Discover the true gruesome history of Rochford this October half-term.
The Rochford Historic Halloween Trail returns from Monday 26 October to Sunday 1 November 2026, following last year’s successful event, which attracted more than 750 participants.
This free, self-guided family trail will lead you around Rochford town centre, visiting participating local businesses and community locations along the way.
At each stop, you’ll discover a story from Rochford’s past, solve a riddle and search for a hidden letter. Collect all the letters to uncover the mystery phrase and complete the trail.
Visit the dedicated Halloween Trail website for the latest information, participating locations, downloadable trail materials and closing-day updates:
www.thedesigncabin.community/halloween
How to take part
Collect the official trail map and answer sheet from Rochford Library, or download a copy from the Halloween Trail website
Visit the participating locations around Rochford
Read the historical stories and solve the riddles
Find the hidden letters
Collect all the letters to uncover the mystery phrase
The trail can be completed at your own pace throughout the October half-term holidays. Posters will be displayed in the windows of participating locations, allowing families to continue the trail even when individual businesses are closed.
Please check each business's opening hours if you would like to visit them in person.
Closing day – Sunday 1 November
Join us on Sunday 1 November for the official closing day of the Rochford Historic Halloween Trail, featuring additional activities and special opportunities to explore Rochford’s history.
Guided tours of Rochford’s Old House
Rochford Town Team will be offering guided tours of Rochford’s Old House, giving visitors the opportunity to learn more about this important historic building.
Tour times, availability and booking information will be published on the Halloween Trail website.
Rochford Town Rooms
Rochford Town Council will open the Rochford Town Rooms, where visitors can view the Rochford tapestry and a special pop-up museum display celebrating the town’s history.
Rochford WI Hall

Hi I’m Amy! I’m a member of the Love Essex team and today I wanted to share my best tips for making the food you buy last longer.
Busy family life can make keeping on top of your food harder, with other priorities often jumping the queue. What if I told you that using your weekly food shop wisely can help to save you time and money during your busy week?
Maximising the life of your food shop can help you to make the most of everything you buy – whilst also saving you those mid-week emergency trips to your local supermarket or corner shop.
It also means you can get the most value out of the food you already love and buy!
When we talk about saving money by reducing your food waste here at Love Essex, people often think it means completely changing their shopping habits. That’s not the case – our goal is to help you make the most of everything you buy, wherever you might choose to buy it from.
A few changes can help your home to become more efficient and organised with food, helping your busy family weekdays to run more smoothly.
Try some of these easy tips below and see if you can avoid that mid-week dash for a last-minute dinner:
Batch cooking
I like to think of batch cooking as a way to maximise what I’m already planning to cook, rather than a whole activity in itself. It’s Monday night and I’ve planned to make chicken curry for dinner; I’ve a nice big packet of chicken breasts and all my vegetables ready to go. I’m cooking for four, so calculated I only need three to four chicken breasts. This leaves me with two left in the packet...
My tip, add the additional chicken breasts and make an additional two to three portions. Pop these in the freezer and add a post-it note to your fridge door as a reminder for later in the week. I now have a meal for another night ready to reheat and I’ve saved myself from trying to find a way to use up two raw chicken breasts - it’s a win-win!
Space-saving Tupperware
If there’s one thing that catches me out with meal preparation, it’s freezer space to store it all. A quick audit made me realise that most of the Tupperware boxes I was reaching for were far too big for storing a single portion.
If you’re freezing a single or smaller portion, use a smaller Tupperware and fill it right to the top. That way you’re not wasting precious space by freezing fresh air!
The self-serve method
I can’t take credit for this tip, but since Emily in our team shared it with us, it’s become a game changer in my house.
When dishing up family dinners, place your dinner in a large dish in the centre of the table (this can be the dish it was cooked in, to save washing up!). Encourage everyone to help themselves but taking some little and often until they’re full. Younger children may need some help with this – but it’s also a great way to involve them with dinner time.
Any leftover food is then untouched in the central dish, meaning it can be saved, frozen and reheated for another dinner. This saves it from being scraped into your food caddy at the end of the meal. You wouldn’t scrape food off someone’s plate and take this for your lunch the next day, but with this method it remains untouched and ready to go.
Try one of these tips with your next weekly food shop and see if they help your food go that bit further.
More tips and tricks
You can get loads more tips and tricks by signing up to our free money saving food challenge. These will help you build easy, smart food habits to get the best value out of your weekly food shop.
And there's great prizes to win too!

Hi, I’m Alice. I live in Colchester and I’m a mum of one. Like most parents I have a busy schedule and spend a lot of my time running around with (and after) my energetic toddler.
When I was first approached by the Love Essex team to write a blog, I didn't know whether sharing my journey with food recycling would be useful to anyone. But if my experience can resonate with others and help them to make their daily routine just that bit easier, then I’d definitely call that a win.
The past
I never used to recycle my food separately, it was never particularly on my radar as an option. I recycled my plastics, glass, paper etc, but I always thought separating my food was a bit gross and just extra effort. I grew up in a large family where leftovers were always quickly snatched up by the sibling who finished their dinner first, and we were expected to finish our meals and not waste food.
Things did and still do get wasted from time to time. Whether I’ve forgotten about them in the fridge, disliked something I’ve made following a recipe that looked SO much better than how it tasted, or the normal things you throw away after prepping a meal, like peelings, bones, and shells. Before, these things would have been emptied into my bin bag and off they would have gone to the smelly bin fairy every two weeks.
My motivation
I think the motivation for me starting to recycle my food was the birth of my son. This may sound like I was suddenly interested in making the world a better place and making more environmentally conscious decisions for him and his generation… and it totally was… eventually. But being completely honest, it was the sudden arrival of poop, and a lot of it!
My bins, due to the new influx of nappies, filled up faster than they’d ever done before and I was looking for ways to free up space in my bin bags as much as possible. When I found out that food was collected weekly, I saw this as another opportunity to free up some space. It also beat having a smelly bin in my kitchen for longer than a week - there’s nothing quite like being greeted by flies and a stale-smelling bin full of last night’s leftovers in the morning!
Getting started
To start with, I didn’t look into council-provided information about food recycling, but turned to my family to ask what they did and how. This is when I found out I had to order a new caddy from Colchester City Council’s website. I went for an external one only, as I wanted to find something that would match my kitchen decor… and I knew I was going to obsess over finding one that I would enjoy looking at.
Liners aren’t provided for free by my local council, but I wanted to use them to keep my kitchen caddy cleaner and contain any food juice. This means I grab liners as part of my food shop at the supermarket, just like I do with bin bags when they run out.
I’ve heard horror stories of maggots and flies that also put me off trying food recycling. But I transfer any food collected in my kitchen caddy to my outside one regularly, so I’ve never witnessed this myself. If they develop in the outside one, it’s only the poor bin crew that have to deal with this (great job guys – you’re braver than I am!) 💪
My routine
This is now my routine, and I can’t believe it’s taken me so long to do it! Even though I don’t have to worry about hordes of nappies anymore, I put all food that’s not eaten in my caddy. Then I give my kitchen caddy a quick wash to keep it fresh and I’m good to go again.

Hi, I'm Lindsay and I'm a mum of two school-age children.
Those of you with children in school know first-hand how expensive school uniform can be to buy new. Jumpers, cardigans, shirts, trousers, skirts, shoes, summer dresses, the list goes on. Then there can be the replacement of items as they inevitably get lost, worn through, or grown out of. It can feel like an ongoing battle!
For families in Essex who struggle financially, this cost can have bigger impacts. That's why support like the Chelmsford Free School Uniform event which took place in August are so crucial.
The Chelmsford Free School Uniform event
I spoke to Kirsty Roberts, Community Connector from the Mid Essex Child and Family Wellbeing Service about the event and why it is making such a difference in Chelmsford and beyond.
Why did Chelmsford Child and Family Wellbeing Service decide to set-up an annual free school uniform event?
Following the success of our Free School Uniform events over the past three summers, we decided to run another one for summer 2026.
Many local families are struggling financially with the cost of living and the high costs of buying school uniform, amongst the cost of school holidays, food and childcare. For many, this can be a huge worry and can also leave families short of money for essentials like food and energy at a time when money is already tight over school holidays.
Our service is also really keen to support sustainability and reduce waste. Many children grow out of uniform so quickly, so this is a great way to see it passed on to others.
Tell me more about the school uniform event which took place in August
We worked closely with Christ Church Chelmsford who hosted and supported the entire event. We had a couple of weeks where donation bins were out at the church and local people donated pre-loved uniform. All uniform was set up in the church youth hall and local people were invited to come along and help themselves to any items they needed.
The event was open to all and advertised through our own service, through all the local primary and secondary schools, and through partner organisations.
How much school uniform was collected and redistributed?
We had huge amounts of donations this year, which we were extremely grateful for. The event supported 139 children.
All leftover uniform went to other local uniform events or uniform banks.
What difference does the event make to families?
Local children have access to free pre-loved uniform to ensure they have the items they need for starting (back at) school in September. Things such as appropriate winter coats mean that children will be kept safe when walking home in colder weather and having correct school uniform means that they will not miss out on learning time. “It will be a massive relief and a burden

https://www.loveessex.org/rss.xml.title: What is contamination and why should I care?
https://www.loveessex.org/rss.xml.text:
What is contamination and why should I care?
Stephen
Fri, 10/02/2026 - 15:29
16 October 2026
Recycling
Kerbside collections
Waste prevention
Hi, it's Lindsay again. I've been a member of the Love Essex team for two and a-bit years now. I didn't come from a waste background, so there were plenty of words within the world of waste I needed to learn about when I started the role.
One of them was contamination.
What is contamination?
I generally knew what it was but not specifically within waste and recycling. I also didn't know why it was also talked about as such a big issue and why I should care about it.
Contamination is when the wrong thing gets mixed in with the recycling, or when recycling is too dirty to be recycled.
How does this relate to me dealing with my recycling and waste at home?
Your recycling services may have changed lately, so now is a great time to learn more about it.
Let's face it, contamination isn't really a word we use on a day-to-day basis, so why are we using it to explain what we shouldn't do with our recycling and waste? Let's explain it in a clear and understandable way.
Recycling needs to be clean and in the right place. Think about a plate of food. If mud got mixed in with it, you probably wouldn't want to eat it.
Recycling works in a very similar way. If it's dirty or in the wrong place, it can't be recycled.
Can a load of recycling really be rejected if it's contaminated?
I had heard this and had thought, 'surely not' but it is true. The same as the plate of food example above, the company recycling the items won't want it. Sometimes it can be so bad that:
it’s not safe for workers to sort if it includes items like dirty nappies, sharp pieces of waste or mouldy food
it could damage the sorting machines
food and liquids have spread onto paper and cardboard, making them unusable
the good recycling is mixed up with too much rubbish
This means that the whole load of recycling is then treated as “general rubbish”. This costs more money to dispose of and more resources are wasted, instead of being used to make new items.
What can I do to avoid contamination?
Here are some simple actions:
check your recycling information from your local council and find out what goes where
make sure food and drink containers are empty - if food has gone off, add it to your food recycling caddy
rinse food containers before recycling them - think yoghurt pots, glass jars and aluminium cans
make sure cardboard, such as pizza boxes are clean - it can't be recycled if it's greasy. If the base is greasy and the top is clean - rip it apart
One final rule
If in doubt, leave it out.
'Wishcycling' is a very common thing and it's totally understandable why people do it. We want to be able to recycle as much as possible, so we add it to the recycling and hope for the best.
Unfortunately, if it can't be recycled along with the rest of the things you've added, it's contamination.
If you're unsure, use the Love Essex Search function . Just start typing what you want to dispose of, select it from the drop down list, add your postcode and it will tell you what to do with it.
If you're still unsure, you can send us a message via Facebook or Instagram .
Have you learnt something new about contamination? Let us know in the comments below with that one thing you're unsure on how to recycle 👇

Hi, I'm Lindsay and I love Halloween, but it's not always been that way!
Back in 2018, I was lucky enough to go to Canada for a holiday, and it happened to be around Halloween. Up until this point, I didn’t care for Halloween. It had never been a part of my childhood. But let me tell you, Canadians go big on Halloween!
Whilst all the displays etc were great to see, what I loved most was the community it built. Kids felt safe to walk around the neighbourhood and knock on their neighbours' doors. Everyone loved it. Children collecting sweets in a pillowcase or a grown-up giving them out to excited looking kids - it was heartwarming to see.
Since then, Halloween has grown in popularity in the UK. Pumpkins have become a staple part of the spooky season in Essex. They’re used for pumpkin competitions or as a symbol to show you welcome trick or treaters. They’re now an annual buy for us.
But many of them still go to waste as they're just seen as a decoration. They eventually end up taking up space in your food recycling caddy, but they are so much more than this!
When we started taking part in Halloween when my kids were old enough, buying a pumpkin (for a couple of years we even grew them) was part of the celebration. After a few years, it occurred to me that the pumpkin, and the money I had spent on it, was just getting wasted. So, I rethought how we could get the most out of it!
No-carve pumpkin decorating
One thing you can do to save your pumpkin from your food recycling caddy, is to not carve it! Don't hate me and think I'm trying to remove the fun. I personally find carving a pumpkin really stressful, fiddly, and also a bit dangerous when the kids are small. By removing this step, it makes it so much easier! If you google no-carve pumpkins and click on images, you’ll be greeted by a whole range of ideas!
The easiest two ways to decorate them in the no-carve way are to:
glue or stick the design on the outside. I found cocktail sticks useful for this
use non-toxic, food safe paint to decorate the outside
By doing this, it protects the inside of the pumpkin so that it can used once you have finished using it as a decoration. Here are some ideas that we've done throughout the years:
Remember not to leave the pumpkin for too long on your doorstep, so that you can still use it for cooking.
Roasting a pumpkin
I have found that the easiest way to use and store the pumpkin, is to roast it.
preheat your oven to 180 degrees Celsius
cut your pumpkin in half
scoop out the seeds and guts (stringy stuff holding the seeds in place)
place the two pieces cut side down on a baking tray
place in the oven for 45 to 60 minutes – you’ll know it’s ready if the pumpkin flesh is soft and you can slide a fork in easily
once the time is up, take the pumpkin out of the oven and leave to cool
remove the skin. As it has been roasted, the skin will be much easier to peel off but you might still need to use a knife to tease it off
I choose to mash my pumpkin, as it can then be used in most recipes
there’s often a lot of pumpkin, so I split it into more manageable amounts. For example, 100g. I use reusable cupcake cases to do this
place the portions in the freezer
once the portions are frozen, remove the cases and put in a freezer bag ready to be used in a recipe. I usually use the microwave to defrost the portions to then add to a recipe
There are so many great recipes out there that use pumpkin. Even if you don’t like pumpkin, you often can’t taste it and it has great nutritional value!
One of my favourite recipes is pumpkin muffins or it’s always great as a soup. Try one of the great recipes our blog.

Funding opportunity for projects reducing food waste
The Love Essex Fund is offering funding to projects in Essex that help to reduce household food waste.

A total of eight projects were successfully awarded funding. The successful initiatives represented a diverse range of organisations, including schools, local businesses, charities, and not-for-profit groups.
The successful projects
Reflecting communities from across the county, each project put forward innovative ideas aimed at reducing food waste within Essex.
The Boaz Project Colchester
The Boaz Project Colchester are creating food nights where the community comes together to teach practical cooking skills and share a meal together.
Create Shake n Bake
Create Shake n Bake are creating an eight-week online cookery programme called 'Create Shake n NO Waste'.
Households will follow along at home and learn to reduce food waste through practical, affordable cooking skills.
Essex Rocks Creative CIC
Essex Rocks Creative CIC are creating a free community resource guide packed with practical recipes, food-saving tips, storage advice, and simple ideas to help households reduce food waste and save money.
Ghyllgrove Primary School

Wivenhoe Library of Things will be adding an ice cube maker, mini freezer, food vacuum sealer, and soup maker to their rentable items to support families with batch cooking.

https://castlehedingham-pc.gov.uk/feed/.title: Essex County Fire and Rescue Service
https://castlehedingham-pc.gov.uk/feed/.text:
Be ready for whatever the weather brings
There’s been plenty of conversation recently about being prepared for emergencies, with the Government’s new Be Ready campaign encouraging households to think about how they would cope if everyday services were disrupted for a few days.
But what does being prepared actually look like, particularly if you live in a rural community?
At Essex County Fire and Rescue Service (ECFRS), we know that living in the countryside can bring its own challenges when extreme weather strikes. From flooding and storms to prolonged dry spells and wildfires, severe weather can affect our homes, roads and the services we rely on.
We want to encourage residents to take a few simple steps to help keep themselves, their homes and their neighbours safe.
A few things you can do today:
Think ahead: Keep a torch, spare batteries, a charged power bank, essential medication and some long-life food and bottled water at home in case of a power cut or disruption to supplies.
Know your local risks: Check whether your property or nearby roads are prone to flooding. Think about alternative routes if roads become impassable.
Reduce fire risks: During dry weather, keep grass and vegetation around your property under control. Take extra care with barbecues and never leave them unattended.
Prepare for storms : Check gutters, drains, fences and roof tiles, and secure garden furniture and other items that could be blown around in strong winds.
Look out for neighbours: If you live in a more isolated location, agree how you could check in on elderly or vulnerable neighbours if bad weather affects power, phone signal or road access.
A little preparation goes a long way
Being prepared doesn’t mean expecting the worst or buying lots of extra equipment. It’s about thinking ahead, knowing what to do and looking out for one another.
Rural communities are often well placed to support each other, and a little local knowledge and preparation can make a real difference when an emergency happens.
For more advice on staying safe in rural areas, visit www.essex-fire.gov.uk/rural.

https://brightlingseatowncouncil.gov.uk/.title: Press Release: Bayard Recreation Ground: Action Needed to Protect Our Football Pitches
https://brightlingseatowncouncil.gov.uk/.text:
Bayard Recreation Ground’s football pitches are in danger of deteriorating further unless action is taken now.
Until July, the pitches had a good-to-average rating, with around 65% grass coverage. Following the dry summer, this has fallen to less than 30%, with much of the remaining surface covered in dead grass.
The Recreation Ground will be closed on Monday 19 th October 2026 for reseeding but open for Playgroup access only.   In order for the seed to germinate, the ground will be closed to the public for approximately six weeks.  Strict access will be allowed from Tuesday 20 th October 2026 from Bayard Avenue to Regent Road only via an access path during this time.  Without intervention, continued use could cause further damage, potentially leaving the whole ground as a muddy, unusable surface.
Access will remain available to the Play Group and for walking along the designated areas and paths. Visitors are asked to respect the restricted areas while the works are carried out.
With Brightlingsea Regent Youth continuing to expand and more teams needing facilities, a long-term solution is also essential. An all-weather pitch at Lower Park could provide a valuable, year-round playing facility for the town’s young people, while reducing pressure on existing grass pitches.
We need to protect Bayard now and plan for the future to ensure our young people have the facilities they deserve .
We apologise for any inconvenience caused.

https://brightlingseatowncouncil.gov.uk/.title: Promenade revamp works to get underway in Brightlingsea
https://brightlingseatowncouncil.gov.uk/.text:
Tendring District Council (TDC) will be improving the surface of the promenade around the paddling pool area, giving this popular stretch of seafront a cleaner, more even finish.
The work will also help address long-standing wear and tear, with the new surface gently sloping from the seawall towards the beach to improve drainage.
Councillor Mick Barry, TDC’s Cabinet Member for Leisure and Public Realm, said: “This upgrade is great news for Brightlingsea’s seafront and for everyone who enjoys spending time here.
“By improving the look and feel of the promenade, we’re creating a space that’s cleaner, more welcoming and even better suited to families, walkers and beachgoers.
“We know this has been a longstanding concern for local residents and councillors, and we’re pleased to have responded and secured the investment needed to carry out these important works.”
The improvement works are due to start in October, with the scheme expected to be completed in November, although timings may vary depending on tides and weather conditions.
As part of the work, the height of the prom will be raised slightly to make it easier for people to move around and to improve accessibility for all visitors.
Councillor Adrian Smith, Cabinet Member for Environment – which includes responsibility for Coast Protection and Engineering – said: “This project is a great opportunity to give one of Brightlingsea’s busiest seafront areas the upgrade it deserves.
“By resurfacing whole sections rather than patching defects, we can improve drainage and create a finish that’s smoother and easier to maintain.
“Brightlingsea’s Blue Flag beach is a real source of local pride, and these improvements will help to build on that status.”
Access to sections of the promenade may be temporarily restricted at times while the work is carried out.

https://www.judiciary.uk/feed/?post_type.title: Davina Ruprah, Kiranjeet Sagoo and Sachin Kalia (1): Prevention of Future Deaths Report
https://www.judiciary.uk/feed/?post_type.source: Prevention of Future Deaths reports feed
https://www.judiciary.uk/feed/?post_type.text:
Date of report: 26/03/2026
Ref: 2026-0439
Deceased name: Davina Ruprah, Kiranjeet Sagoo and Sachin Kalia (1)
Coroner name: Nadia Persaud
Coroner Area: East London
This report is being sent to: Essex police
REGULATION 28 REPORT TO PREVENT FUTURE DEATHS 1 CORONER
I am Nadia Persaud, Area Coroner for the coroner area of East London 2 CORONER’S LEGAL POWERS
I make this report under paragraph 7, Schedule 5, of the Coroners and Justice Act 2009 and Regulations 28 and 29 of the Coroners (Investigations) Regulations 2013.
http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2009/25/schedule/5/paragraph/7
http://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2013/1629/part/7/made  3 INVESTIGATION and INQUEST
On the 25 July 2024 I commenced an investigation into the deaths of Davina Kaur Ruprah (aged 24), Kiranjeet Sagoo (aged 36) and Sachin Kalia (aged 19). The investigation concluded at the  end of the joint inquest hearing, on 16 March 2026 with the jury reaching a narrative
conclusion:
The cause of death was a Road Traffic Collision caused by the driver losing control whilst driving at high speed in adverse weather conditions.
The fatal collision could have been avoided if:
The ford transit van was not parked within the central reservation after the first incident at 21:12.
If the MPS attending officers had been provided with the correct location and arrived in sufficient time to clear the first incident.    4 CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE DEATH
Date: 15th July 2024
Location: Wennington junction, Westbound, Rainham, London
At 21:12 a BMW One series collided with a Ford Transit. The BMW One series driver was driving in excess of the speed limit, and lost control, causing the collision and for the Ford Transit to  come to rest on the central reservation, slightly protruding onto lane three. This posed a hazard to passing motorists, but we do not consider it to be a major hazard for vehicles being driven at  an appropriate speed, based on the number of vehicles that safely passed the Ford Transit. An emergency call was made to the Metropolitan Police Service (MPS) at 21:19, identifying the  site of the first collision at the Wennington junction between the A13 and the A1306. The MPS call handler did not note the Wennington junction as the location of the incident in the “remarks” section available to her, and the computer system only listed the incorrect Dagenham junction between the A13 and the A1306 as a possible location. This meant that the  MPS attending officers were despatched to the incorrect location so found no trace of the  incident despite checking one further junction in either direction.
Had the officers been provided with the correct location they would likely have arrived before  the time of the second collision.  If they had arrived before the second collision, the officers were trained to park their car in the “fend off” position, so as to slow the traffic in the lanes 2 and 3 and minimise the risk to other road users. They may have also elected to remove the Ford Transit from the central reservation. Therefore, had the MPS officers attended the correct  location, it is likely that the fatal collision could have been avoided. A 999 call was also made to Essex Police. The call handler incorrectly identified the location of the incident to be on Essex Police ground. The correct location was within Metropolitan Police  ground.  Essex police staff did not contact the Metropolitan Police Service.  There were no resources available within Essex police to respond to the 999 call, prior to the second collision  occurring.
At 22:04, a BMW Four series reached the location of the first collision, travelling well in excess of the speed limit, in lane 2 of the A13 westbound. The BMW Four series driver, undertook emergency braking and lost control of the car. It is possible, this was due to the combination of a slower moving vehicle ahead in lane 2, and the  Ford Transit. https://fiveestuaries.co.uk/feed/.title: Joint Substations Design Guide published

Throughout 2025 and 2026 Five Estuaries, along with North Falls Offshore Wind Farm, have been working with stakeholders and the community around the substation site to create a Joint Substations Design Guide.
The Design Guide will be provided to the commissioned substation designers, setting a fixed framework for the final substation designs. The purpose of the document is to:
Outline the overarching design principles for each substation.
Establish a series of shared commitments that the final substation designs must follow.
Cover key elements such as site layout, building form and materials, ensuring a consistent and coordinated design approach across both projects, particularly if separate contractors are commissioned.
We are grateful to the local community, our landowners and other stakeholders who have been vital to the development of the Design Guide and provided valuable insight to help shape the final document.
What is the Design Guide?
The Design Guide has been prepared to support the development of detailed proposals for both projects co-located onshore substations. Before the submission of their Development Consent Order (DCO) applications, both projects prepared ‘design approach documents’ to outline individual plans and to evidence the ‘good design’ followed, in accordance with the overarching national planning policy for energy.
This Design Guide brings together the two projects’ individual approaches and plans for their substation sites into one combined document. It will be the primary reference document for guiding the detailed design and delivery of the substations and associated infrastructure; the intention for it to be used consistently by all designers, consultants, and contractors involved in the project to ensure a coordinated, high-quality, and policy-compliant outcome.
The Design Guide is comprised of nine parts:
Section 1: Introduction – This section sets the scene for the design guidance included in the subsequent parts of the Design Guide.
Section 2: The projects – This section provides context for the projects and outlines clear regulatory, technical and performance requirements for future detailed design.
Section 3: The site – Describes the site, its character, visual amenity, public rights of way, heritage, drainage and ecology.
Section 4: Layout – Explains the substations site, the constraints within and around it and technical requirements such as CCTV, wayleaves and easements, lighting and fencing. Building layout options were presented.
Section 5: Design and materials – Explored building types, reflecting on local precedents. Options were presented on roof styles, elevations and materials as well as security and perimeter fencing.
Section 6: Sustainability – Covering sustainable design and construction principles and design features.
Section 7: Colour – Information on the Environmental Colour Assessment which was undertaken to inform colour options presented to be applied to the exterior of the substation buildings. Also included options on application style.
Section 8: Landscape and ecology – Providing coordinated advice for the landscape scheme including planting approach, species selection and the inclusion of micro-habitats.
Section 9: Engagement – This section provides an overview of the engagement process taken to create the Design Guide and a summary of the feedback received at each stage as a result.

The engagement process
The development of the Design Guide was iterative, subject to review by key stakeholders, interested parties and an independent design review panel. This meant that the content evolved as stakeholder feedback was gathered, and the shortlist of options was refined.
Through two separate phases of engagement, we consulted local residents and landowners , parish councils and local authorities on the aspects of the guide that were subject to optionality .

We are pleased to share a significant milestone in the development of the Five Estuaries Offshore Wind Farm. Today the project has officially received Development Consent from the Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero.
Five Estuaries is owned by various shareholders including RWE, which is leading the development of the project on behalf of the project partners. The offshore wind project is owned by RWE (33.33%), a Macquarie-led consortium (25%), ESB (20.83%) and Sumitomo Corporation (20.83%.)
An extension to the operational Galloper Wind Farm, the project is to be located in the southern North Sea across two seabed areas covering approximately 128 km². Five Estuaries is consented to comprise up to 79 wind turbines, with a maximum tip height of 370 metres, plus foundations.
Under the approved plans, electricity generated by the wind farm would be transmitted ashore via subsea cables to Sandy Point, located between Frinton-on-Sea and Holland-on-Sea in Essex. From there, underground cables will connect to a new substation west of Little Bromley, eventually joining the East Anglia Connection Node on the proposed National Grid’s Norwich–Tilbury transmission corridor.
Danielle Lane, RWE Director of Development for UK and Ireland, commented:  “We are delighted to have received development consent for Five Estuaries. This achievement reflects years of dedicated community engagement and collaboration with local stakeholders.”
Once fully constructed, Five Estuaries would be capable of generating sufficient electricity to power the equivalent of up to 1 million typical UK homes annually. During construction and operations, the project would support hundreds of new and existing skilled jobs, both directly and across the wider supply chain. Strategically, the project could also play an important role in helping ensure UK security of supply of domestically generated clean power and support the Government’s transition towards a decarbonised electricity system.
We are incredibly grateful to all stakeholder organisations and communities that we have engaged with over the past five years as we have developed the project. We would like to take this opportunity to thank those who have helped us to refine and adapt the proposals to create the best possible project for this site, for the community and the environment.
You can view the Development Consent Order and supporting information on the Planning Inspectorate website here or see where you can view a printed copy here .
We are committed to working collaboratively with all stakeholders, local communities, and interest groups throughout the next phases of the project to ensure it delivers real value locally, regionally, and nationally.
We will continue to keep you informed as the project progresses into the construction and delivery stages. In the meantime, should you have any questions or wish to stay engaged with the project, please don’t hesitate to contact us.
Thank you for your continued interest and support.

https://fiveestuaries.co.uk/feed/.title: Five Estuaries and North Falls Archaeology Surveys
https://fiveestuaries.co.uk/feed/.source: Five Estuaries offshore wind farm (Tendring landfall)
https://fiveestuaries.co.uk/feed/.text:
Five Estuaries and North Falls are jointly carrying out archaeological trial trenching surveys starting in the week commencing the 8 September 2025.
The works will be taking place within our proposed development boundary between Bentley Road and Ardleigh Road (as shown on the below plan), within the parish of Little Bentley, on private land in agreement with the relevant landowners.
Archaeological trial trenching involves the excavation of trial trenches across a site to estimate the archaeological potential.
The surveys will be taking place near Little Bromley 17 Public Right of Way; however, this will remain open throughout the works with fencing and signage as appropriate.
This is the second stage of trial trenching following those that we undertook within the proposed substation area in 2023 and will continue next year at other areas along the proposed cable route. This is not the start of either of the project’s construction as we are still awaiting consenting decisions.
The surveys are being carried out jointly by Five Estuaries and North Falls to help the projects understand the archaeology that is present to inform the next stage of mitigation, and whether any more detailed set piece excavations may be required (if significant archaeology is identified), which can be planned in prior to the main works starting. This approach is detailed in the Archaeological Mitigation Strategy: EN010115-001695-10.47 Archaeological Mitigation Strategy (AMS) – Revision B (Clean).pdf .
The locations of the trenches have been informed by using desk-based sources (such as aerial photography and existing records) and the geophysical surveys we carried out in 2023. The trenches target potential archaeology as well as blank areas to be explored.
The works are expected to take around six to eight weeks, being complete by mid-October, subject to weather conditions.
The works will be undertaken by our contractor Wessex Archaeology. The trenching will take place between 8am and 5pm Monday to Friday. All staff carparking will be located within the work area, or at offsite locations as agreed with landowners and designated accesses will be used. Equipment will be secured onsite when works are not taking place in agreement with the relevant landowners. The topsoil and subsoil will be segregated during the trenching, and the field will be fully reinstated on completion of the works.

Returning mobility equipment
Patients who have been given mobility equipment to use are being asked to return it when no longer needed.
Crutches, metal walking sticks and walking frames are among some of the items patients can return if they’ve borrowed the equipment or been issued the equipment from Ipswich or Colchester hospitals.
Each item of equipment is deep cleaned, checked and maintained or repaired before being issued to another patient.
Items that can be returned include:
Crutches
metal walking sticks
walking frames
perching stools
commodes
shower chairs
toilet frames
How you return equipment is different depending on the area.
Returning equipment in east Suffolk/Ipswich:
Drop it into the large blue recycling container outside Entrance 6 or the Garrett Anderson building at Ipswich Hospital (you can park for free in the drop off bay if quickly returning equipment in the container)
Contact Suffolk Medequip for a free collection. Arrange a collection by phone on 01473 351 805 or email Suffolk Medequip.
Take it to Medequip’s depot at Unit 31, Bluestem Road, Ransomes Europark, Ipswich, IP3 9RR
Return it to the Live Well Hub in Leiston at Waterloo Centre, Waterloo Avenue, Leiston, IP16 4HF
Return it to The Dales in Ipswich at 216 Dales Road, Ipswich, IP1 4JY.
Returning equipment in north Essex/Colchester:
Return crutches, walking frames and metal walking sticks to the large blue recycling container outside the front entrance of Colchester Hospital or to the large blue recycling containers outside the side entrance doors to the ESEOC Dame Clare Marx Building at Colchester Hospital.
Any medical equipment that was delivered directly to your house should have a Medequip or ECL sticker on it. If so, you can contact Medequip for a free collection. Their details are listed below.
Phone 0333 034 2048, or  email Essex Medequip via email.
This includes:
hospital beds
toilet frames
perching stools
commodes
hoists
slings
slide sheets
wendylet (special bed sheet) etc.
You can also return equipment with an ECL or Medequip sticker direct to the depot at Unit 2, Horizon 120 Business Park, Horizon Boulevard, Braintree, Essex, CM77 7AY.
If you’ve left Colchester Hospital with a piece of medical equipment that isn’t a walking aid and doesn’t have a Medequip or ECL sticker on it, please do not return it to Medequip but contact the team at the hospital who supplied it.
Material moon boots or arm supports cannot be returned as they cannot be cleaned for future patients.
Please don’t return equipment to our community hospitals or to our community teams – they aren’t able to take back equipment there.

https://www.esneft.nhs.uk/feed/.title: Wishing Rolo a happy retirement
https://www.esneft.nhs.uk/feed/.source: East Suffolk & North Essex NHS (Colchester Hospital)
https://www.esneft.nhs.uk/feed/.text:
For years he’s been taking the lead at Ipswich Hospital, but now Rolo the dog is set to bid farewell and take a well-deserved retirement.
A rescue dog who was saved from certain death on a puppy farm in Essex, Rolo has been charming patients, visitors and staff alike for six years, accompanied by his owner Claire Dean.
A television celebrity – Rolo has featured on the BBC and was a finalist for the BBC Make a Difference Awards Unsung Hero – the PAT (Pets as Therapy) dog visits wards and clinics bringing a smile to the faces of the people he meets. He helps patients in many ways, both physically and mentally, including with their speech and language and rehabilitation.
Claire said: “He is going to be 13 shortly and that is quite old for a working dog. I would rather him have a final day working rather than having to call up and say he’s not coming in anymore because he’s not well.
“He is slowing down a bit but only after he has done his stint at the hospital – people can’t believe he is coming up for 13 as he walks so well, especially given the fact he’s had two cruciate ligament surgeries.
“He is very agile and is always looking around to see who he can interact with – waiting for me to give him the go-ahead.
“I liken his job to us humans when we go to a museum or an art gallery, after a couple of hours or so he needs a break.
“He is constantly stimulated, seeing people he knows and doesn’t know, and he is very aware and alert. When he goes on a ward he changes the whole atmosphere.”
Rolo is cuddled by his owner Claire.
Rolo, whose final day at the hospital in on 17 November, was rescued by the RSPCA, in one of three litters and was very poorly initially.
However, after some tender loving care from the charity he recovered sufficiently enough for him to be adopted by Claire.
Claire said: “His story has been shared widely. As a result of seeing a BBC report on television about Rolo, a hospital in Gloucester then decided to recruit for their own PAT dog to serve their stroke ward.
“Many people have misconceptions about rescued dogs, but I know how amazing rescues can be. His two siblings weren’t as lucky as him and that is why I am a big advocate of rescue dogs and rehoming them.
“It’s not just about the work he does in the hospital but also what he represents as a rescue advocate and how, his story will encourage other potential dog owners to consider adopting a rescued dog.”
ESNEFT voluntary services manager Robbie Payne said: “We are incredibly grateful that Claire and Rolo chose to volunteer with us.
“They have shown dedication, compassion, kindness and care for our patients and staff which is greatly valued by all those who have met with them.
“Rolo has certainly earned a rest in his senior years and leaves with our heartfelt thanks.”
RSPCA Essex and London Chief Inspector Clare Dew said: “We’re so proud of Rolo and everything he’s achieved with Claire.
“He was clinging onto life when he was rescued from a puppy farm by our teams and he was lucky to pull through.
“But he was even luckier to find such a loving, dedicated family and to land a job that he has enjoyed so much, for so long, bringing joy to people at the most difficult time of their lives.
“He’s a real rags to riches story and just goes to show that there’s nothing a rescue dog can’t do.”

https://www.esneft.nhs.uk/feed/.title: New type of hip surgery helps patients
https://www.esneft.nhs.uk/feed/.source: East Suffolk & North Essex NHS (Colchester Hospital)
https://www.esneft.nhs.uk/feed/.text:
Patients are benefiting from a different type of surgery for their hip replacements.
Surgeons use a technique, which means the surgery is performed through the front of the thigh.
Hazel Grainger, 63, was the first patient to have the anterior hip replacement surgery at the Essex and Suffolk Elective Orthopaedic Centre (ESEOC) at Colchester Hospital.
The surgeries were carried out by consultant surgeons Mr Michael Field and Mr Anand Shah – marking a major first for East Suffolk and North Essex NHS Foundation Trust (ESNEFT) which runs ESEOC.
The anterior method helps preserve a patient’s muscles allowing them to recover quickly in the first six weeks and can mean the operation is less painful. In America over half of all hip replacements are now done using the anterior approach, with many patients going home the same day.
Dental nurse Hazel, from Felixstowe, said it’s a relief to have had her hip replaced. She said: “The pain got so bad that I was unable to do my job. I am now pain-free and was back at work within four weeks.”
The operation is performed by accessing the hip joint through a cut at the top of the thigh at the front. This approach was first used in the 1800s when surgeons first performed procedures on hips to treat tuberculosis.
Mr Field said: “It’s an exciting first for ESNEFT to be able to bring this new service to the Trust when there is an increasing awareness, interest and demand from patients to have it.”
Mr Field, right, with three patients to have the surgery done, including the first, Hazel Grainger (second left)

https://www.esneft.nhs.uk/feed/.title: Mum and son with same blood cancer join research study
https://www.esneft.nhs.uk/feed/.source: East Suffolk & North Essex NHS (Colchester Hospital)
https://www.esneft.nhs.uk/feed/.text:
A mum and son who have both been diagnosed with the same type of blood cancer are taking part in research to evaluate the impact of new treatment.
Pat Sawyer, 85, and Mark Sawyer, 62, were both diagnosed with blood cancer through routine blood tests before surgery. Pat for an operation to her hand, Mark for a gallbladder operation.
The pair are now both part of the Mithridate research trial at East Suffolk and North Essex NHS Foundation Trust, one of the trusts that is part of the study.
Mark (left) with Pat and Reg Sawyer, Pat’s husband and Mark’s dad
Pat, a grandmother of five from Kirby-Le-Soken, said: “It’s a coincidence Mark and I have the same cancer. Apparently it’s not hereditary, but it feels strange we both have the same type!
“My doctor said I could start on the trial, which I was quite happy to do it. It might help me and help my son or other patients in the future.”
The Mithridate trial is looking at the effectiveness of different types of treatment.
As part of the trial Pat is taking a treatment called Ruxolitinib. Mark is taking Hydroxycarbamide.
Pat and Mark
Mark, who has three grown-up children and four grandchildren, said: “My understanding of the cancer is that my blood is too thick and wasn’t pumping round my body as it should. Now I look back I did have cold hands and feet, which was due to circulation. I was also feeling quite tired.
“When I was told I could join the study I thought why not. If it gives some insight into medicines that can help that’s great. I’m pleased I can be involved in helping.”
As part of the study both Pat and Mark are monitored regularly – Mark at Colchester Hospital and Pat at Clacton Hospital.
Mark, who lives in Frinton-on-Sea and runs his own maintenance business, added: “Being part of the research means I’m being monitored frequently which is good. I cannot fault the service and treatment I’ve had.”
As Pat is nearer to Clacton Hospital she travels there to see her consultant and the principal investigator of the Mithridate study Dr Khalid Saja.
Dr Khalid Saja, a consultant haematologist and clinical lead for Haematology, said: “This trial is comparing the effectiveness between two treatments for patients diagnosed with polycythaemia vera – an existing treatment, or what we call standard-of-care, and a new treatment called Ruxolitinib.
“This is a randomised trial, so participants can either receive one of the currently existing medications or receive Ruxolitinib. Then the study will review which medicine is best for patients.”
Mark and Pat have given their consent to share their story about their involvement with the study.

https://www.esneft.nhs.uk/feed/.title: Looking ahead: What the CQC’s well-led report means for ESNEFT
https://www.esneft.nhs.uk/feed/.source: East Suffolk & North Essex NHS (Colchester Hospital)
https://www.esneft.nhs.uk/feed/.text:
The Care Quality Commission (CQC) has published its well-led assessment for East Suffolk and North Essex NHS Foundation Trust (ESNEFT).
The review took place in November last year. It provides a snapshot of the Trust as it was at that time and since then, there have been many significant changes.
The report recognises the Trust’s clear vision and strategy, strong partnerships with local organisations, commitment to sustainability and the dedication shown by teams across ESNEFT.
The assessment also identified several areas of focus. These include:
Making it easier for colleagues to speak up
Creating a more inclusive workplace
Strengthening how risks are identified and managed, and
Making sure learning leads to lasting improvements.
In a joint statement, ESNEFT’s Chief Executive Paul Scott and Trust Chair Tracy Dowling, said: “We accept and recognise the findings of the CQC’s well-led assessment and the opportunities it highlights for us, as a new leadership team, to continue improving.
“It is important to remember that inspectors visited almost a year ago and the report reflects ESNEFT as it was at that time. Since then, there have been some considerable changes at the Trust. This includes the arrival of a new Chief Executive, Chair and Director of Governance. Work is also continuing to strengthen our leadership team.
“The report recognises many of our strengths, including the dedication of our staff, our strong partnerships and our clear vision for the future. We are grateful to colleagues across ESNEFT for the commitment, professionalism and compassion they show every day.
“We have already acted on several of the issues raised during the assessment, and more improvements are underway. We now remain focused on strengthening governance, supporting an open and inclusive culture, and continually improving our services.
“Looking ahead, one of our key priorities is a significant programme of engagement with patients, communities and our staff to help shape the culture, behaviours and values that will define ESNEFT in the future.
“While there is more work to do, we have a strong foundation to build on. We are committed to becoming the organisation our patients, communities and staff rightly expect and deserve.”
About the assessment
The well-led review took place from 24 to 27 November 2025. It followed CQC inspections of medical care (including older people’s care) and urgent and emergency services at both Colchester and Ipswich hospitals.
The inspection came at a time of major organisational change after the introduction of a new electronic patient record at ESNEFT. It was also the start of a challenging winter period for teams.
The overall rating of ESNEFT’s well-led domain (how the Trust is run) has dropped from good to requires improvement.

https://www.pah.nhs.uk/feed/.title: New way to complete waiting list questionnaires through My Alex Health
https://www.pah.nhs.uk/feed/.text:
We are changing the way we send digital questionnaires to adult patients who are waiting for treatment.
The questionnaires, previously sent through Healthcare Communications Envoy, will now be available through My Alex Health , our secure patient portal. This change will help make our communications more consistent, familiar and easier for patients to recognise.
What to expect
If you are an adult waiting for treatment and meet the relevant criteria, we will send you a questionnaire every 12 weeks. It lets you know that we are aware you are still waiting and gives you an opportunity to confirm whether you still need to be seen by the relevant specialty or whether you no longer require care from us.
The questionnaire takes around two minutes to complete. If you do not complete the questionnaire, your care will continue and you will remain on the waiting list.
How to access the questionnaire
You will receive a text message from ‘NHS PAHT’ asking you to complete the questionnaire in My Alex Health . If you are already registered, the message will explain how to access it. If you have not yet registered, you will receive a separate message with information to help you sign up. You can read more about the benefits here >
My Alex Health is our secure online patient portal, where patients can access information about their care with us and complete assessments and questionnaires from home.
If you do not feel confident completing the questionnaire online, you do not need to worry. Your care will continue and you will remain on the waiting list. You can ask a trusted family member, friend or carer to help you complete it if you wish.
Questionnaires for children and young people
For now, this questionnaire will only be sent to adult patients. We plan to develop a separate questionnaire for children and young people in the future.

https://www.pah.nhs.uk/feed/.title: Major expansion at St Margaret’s Community Diagnostic Centre (CDC) will bring more diagnostic care closer to home
https://www.pah.nhs.uk/feed/.text:
More diagnostic services will be available at St Margaret’s Community Diagnostic Centre (CDC) in Epping from the week beginning 14 December, giving patients better access to tests and care closer to home.
The new services build on the blood testing service, which will move from the main outpatients’ department at St Margaret’s Hospital to the CDC (pictured, top) on 16 November . Delivered by the experienced Health Services Laboratories (HSL) phlebotomy team, the service will offer a modern setting and more appointment availability, with capacity for around 230 blood testing patients each day. GP-referred patients can continue to book through Swiftqueue. Blood testing also remains available at the Harvey Centre in Harlow, Herts and Essex Hospital in Bishop’s Stortford, and at some health centres and GP practices.
The other services will be within the new CDC extension (pictured, below). Two X-ray rooms will open from the week beginning 14 December ( see map ). The walk-in service will be open from 8am to 7.30pm, Monday to Friday, and 9am to 4.30pm at weekends. Patients referred by their GP will not need an appointment, while patients referred by a specialist outpatient clinic can attend during these times. X-ray services will move to the CDC from their current location in the St Margaret’s Hospital outpatients’ department.
A fourth ultrasound room will also open from the week beginning 14 December. It will provide consultant- and sonographer-led non-obstetric (non-pregnancy) ultrasound, as well as procedures such as ultrasound-guided steroid injections. Appointments are required following referral via GP or specialty.
FibroScan appointments will also start from the week beginning 14 December. FibroScan is a quick, non-invasive test that checks liver stiffness and fat levels. It is commonly used to assess and monitor conditions including fatty liver disease, alcohol-related liver disease and viral hepatitis. Transnasal endoscopy (TNE) appointments will start in early 2027. TNE uses a thin, flexible camera passed through the nose to examine the food pipe, stomach and first part of the small intestine. Both services require an appointment following specialist referral.
A dedicated nurses’ station will support patients recovering after interventional diagnostic procedures—minimally invasive procedures that use imaging to guide diagnosis or treatment, such as ultrasound-guided injections. Pre-assessment clinics will also run from the centre, checking patients’ health and readiness before a planned procedure. The haematuria one-stop clinic will continue at weekends, providing the tests needed in one visit for patients with blood in their urine.
In addition to the blood testing activity, around 350 more patients are expected to use the CDC each day from 14 December as the new services open. Self-check-in and digital wayfinding will continue to help patients move through the centre easily, and parking arrangements at St Margaret’s Hospital remain unchanged.
Thom Lafferty, Chief Executive, said: “This major expansion at St Margaret’s CDC marks an important step forward in how we provide diagnostic care for our communities.
“By bringing together blood testing, X-ray, ultrasound and specialist diagnostics in one modern centre, we will give thousands more patients faster, easier access to the tests and treatment they need, closer to home.
“This is more than an increase in capacity. It is about creating a joined-up, efficient and welcoming service that supports earlier diagnosis, improves the patient experience and delivers more care in the right place.”
Pictured: St Margaret’s Community Diagnostic Centre (top) and the St Margaret’s Community Diagnostic Centre extension (below).

https://www.pah.nhs.uk/feed/.title: Blood testing service to relocate to the new St Margaret’s Community Diagnostic Centre (CDC)
https://www.pah.nhs.uk/feed/.text:
The blood testing service currently delivered from the main outpatients’ department at St Margaret’s Hospital, Epping, will be relocating to the new St Margaret’s Community Diagnostic Centre (CDC) on 16 November.
This will offer patients a new, modern purpose-built environment, in a more convenient setting alongside other diagnostics services and additional appointments, increasing access to care closer to home.
The introduction of blood testing is the latest expansion of services at the CDC, which saw its first patient in March and officially opened in May. The centre is designed to transform care for the communities we serve by supporting quicker, more local access to diagnostic tests and treatment closer to patients’ homes.
Blood testing services will continue to be available at the Harvey Centre in Harlow and Herts and Essex Hospital in Bishop’s Stortford, as well as a number of health centre and GP practice clinics already in place.
The service will continue to be delivered by the experienced phlebotomy team from Health Services Laboratories (HSL). The centre is expected to see around 230 patients a day.
Although the location is changing from 16 November ( see map ), patients referred by their GP for a blood test will still be able to use the same Swiftqueue system to book their appointment for the St Margaret’s CDC. Parking arrangements remain the same at the St Margaret’s Hospital site.
Thom Lafferty, Chief Executive, said: “Expanding the range of services available at St Margaret’s CDC is an important part of our commitment to providing more care closer to home.
“Relocating blood testing to the CDC will give patients a modern, purpose-built environment and enable us to offer more appointments, while creating a more efficient experience.
“Alongside our blood testing services at the Harvey Centre in Harlow and Herts and Essex Hospital in Bishop’s Stortford, this will improve access to diagnostic care across the communities we serve.”

https://www.pah.nhs.uk/feed/.title: New welcome pack introduced to help patients feel informed and supported during their hospital stay
https://www.pah.nhs.uk/feed/.text:
We have introduced a new welcome pack to give inpatients clear, practical information and reassurance throughout their hospital stay.
Designed to help patients feel informed and supported, the pack brings together essential information about their care, everyday life on the ward and preparing to leave hospital safely.
It focuses on topics that can make a significant difference to a patient’s experience and recovery, including getting a good night’s sleep, speaking up about pain or discomfort, staying active where it is safe to do so, and understanding what will happen before and after discharge.
The pack also supports our ‘Don’t put up with it, tell us’ campaign, encouraging patients and families to speak to staff if they need help, have a concern or feel that something is not right. It signposts further support, including Martha’s Rule and the Patient Advice and Liaison Service (PALS).
Jo Ward, Chief Nursing Officer (Interim), said: “We know that coming into hospital can feel worrying, and clear information can make a real difference. Our new welcome pack is designed to help patients and their families know what to expect, feel more confident and play an active role in their care and recovery.
“It covers some of the issues that matter most during a hospital stay, including rest and sleep, managing pain and preparing to leave hospital safely. Just as importantly, it reinforces our ‘Don’t put up with it, tell us’ message: if you need help, have a concern or feel something is not right, please speak to us. Our teams are here to listen, respond and support you.”
The pack includes QR codes linking to further information and explains how patients can access support during their stay and after discharge. Alternative formats are available through the ward team.
You can read the welcome pack here .

https://www.pah.nhs.uk/feed/.title: Community appointment day helps patients access joined-up musculoskeletal (MSK) support
https://www.pah.nhs.uk/feed/.text:
More than 100 patients from Harlow and surrounding areas, living with lower limb musculoskeletal (MSK) conditions benefited from a MSK Community Appointment Day (CAD) jointly organised by The Princess Alexandra Hospital NHS Trust (PAHT) and Essex Partnership University NHS Foundation Trust (EPUT), at The Latton Bush Centre in Harlow, last week (28 September) which brought together clinicians, community services and voluntary sector organisations to provide personalised support in a single visit.
Endorsed by Getting It Right First Time (GIRFT), a national NHS programme designed to improve treatment and care of patients, MSK CADs offer a one-stop approach to care, helping patients access assessments, tailored exercise plans and holistic support closer to home. The model aims to support earlier intervention, improve patient outcomes and reduce the need for multiple appointments and referrals to other services.
Throughout the day, patients took part in ‘What Matters to You’ conversations to identify their own personal goals; had physiotherapy assessments and exercise sessions designed to help them better manage their condition and take an active role in their recovery.
A wide range of organisations were on hand to provide advice and support, including Essex Wellbeing Services, Active Essex, Rainbow Services, Integrated Neighbourhood Teams (Harlow North and South), Sexual Health, the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), Arthritis UK, community Diabetes Team, community dieticians, eye clinic liaison officers and Housing Services. Their presence showcased the breadth of support available to patients beyond traditional healthcare services and highlighted the value of integrated working across the health and care system.
Early intervention was the key aim of this MSK Community Appointment Day, to address issues promptly and help prevent conditions from worsening where possible, reduce chronic pain and support faster recovery. By focusing on individual goals and priorities, the event has encouraged a more personalised approach to care and wellbeing; demonstrating how a collaborative care approach can not only improve the patient experience, but support self-management and help reduce pressure on community and secondary care services.
David and Camilla from Church Langley, patients seen on the day, said:
“Amazing day, so well organised. We saw the physio who helped us with exercises, she also fed back details about an X-ray. The dietitian really helped with advice on how to increase our protein input. Thank you everyone.”
Jim McLeish, Chief Clinical Transformation Officer at PAHT said: “It was fantastic to witness first-hand the positive difference this was making for patients; a service that not only helps improve access to care but also helps to reduce waiting times and responds to individual needs in a more convenient and patient-centred way.
“The MSK CAD is a great example of our ambition to bring care closer to patients, with NHS organisations, community services and voluntary sector partners working together to provide joined-up support. The success of the day is a real credit to everyone involved, and I would like to thank all those who helped organise and deliver such an important event for our patients.”
Nicole Rich, Director of Community Physical and Mental Health Services at EPUT said: “I am delighted that the day was a great success.  Getting out into the community means we can see more patients and treat them earlier and closer to home which is one of the top priorities for EPUT.”
The feedback from patients and partner organisations will help inform future Community Appointment Days as the programme continues to support people living with MSK conditions in West Essex.

https://www.eput.nhs.uk/feed/.title: Essex NHS charity helps Rayleigh care home residents enjoy life’s little pleasures
https://www.eput.nhs.uk/feed/.text:
Residents at Rawreth Court dementia care home, run by Essex Partnership University NHS Foundation Trust (EPUT), are benefiting from a range of new activities and improvements made possible through The Trust’s charity.
From seaside trips and afternoons at the bowling alley, residents are enjoying more opportunities to stay active, make choices and enjoy the little things that make life meaningful, thanks to EPUT’s charitable fund.
Also on the schedule are visits to garden centres, local attractions, bowling and Southend Pier. Whether it’s enjoying tea and cake, exploring somewhere new or revisiting a familiar place, the outings provide opportunities to socialise and maintain a connection with the wider community – helping to support residents’ independence, wellbeing and quality of life.
The CQC recently upgraded its overall rating for the nursing home from requires improvement to good, following an inspection in August. It is now rated good in all areas.
For people living in residential care, continuing to enjoy familiar activities and experiences can be particularly important. Getting out and about can help reduce feelings of isolation, lift people’s mood and give residents something to look forward to.
Back at Rawreth Court, charitable funding is also helping to make every day routines more enjoyable and accessible.
A new picture-based menu board is helping residents make choices about what they would like to eat, using images of meals to make information easier to understand. The board also includes a clock and mealtimes, helping residents recognise daily routines and feel more confident about what is happening throughout the day.
Alina Kutraite, Registered Nursing Home Manager at Rawreth Court, said: “Moving into a care home shouldn’t mean giving up the things you love doing. We want our residents to continue enjoying life, whether that’s going out for the day, visiting somewhere familiar or simply being able to choose what they’d like for dinner.
“For people living with dementia, these everyday experiences and choices can make a real difference. They help people feel more confident, comfortable and independent, while giving them opportunities to connect with others.
“We’re incredibly grateful for the charitable funding, which has helped us introduce these improvements and give our residents more opportunities to enjoy the things that make them happy.
“It’s often the little things that mean the most, and seeing the enjoyment these experiences bring to our residents makes it all worthwhile.”
The EPUT charity has also supported new sensory activities and cognitive games to help stimulate memories, encourage communication, and provide comfort and reassurance during moments of anxiety or distress.
These activities build on Rawreth Court’s commitment to providing personalised, compassionate care, including its dedicated Namaste Care room .
Together, these charity-funded initiatives are helping residents maintain their independence, stay connected to their communities and continue enjoying the experiences that bring them happiness.

https://www.eput.nhs.uk/feed/.title: Former Army medic to run marathon for mental health charity
https://www.eput.nhs.uk/feed/.text:
A former Army medic is running next year’s London Marathon for an armed forces charity that he credits with saving his life.
Kevin Russell is a Mental Health Act Manager at Essex Partnership University NHS Foundation Trust (EPUT).
It will be his first major run since completing the Edinburgh Marathon in 2019. He is raising money for Combat Stress, which delivers specialist treatment and support to former service personnel across the UK with military-related trauma
“I am literally starting from scratch again as I haven’t been running for the last few years,” he said.
“I applied every year for the London Marathon and never got in, then Combat Stress offered me a place.”
Kevin, who lives in Basildon, sought help from the charity in 2022 after suppressing emotions and flashbacks he experienced from his time in military service for 17 years.
He underwent a two-year treatment programme with Combat Stress, which helped him to learn more about post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and coping skills to help manage his triggers. It prompted him to seek an official diagnosis of PTSD from EPUT’s mental health services.
The dad-of-two said Combat Stress saved his life and he is doing as much as he can to raise awareness of the impact of PTSD on military personnel and veterans. He won the charity’s Veteran Storyteller of the Year award in February for sharing his story and continues to share his experiences to tackle stigma and encourage people to seek help.
Kevin was 21 when he joined the Royal Army Medical Corps as a combat medic and he served tours in Oman, Iraq, Bosnia, and Afghanistan. He left the Army in 2006 after being deeply affected by the aftermath of two incidents in Kabul involving multiple casualties, including children.
He joined the NHS and has worked at EPUT and its predecessor Trusts ever since.
In his current role, Kevin helps clinicians ensure the correct processes are followed when people are detained for treatment under the Mental Health Act and provides advice to the patients’ families.
He said: “Being a patient with Combat Stress, I understand what it’s like being on the other side of the fence, the one needing help, having to have things explained to them and having treatment.
“I also understand from the other side of being the person to help people and tell them what’s going on.”
Remembrance Sunday and Armistice Day are a poignant time for Kevin, who attends a Remembrance event every year.
He was one of 10,000 participants in the Cenotaph Parade, which followed the National Act of Remembrance led by HM The King on Remembrance Sunday (8 November).
Kevin, who took part with other veterans representing Combat Stress, said: “It’s just incredible being there, just being with other veterans and with people who ‘get it’ and you don’t need to say anything.
“I think it’s important to take time on Remembrance day, even if you don’t know anyone connected to the military, to not only remember those who have paid the ultimate price but also those for whom things are still carrying on for them, the war is still going on in their head. And those who have got physical injuries that affects their life.
“Just saying thank you to a veteran or acknowledging they’re there, it’s just nice to take that time.”
Kevin hopes to raise at least £2,500 for Combat Stress at next year’s London Marathon. Anyone who would like to sponsor him can visit his fundraising page .
Robert Marsh, Director of Fundraising at Combat Stress, said: “We are so grateful to Kevin, whose selflessness and determination continue to be invaluable to the veteran community.
“His efforts continue to inspire veterans to come forward for help, while also shining a spotlight on, and raising vital funds for, our life-changing specialist treatment.
“We are delighted that he is running the marathon for Combat Stress this year, and we will be cheering him on every step of the way.”

https://www.eput.nhs.uk/feed/.title: Charity gifts £3,000 to patients for Christmas
https://www.eput.nhs.uk/feed/.text:
Fundraisers have donated a Christmas gift of £3,000 to boost the wellbeing of patients receiving care from a number of services at Epping’s community hospital.
The League of Friends of St Margaret’s Hospital in Epping presented £500 each to mental health community outpatient teams and five wards run by Essex Partnership University NHS Foundation Trust (EPUT).
The teams provide physical and mental health care at the Epping Forest Unit and mental health unit. Some patients receive longer term care, which may include extended stays on wards.
Pam Mulholland, chair of the League of Friends, said: “Although the main objective is to help with Christmas festivities, any money left over can be used by the wards to help patients through the year.
“Some patients have no visitors at all and don’t get any presents for Christmas, so this means they can get a gift on Christmas Day.”
Pam and Epping Town Council mayor Razia Sharif met staff to present the donation and find out more about their work. They also met patients and relatives on Roding ward, one of the Trust’s mental health wards.
Razia said the annual Christmas donation was a “wonderful tradition and a great part of the community spirit” in Epping.
She said: “Every year we give the ward teams several hundred pounds each to spend as they wish, whether to make the wards look better or for something they do for themselves or patients.”
Emmanuel Olaniregun, Ward Manager for Roding ward, said the support was “invaluable.”
He said: “Some of our patients are admitted with very few personal belongings and may have limited or no family support. This funding enables us to provide essential items such as clothing and toiletries, helping patients maintain their dignity and feel more comfortable during their stay.
“Although the Christmas donation helps us bring some festive cheer to patients, its benefits extend throughout the year. We use the funding to support meaningful activities, provide small treats, and celebrate special occasions such as birthdays, particularly for patients who may not have family or friends to celebrate with them.
“These may seem like small gestures, but for someone experiencing mental health difficulties, they can make a significant difference to their emotional wellbeing, sense of belonging and overall experience of care.
“We are extremely grateful to the League of Friends for their continued generosity. Their support helps us go beyond essential clinical care and provide the personal touches that make our patients feel valued, respected and remembered.”
Lesley Hanks, Operational Manager for Community Inpatient Services, added: “I’m incredibly grateful to the League of Friends for their generous donation.
“Their continued support makes a real difference to our wards and to the experience of patients in our care.”

https://www.eput.nhs.uk/feed/.title: Can you help us to shape a service user network for people living with an eating disorder?
https://www.eput.nhs.uk/feed/.text:
Essex Partnership University NHS Foundation Trust is looking for adults in Essex who have lived experience of a primary eating disorder to help shape the Trust’s Eating Disorder Service User Network (SUN).
The SUN aims to support and empower people who are living with an eating disorder on their recovery journey and provide a space for them to connect and share their experiences.
The Trust will be holding an online focus group for people to share their thoughts and ideas for what the SUN will offer and how it will be run.
If you are interested in participating, please register your interest by completing the short registration form  before Tuesday 17 November.
The SUN will currently not be open to people who experience irregular eating behaviours as a result of other mental health difficulties because we appreciate they will have different needs, however we are open to suggestions from the focus group.
Anyone with questions about the SUN or the focus group can contact epunft.edsun@nhs.net
