https://www.eput.nhs.uk/feed/.title: Pop-up shop provides free clothes for hospital patients
https://www.eput.nhs.uk/feed/.text:
Volunteers are appealing for more helpers and donations to expand a project that provides free clothes for people receiving mental health inpatient care.
Roots of Hope community interest company recently set up a weekly pop-up shop and crisis boxes of clothes for patients admitted to Chelmsford wards run by Essex Partnership University NHS Foundation Trust (EPUT).
The shop is held every Friday from 10am to 2pm at The Crystal Centre in Chelmsford.
Patients from the Crystal Centre and the Trust’s other mental health wards nearby can choose from new and second-hand clothes for free. Staff can buy clothes for a donation and the money raised is used to buy new underwear for patients.
Charlotte Spooner, who founded Roots of Hope with colleague Amanda Crossley, said the shop is already making a difference: “We’re in our second week now and it’s just been so lovely. Patients can come off the ward with staff, have a chat with us, and browse.
“There is still a great need for clothes – some people have hardly anything.
“The shop gives people boost. We’re hearing from patients about how it’s brightened up their day, that they were feeling really sad and now they’re feeling really happy, positive and hopeful.”
Charlotte first started collecting second-hand clothes for patients two years ago when she was a Peer Worker at EPUT. Peer Workers are staff who use their own experience of mental health challenges to support patients and ensure their needs are met.
Some patients had very little clothing because they couldn’t afford them or didn’t know anyone who could bring them some from home.
She and Amanda set up Roots of Hope last year so they could apply for external funding to expand the project. The non-profit organisation has a small team of volunteers, and needs more help to run the shop, and donations to buy new underwear for patients.
Andy Martin is one of their new volunteers and said it was “phenomenal” helping out on the shop’s first day on 16 October.
He said: “It’s just such an amazing thing to do for people who don’t have much and it gives them hope.
“You really feel like you’re doing some good and putting back into the community.”
Roots of Hope are looking for volunteers to help run the shop, and always welcome financial donations and donations of good quality clothes and new underwear.
They are especially in need of leggings, T-shirts, pyjamas, slippers, slip-on shoes, coats, hooded tops, men’s jogging bottoms, and men’s shirts and tops.
Visit the Roots of Hope Linkt.ree page to find out more about Roots of Hope. A fundraising page  has also been set up for anyone who would like to make a donation.
Anyone who is interested in volunteering opportunities at EPUT can email epunft.volunteers@nhs.net

https://www.eput.nhs.uk/feed/.title: Allotment project helps mental health patients grow in confidence and independence
https://www.eput.nhs.uk/feed/.text:
From growing their own vegetables to enjoying mindfulness in nature, people receiving mental health support in Essex are benefiting from an allotment project helping them build confidence, learn new skills and connect with others.
The Community Allotment Group, run by Essex Partnership University NHS Foundation Trust’s (EPUT) Mid Essex Community Occupational Therapy team, has been transformed thanks to charitable funding.
The weekly group gives people receiving community mental health support opportunities to enjoy gardening, develop friendships and build a sense of achievement in a relaxed, supportive environment.
This week is Occupational Therapy Week , showcasing how occupational therapists enable participation in the activities that matter most, improving health, wellbeing and quality of life through expert support at every stage of life.
New freshly painted raised planting beds, gardening equipment and donated garden furniture have transformed Beeches Road Allotments in Chelmsford into a more welcoming and accessible space. Funded through EPUT Charitable Funds, the improvements have made a particular difference for patients with physical health conditions or reduced mobility, enabling more people to comfortably take part in planting, tending and harvesting produce.
One patient said: “I really enjoy coming to the allotment, it gets me out of the house and gives me a space to talk to people that accept me.”
Patients have also helped paint the raised beds bright yellow, giving them a sense of pride and ownership over the space.
Megan Treadwell, Senior Occupational Therapist at EPUT, said: “The allotment is about so much more than gardening. It’s a place where people can build confidence, make connections and develop skills that support their recovery and everyday independence.
“One of our biggest achievements this year has been making the space more accessible. Previously, some patients struggled to take part because of physical health difficulties, but the new equipment means we can adapt activities to suit their needs.”
Patients have enjoyed a successful growing season, harvesting pumpkins, cucumbers, green beans, beetroot and other produce to take home.
The benefits extend beyond gardening, with patients developing practical life skills such as planning meals, shopping for ingredients and preparing food independently.
One patient shared: “I now grow things at home with mum because I learnt at the group.”
Megan added: “It’s incredibly rewarding when someone takes home something they’ve grown and comes back to tell us what they’ve made with it. We’ve had patients bring in homemade rhubarb jam and share their recipes with others. These might seem like small things, but they represent real progress.”
The funding has also enabled the team to introduce a separate mindfulness and movement group, offering gentle exercise, relaxation and grounding activities outdoors for people who may not be interested in gardening.
The project’s success has also helped inspire a second allotment group at St Peter’s Hospital in Maldon, launched in July, giving more people opportunities to experience the therapeutic benefits of gardening.
Megan said: “Being outdoors in a peaceful, informal environment can make such a difference. Some people find it easier to open up away from a traditional clinical setting.
“Thanks to the charitable funding, we’ve been able to make the allotment more inclusive and extend these opportunities to more people.”
EPUT Charitable Funds supports projects that enhance the experience of patients, families, carers and colleagues beyond what NHS funding can provide.

https://www.eput.nhs.uk/feed/.title: People with lived experience helping hundreds access mental health support in Essex
https://www.eput.nhs.uk/feed/.text:
Hundreds of people across north east Essex are being helped to improve their mental health, build confidence and access vital support thanks to a service bringing people with lived experience directly into NHS care.
The Peer Support Service, delivered in partnership by Essex Partnership University NHS Foundation Trust (EPUT) and local charity SUMMIT, supports people across Colchester and Tendring who are experiencing mental health difficulties.
The service brings together six peer support workers who use their own experiences of mental health challenges to build trusting relationships, offer encouragement and help people overcome barriers to accessing care.
From August 2025 to August 2026, peer support workers helped people attend 385 important healthcare appointments, including 330 GP appointments and 55 outpatient appointments. This has resulted in estimated NHS savings of £22,000 by helping to prevent missed appointments.
The team also supported five people experiencing mental health crises, helping to avoid visits to A&E and potential hospital admissions.
Peer support workers offer personalised support, usually over 20 to 24 weeks, helping people attend appointments, access counselling, manage financial and housing difficulties, and reconnect with their communities.
Over the past year, the service has helped people address more than 1,550 issues, ranging from accessing benefits and housing support to finding specialist counselling, befriending services and help with drug and alcohol difficulties.
A further 345 people were supported to access other health services, helping them get the care they needed.
For many people, having someone alongside them who understands what they are going through can make a life-changing difference.
One person supported by the service said: “I have been really struggling with my mental health and now, with the support from my peer support worker, there is hope for the future.”
Another said: “I don’t know where I would be if they hadn’t come into my life, I feel I can breathe again.”
The service also helps people overcome loneliness and isolation by building their confidence to take part in everyday activities and connect with others.
SUMMIT has established peer support groups in Colchester and Tendring, giving people a welcoming space to meet others, share experiences and continue receiving support after their individual sessions have ended.
One person said: “I feel so much more confident going out on my own now.”
Another added: “I feel like someone is listening to what I need.”
Ann Sheridan, Executive Nurse at EPUT, said: “We are proud to work alongside SUMMIT to provide this valuable service, which shows just how powerful lived experience can be in supporting people’s mental health.
“Having someone who understands what you are going through can make a real difference, particularly for people who may have struggled to access support in the past. These results show the positive impact peer support workers are having in helping people build confidence, stay connected with their care and get the help they need.”
Gaynor Jarrett, CEO of SUMMIT, said: “Peer support is about helping people feel heard, understood and supported by someone who has experienced their own mental health challenges.
“Behind these figures are people who are finding the confidence to leave their homes, attend appointments, make new connections and feel more hopeful about their futures.
“We are incredibly proud of our peer support workers and the difference they are making to people’s lives across Colchester and Tendring.”
The service has now been running for two years, with referrals increasing as more NHS mental health teams and community services have begun accessing the support.
The service highlights the importance of working closely with health services, charities and community organisations to help people access support earlier and prevent their mental health from deteriorating.

https://www.eput.nhs.uk/feed/.title: Creative workshops help young people at risk of psychosis build confidence and connections
https://www.eput.nhs.uk/feed/.text:
Young people at risk of developing psychosis are discovering the therapeutic benefits of arts and crafts, helping them build confidence, express themselves and connect with others.
Patients supported by Essex Partnership University NHS Foundation Trust’s (EPUT) At Risk Mental State (ARMS) Service in south west Essex are being given opportunities to take part in creative workshops and community activities to support their mental health and wellbeing, funded by EPUT’s charity.
The service supports people aged 14 to 35 across Basildon, Thurrock and Brentwood who may be experiencing unusual thoughts, feelings of paranoia or hearing voices. These experiences can also lead to social isolation and make it difficult to take part in group activities.
Thanks to EPUT’s Charitable Funds, the team is helping patients overcome these barriers by providing opportunities to try new experiences in a supportive environment.
One activity was a Japanese-inspired Kintsugi workshop at Minus Cloud Nine in Brentwood, where patients learned the art of repairing broken pottery using gold-coloured materials.
Kintsugi, meaning ‘golden joinery’, celebrates imperfections rather than hiding them. By highlighting cracks in gold, broken pieces are transformed into something beautiful and unique, carrying a powerful message about self-acceptance and how difficult experiences can become part of our personal story.
Led by psychotherapist Charlotte, the workshop encouraged conversations about mental health and wellbeing while giving participants the chance to learn a new skill and create something they could feel proud of.
Arts and crafts can have important therapeutic benefits for mental health, helping people relax, express emotions and build confidence. Taking part in group activities also creates opportunities to form friendships, reduce isolation and develop a sense of belonging.
For people who may find social situations particularly challenging, simply attending and taking part can be a significant achievement.
Martine Pridgeon, Senior Occupational Therapist at EPUT’s ARMS Service, said: “For some of the people we support, getting out into the community and joining a group activity can feel like a really big step, so seeing them take part and enjoy themselves was lovely.
“The Kintsugi workshop had such a meaningful message behind it. The idea that something broken can become beautiful in a different way is a lovely reminder that our experiences and imperfections are part of what makes us who we are.
“Creative activities give people a chance to express themselves, build confidence and connect with others in a relaxed environment. Even small steps like attending a workshop can make a real difference to someone’s wellbeing.
“One patient said they thought the workshop was really relaxing and that it was nice to focus on something with a clear head, another commented on how nice it was to meet new people, and a patient’s mother said that he had talked about it a lot afterwards and mentioned how much he had enjoyed it.”
The team is now hoping to organise more activities, including a mandala dot-painting workshop, to give more patients opportunities to explore their creativity, meet others and feel more connected to their communities.
The project is supported by EPUT Charitable Funds, which helps fund activities and improvements that go beyond what the NHS would normally provide, making a positive difference to patients’ experiences and wellbeing.

https://www.eput.nhs.uk/feed/.title: Nurse completes charity walk in father’s memory
https://www.eput.nhs.uk/feed/.text:
A mental health nurse has raised £260 for a cancer charity in memory of their father.
Sophie Phillips works in Ardleigh ward at The Lakes mental health unit in Colchester, a service run by Essex Partnership University NHS Foundation Trust.
Sophie and their twin brother Alex Gorden completed Cancer Research UK’s Shine Night Walk in Cambridge on Saturday 17 October.
Sophie said: “I completed the 10km walk in 2 hours and 1 minute. I have raised £260 for brain cancer research, which I’m really pleased about.”
Alex raised more than £130 for research into ovarian cancer.
Their father Austen sadly died in May 2022 after being diagnosed with a stage 4 glioblastoma tumour in January that year.
Sophie wants to raise money towards finding a cure for people diagnosed with cancer, especially brain cancer.
Statistics from Cancer Research UK  show that more than 12,500 people in the UK are diagnosed with brain cancers or tumours every year.

https://www.eput.nhs.uk/feed/.text:
A medical secretary has completed her first half marathon and raised double the amount she hoped for the National Deaf Children’s Society.
Grace Bryant works in the Basildon Mental Health Urgent Care Department, a service run by Essex Partnership University NHS Foundation Trust that provides 24 hour help seven days a week for adults experiencing a mental health crisis.
She completed the Royal Parks Half Marathon in London on Sunday 11 October in 3 hours and four minutes.
Grace, whose son was born profoundly deaf in his left ear, said: “It was really good fun. It’s a great atmosphere and everyone’s support keeps you going.
“I’ve managed to double my target now and have raised £700, so I’m super pleased with that!”
Last October she completed the National Deaf Children’s Society 100-mile challenge and raised more than £200.

While there is more to do, the Trust has made significant progress through innovation:
Our 111 mental health crisis phone line ensures people in need can access support 24 hours a day, 365 days a year
People with lived experience have been employed in designated roles across the Trust, ensuring patient voice is heart of the organisation and all that we do.
A number of new initiatives have been launched, helping people access the support they need when they need it most. These include a mental health urgent care department, By Your Side maternal mental health service, Rough Sleeper team, mental health crisis ambulance cars, virtual wards and neuromodulation service.
EPUT was formed on 1 April 2017 and provides community health, mental health and learning disability services across Essex, Luton and Bedfordshire and Suffolk.  We employ more than 7,200 staff working across more than 200 sites.

https://www.essex.icb.nhs.uk/feed/.title: We take them for granted, but where would we be without them? Antibiotics: the backbone of modern medicine
https://www.essex.icb.nhs.uk/feed/.text:
Antibiotics are one of the foundations of modern healthcare. They treat serious bacterial infections and make many of the treatments we now take for granted, from major surgery to cancer treatment, much safer.
This World Antimicrobial Resistance Awareness Week (18–24 November), Dr Matthew Sweeting, Executive Medical Director at NHS Essex, explains why we all have a role in protecting antibiotics for the future.
Imagine breaking your leg badly, with an open wound that becomes infected. Today, doctors can treat that infection with antibiotics. Now imagine that the bacteria causing the infection are resistant to the antibiotics we have available. Suddenly, something we would normally expect to treat can become much more dangerous. That isn’t science fiction. Antibiotics continue to save lives every day, but antibiotic-resistant infections are already happening and are becoming an increasing threat.
Help keep antibiotics working
Antibiotics are used to treat bacterial infections and are also essential to much of modern medicine, including surgery and the treatment of serious wounds. But every time we use an antibiotic there is an opportunity for bacteria to adapt and develop resistance. If that happens, the antibiotic may become less effective or stop working altogether, making infections harder to treat.
Antibiotic resistance is one part of the wider problem of antimicrobial resistance , or AMR. Other microbes, such as viruses, fungi and parasites, can also become resistant to the medicines used to treat them.
As healthcare professionals, we have a responsibility to make sure medicines such as antibiotics are prescribed appropriately. But everyone can play a part in helping to keep them working for the future.
This does not mean avoiding antibiotics when they are needed. It means using the right antibiotic, for the right patient, at the right time, and only for as long as needed. The UK Health Security Agency’s Andi Biotic , mascot of the Keep Antibiotics Working campaign, is one way this message is being shared.
Antibiotics and children
Many common childhood illnesses are caused by viruses and will get better without antibiotics. Antibiotics do not work against viral infections such as most coughs, colds and flu.
In Essex, 36.6% of children aged 0 to 9 received at least one antibiotic prescription from primary care in the past 12 months. The NHS England ambition is 25% or fewer by March 2027.
This is not about withholding antibiotics from children who need them. When antibiotics are needed to treat a bacterial infection, they can be essential. It is about avoiding antibiotics when they will not help, while making sure parents and carers know how to manage symptoms and when to seek further help. Your doctor, nurse or pharmacist can advise about the best treatment and what signs to look out for.
Everyone’s responsibility
Small actions today can help keep antibiotics working for our families and future generations.
We can all play our part by:
Using antibiotics wisely. Only take antibiotics when they have been prescribed for you, take them as directed and never save them for another time or share them with someone else. Pharmacists can also help with symptoms of coughs, colds and other minor illnesses.
Preventing infections spreading. Simple measures such as good hand hygiene and staying at home when you are unwell can help reduce the spread of infections.
Keeping vaccinations up to date. Getting the flu, RSV, COVID and other vaccinations you are eligible for helps protect you from serious illness and can reduce the chance of infections leading to hospital treatment.
Healthcare has responsibilities too. We need to continue improving prescribing, reviewing whether antibiotics are genuinely needed and learning from variation in prescribing between services and different parts of the country.
Become an Antibiotic Guardian
We can all make a difference to keep antibiotics working for the future.

https://www.essex.icb.nhs.uk/feed/.title: Essex mum avoids A&E visit thanks to local NHS eye care service
https://www.essex.icb.nhs.uk/feed/.text:
An Essex woman avoided a trip to A&E after getting help from a free NHS service for new eye problems.
The Minor Eye Conditions Service (MECS) helps people with eye problems that have started recently. It is available at participating opticians across Essex, without needing to see a GP first.
Jayne Mason, from Thurrock, discovered the service when her mum developed a red, painful eye.
Her mum was considering going to A&E, but Jayne first contacted her usual optician. When they could not offer an appointment, Jayne searched online and found another practice offering MECS in Pitsea.
After a short telephone assessment, her mum was offered an appointment within 30 minutes.
An optometrist, a healthcare professional who examines eyes, checked her symptoms and reassured her that there was no serious problem requiring further treatment.
“When I visited Mum, she had developed a red, painful eye and was considering going to A&E. Her usual optician couldn’t offer an appointment, so I searched online and found another local practice offering MECS.
“After a quick telephone assessment, Mum was offered an appointment, had a thorough examination and, most importantly, we were reassured that there was nothing seriously wrong.
“The whole experience was excellent. Mum got expert advice quickly and conveniently, and it meant we avoided an unnecessary trip to A&E. It’s a useful service for people to know about.”
Jayne said
How the NHS eye care service can help
The Minor Eye Conditions Service can assess and treat a range of new eye problems, including:
Red or sore eyes
Dry, gritty or uncomfortable eyes
Eye irritation or swelling
Watery eyes
New flashes or floaters in your vision
Eye pain
Ingrowing eyelashes
Small objects in the eye, such as grit
You do not need a referral from your GP.
The service is free for eligible patients and is available through participating optical practices across Essex.
“Jayne’s experience shows how the Minor Eye Conditions Service can help people get the right eye care quickly and closer to home.
“If you develop a new or recent problem with your eyes, such as redness, soreness, irritation or new flashes and floaters, you may be able to get help from a participating local optical practice without seeing your GP first.
“The optometrist will assess your symptoms and can provide treatment where appropriate. If you need care from another NHS service, they can advise you about what to do next.
“We want more people in Essex to know that this service is available and to consider it when they develop a new eye problem.”
Dr Boye Tayo, Clinical Lead for Eye Care at NHS Essex, said:
How to get an appointment
If you have a new eye problem, you can contact a participating optical practice directly.
Find a local practice offering the Minor Eye Conditions Service.
Call the practice and ask for a MECS appointment.
Answer some questions about your symptoms.
The practice will advise you about an appointment or what to do next.
Depending on your symptoms, you may be offered an appointment within 24 hours or within a few working days.
Call before visiting. Do not turn up without an appointment.
Find out more about the Minor Eye Conditions Service and how to get an appointment.
What patients say about the service
In a survey of 641 patients who used the service in mid and south Essex between April and June 2026:
96% said they would recommend it to family and friends.
35% said they would have gone to their GP without the service.
20% said they would have gone to A&E.
The results show how the service can help people find an alternative to visiting their GP or A&E for some eye problems.
When to get emergency help
ome eye problems need emergency medical attention.
Go to A&E or call 999 if:
You suddenly cannot see from one or both eyes.
You have severe eye pain.
You have a serious eye injury.
A sharp object has pierced your eye.
A strong chemical has gone into your eye.
If a strong chemical gets into your eye, keep rinsing it with water while wait

https://www.essex.icb.nhs.uk/feed/.title: Get your flu vaccine before Christmas
https://www.essex.icb.nhs.uk/feed/.text:
If you are eligible for a free NHS flu vaccine and have not had it yet, book your appointment now.
The vaccine can take up to two weeks to build protection. Getting vaccinated by Friday 11 December will give it time to work before Christmas Day.
If you cannot get an appointment by then, you should still have the vaccine. Flu can spread throughout winter.
Why the flu vaccine matters
Christmas is a time when families and friends come together. This can make it easier for flu to spread.
Flu can make anyone unwell. For some people, it can cause serious illness and lead to a stay in hospital.
People at greater risk include older people, pregnant women and people with certain long-term health conditions. Vaccinating children also helps reduce the spread of flu to other family members.
As you make your Christmas plans, please make time for your flu vaccination too. Flu can make anyone unwell, but for some people it can lead to serious complications, a hospital stay and, in some cases, death. If you’re eligible for a free vaccine and haven’t had it yet, book an appointment now rather than leaving it until the festive rush.
If you’re a parent or carer, please also check whether your eligible child has had their flu vaccine. If they’ve missed it, make arranging their vaccination part of your Christmas preparations.
If you can only get an appointment after 11 December, please still take it. Flu can circulate well beyond Christmas, and vaccination can help protect you through the rest of winter.
Dr Matthew Sweeting, Executive Medical Director at NHS Essex
How to get your flu vaccine
Eligible adults can:
book through the NHS website or NHS App
call 119 free of charge if they cannot book online
ask their GP practice about appointments
ask a participating pharmacy about appointments.
Some pharmacies offer walk-in vaccinations. Check with the pharmacy before travelling.
If you are pregnant, you can also ask your midwife about getting vaccinated.
Flu vaccines for children
Children who were aged two or three on 31 August 2026 can get their free flu vaccine at their GP practice or a participating pharmacy.
From 1 December 2026 , children from Reception to Year 11 who missed their flu vaccination at school can also get vaccinated at a participating pharmacy.
Parents and carers can ask the pharmacy about appointments or contact their school vaccination team about a catch-up appointment.
Last year, around 104,000 hospitalisations were avoided through people getting their jabs and protecting themselves, their loved ones, our communities and helping the NHS prepare for winter.
So far this season, over 2 million people in the East of England have already had their flu jab, which is great news, but there are plenty more appointments available.
The flu jab really is your best defence against winter illness. It takes just a few minutes, but it can protect you for months, helping to prevent serious illness, avoid hospital admissions and keeping the most vulnerable people safe.
Now is also a great time to get your 2- and 3-year-olds vaccinated; little ones can get really unwell with flu. Many people don’t know that whilst school age children get their offer in their schools, younger children age 2 and 3 are also entitled to a nasal spray vaccine and they can get it at their GP or at a participating local pharmacy.
Now it is easier than ever to book – there are plenty of appointments available at the time and place most convenient to you giving you and your family the best possible protection over Christmas and through the winter months.”
Dr Eleanor Powers, Head of Public Health Commissioning (immunisation) for NHS England – East of England

https://www.essex.icb.nhs.uk/feed/.title: Use antibiotics wisely and help keep them working
https://www.essex.icb.nhs.uk/feed/.text:
Antibiotics save lives, and we can all help keep them working. By choosing to use antibiotics wisely and only taking them when they are needed, people in Essex can help protect these important medicines for the future.
Antibiotic resistance is increasing. This happens when bacteria change and antibiotics no longer work as well against them. It can make infections much harder to treat.
In 2025, an average of 406 antibiotic-resistant bloodstream infections were reported each week in England. Some of these infections can be life-threatening.
When antibiotics can help
Antibiotics treat infections caused by bacteria. This includes some serious illnesses, such as pneumonia, meningitis and sepsis. They are also important for surgery and some cancer treatments.
Antibiotics do not work against viruses. This means they will not treat colds, flu or COVID-19.
Taking antibiotics when they are not needed can allow bacteria to become resistant. These bacteria can spread to other people and cause infections that are harder to treat.
What you can do
You can help keep antibiotics working:
Do not expect or demand antibiotics for common illnesses such as colds and flu.
Ask a pharmacist for advice about treating your symptoms.
Take antibiotics exactly as prescribed.
Never share antibiotics with another person.
Do not save antibiotics to use later.
Take leftover antibiotics to a pharmacy for safe disposal.
Have the vaccinations you are eligible for.
Wash your hands regularly.
Cover coughs and sneezes with a tissue, then put it in a bin.
Stay at home when you are unwell, where possible.
These actions can reduce infections and unnecessary antibiotic use.
Protecting antibiotics for the future
We all have a role to play in halting the growth of antibiotic resistance. Please don’t go to your GP or other health professional expecting or demanding antibiotics. Instead, follow tried and tested advice for easing symptoms of common illnesses like colds and flu. You can visit the NHS website for further advice or can ask your pharmacist.
If you are prescribed antibiotics, please take them exactly as prescribed. Do not save them for later or share them with anyone else. If you do have any leftover antibiotics, take them to your pharmacist to dispose of them properly. And everyone who is eligible for vaccinations like flu, COVID-19 or RSV should make sure to arrange their vaccine.
If we all work towards protecting our antibiotics, we can make sure that we can continue to use them when they are needed.
Dr Matthew Sweeting, Executive Medical Director at NHS Essex
You can also choose a personal pledge through the Antibiotic Guardian campaign. A pledge could be to use antibiotics only as advised or to return leftover antibiotics to a pharmacy.

https://www.essex.icb.nhs.uk/feed/.title: Lung cancer detection is key to saving lives
https://www.essex.icb.nhs.uk/feed/.text:
Cancer is a vile thing, as we all know. Many of us know someone who has survived it, is living with it or has lost their live to it. Data suggests that nearly half of us will have cancer at some point in our lives. It is a sobering thought.
While better, more effective treatment is helping people with cancer to live longer, early detection through screening programmes also plays a huge part.
Since the introduction of such programmes, mortality rates have fallen. For example, the breast cancer screening programme has contributed to the decline in breast cancer deaths . Every year, breast screening detects around 19,000 cancers in England and prevents the deaths of around 1,300 women across the UK.
Screening is effective because treatment works best when cancers are found at an earlier stage. Screening allows us to find cancers before symptoms appear when they are easier to treat, and before they have spread.
Lung cancer screening – the newest cancer screening programme
Initially, NHS Lung Cancer Screening , previously known as Targeted Lung Health Checks, began as a very localised programme in a small number of areas in England, including Thurrock. The areas were chosen based on the high numbers of people with late-stage lung cancer diagnosis or high smoking rates. It invited people aged 55 to 74 who had a history of smoking, who are considered at higher risk of developing lung cancer.
Since then, the successful programme has expanded to more areas in Essex.
Why it is so important
Lung cancer is the third most common cancer diagnosed each year, but it is the most common cause of cancer death. Almost twice as many people die from lung cancer each year compared to bowel cancer, the second most common cause of death from cancer.
It often has no symptoms until later stages, or the symptoms are easily mistaken for other common conditions.
As treatment for lung cancer works best in the early stages, waiting for symptoms to appear can be too late. People diagnosed with stage 1 lung cancer have around a 65% chance of surviving for five years or more. This drops to around 15% at stage 3 and 5% at stage 4.
This is why screening is so important. It can pick up those early-stage cancers before they cause symptoms. People can then get the treatment they need when it will have the best chances.
In Essex, over 40,000 people have been invited to take part in screening. For most people screened, nothing will be found, but a small number will be diagnosed with cancer. So far, 449 lung cancers have been found through screening, with almost 75% being stage 1 or 2 (332). This impressive figure for early detection is having a profound effect.
Before the introduction of the programme, lung cancer was primarily diagnosed after a referral from a GP, emergency admissions and during investigations for other conditions. Just 23% of lung cancers were found at stage 1 or 2 via these routes in 2020.
Today the combined figure – including GP referrals, emergency admissions, chance discoveries, and lung cancer screening – is 43%; almost double the figure from six years ago. This will make a huge difference for people going through treatment, and we expect to see deaths from lung cancer reducing as a result.
How it works
Eligible people (55-74 and with a history of smoking) registered at participating GP practices receive an invitation letter asking them to schedule a telephone consultation with a specialist nurse. If they are considered at higher risk, they will be offered a low-dose CT scan, which is carried out at a state-of-the-art mobile unit.
The programme showcases the collaboration between many different organisations, including GP practices, hospital trusts and providers of the mobile scanning unit, Colbalt, working to deliver faster diagnosis for patients. Local government partners and the voluntary sector also play a crucial role in highlighting the importance of screening for eligible people.
What next for the programme

https://www.essex.icb.nhs.uk/feed/.title: Lung cancer screening starts in Harlow
https://www.essex.icb.nhs.uk/feed/.text:
People aged 55 to 74 in Harlow who smoke or used to smoke are starting to receive invitations for free NHS lung cancer screening.
The screening can find lung cancer before symptoms appear. Finding cancer earlier can give people a better chance of successful treatment.
Harlow is the first area in west Essex to receive the screening programme. It will also be introduced in Epping Forest and Uttlesford.
What to do if you receive an invitation
If you receive an invitation, follow the instructions in your letter to arrange a telephone appointment with a specialist nurse.
The nurse will ask questions about your health and smoking history. If they find that you have a higher risk of developing lung cancer, you will be offered a low-dose CT scan. This is a quick scan that takes detailed pictures of your lungs.
Not everyone who has the telephone appointment will need a scan.
People who may be eligible should also make sure their smoking history is recorded correctly with their GP practice.
Finding lung cancer earlier
Lung cancer can develop without causing clear symptoms. This means it can sometimes be difficult to spot in its early stages.
Screening aims to find lung cancer sooner, when there may be more opportunities for treatment.
Screening elsewhere in Essex has already found 449 lung cancers. Of these, 332, around 74%, were found at stage 1 or 2. These are the earlier stages of lung cancer.
We are really pleased to announce that the Lung Cancer Screening programme is coming to Harlow. The aim of the programme is to detect lung cancer early so that people can be treated sooner and more effectively – ultimately saving more lives.
Lung cancer is the biggest cause of cancer deaths in the UK. The unfortunate reality is that for many people it can develop for a long time with no clear signs. If there are symptoms, they can be easily mistaken for more common conditions. That’s why screening is so important.
If you receive an invite, make sure to get in touch with us using the contact details in your invitation. For the majority of people everything will be normal, but in circumstances where something is found, screening will give us more opportunity to act sooner.
Dr Sara Astbury, local GP and Clinical Lead for Cancer at NHS Essex
Do not wait for screening if you have symptoms
If you are worried about symptoms, contact your GP practice. Do not wait for a lung cancer screening invitation , whether or not you think you are eligible.

https://www.essex.icb.nhs.uk/feed/.title: “Like a catastrophic plane crash” – mother tells story of nearly losing daughter to undiagnosed diabetes
https://www.essex.icb.nhs.uk/feed/.text:
A Rayleigh mother is raising awareness of the signs of type 1 diabetes after she was told to “prepare for the worst” when her daughter was rushed to hospital.
Zara was on a family trip in August 2025 when she was feeling exhausted. After returning home, the then 13-year-old became sick and struggled to breathe.
She was taken to Southend Hospital and was immediately admitted with type 1 diabetes and diabetic ketoacidosis, a life-threatening condition where the body does not have enough insulin.
This World Diabetes Day (14 November) Zara’s mum Mandy wants to make sure that parents are aware of the signs of diabetes so they can avoid the traumatic experiences her daughter Zara and the whole family went through. She has recently launched a monthly meet and greet group in Rayleigh to provide support and tips for families.
Mandy said:
While the medical team were asking me questions, they told me that they were wiring Zara up to a defibrillator in case her heart stopped. It was at this point that staff told me to call my family to come to the hospital, prepare for the worst, and say my goodbyes because she was not expected to live.
Zara spent a week in hospital as the staff monitored her blood glucose levels and slowly, she began to improve. Mandy said:
Our experience felt like a catastrophic plane crash rather than a managed emergency landing. Her siblings are still adjusting to the emotional turmoil of what they saw.
Zara doesn’t remember much of the time in intensive care but has vivid memories of certain moments and those who she formed the closest bonds with.
I live with a heavy sense of guilt that I failed her by not recognising the signs.
The NHS advises that the easiest way to remember type 1 diabetes symptoms is the 4Ts:
Toilet
Thirsty
Tired
Thinner
In the months before Zara became seriously ill, the signs of her undiagnosed type 1 diabetes appeared slowly. She complained about stomach pains, backaches and felt tired all the time. She was always thirsty, needed to use the toilet more frequently and suffered from dizziness.
Symptoms of diabetes can develop quickly so it is important that parents are aware of what to look out for. Children may start going to the toilet more often and also become constantly thirsty without being able to quench it. They may also feel very tired and have no energy and lose weight or look thinner than usual. If you notice these symptoms, you should seek same day urgent medical assessment via your GP or NHS 111.
If symptoms get noticeably worse, it could be what is known as diabetic ketoacidosis which needs immediate attention. When you have symptoms of undiagnosed diabetes and severe stomach pain, rapid breathing, vomiting and confusion, you should call 999 or go to A&E straight away.
Dr Deepa Shanmugasundaram, GP and Clinical Lead at NHS Essex
Diabetic ketoacidosis or DKA, is a life-threatening condition that can develop when the body does not have enough insulin. It can include feeling sleepy and confused, breathing faster and more deeply than usual, as well as stomach pain, diarrhoea and feeling or being sick.
Mandy said:
I had absolutely no idea what the 4Ts were, what the signs of type 1 diabetes looked like or how life-threatening DKA can be.
Today, Zara is living like any other teenager and managing her diabetes. using a glucose monitor and insulin pump.
To help other families and children with type 1 diabetes, Mandy has set up a monthly meet and greet group in Rayleigh to offer a space to share experiences, tips and advice. Mandy added:
We know that other families have not been as fortunate as us. Tragically, there are parents who have lost their children to DKA from undiagnosed type 1 diabetes.
Read more of Mandy and Zara’s story
Want to know more about the meet and greets?
Mandy runs monthly meet and greets which are open to all families who have a child who has type 1 diabetes. These support children and families by bringing people together. All family members welcome.

https://www.essex.icb.nhs.uk/feed/.text:
The NHS minor injuries unit’s (MIU) move to Thurrock Hospital was welcomed as a positive step for people in and around Thurrock, Basildon, Brentwood following a visit to the site today (13 November).
Visitors today included Jen Craft, MP for Thurrock and patient representatives and allowed them to see the improved patient and clinical facilities. These include a much bigger and more comfortable waiting area with a designated children’s space, and specialist treatment facilities, including a purpose-built wound care room with integrated shower facilities and a dedicated plaster room.
The visitors also saw the adjacent Community Diagnostic Centre which is providing X-Ray facilities for the MIU. They also talked to staff from North East London NHS Foundation Trust (NELFT) who run the service and to representatives from NHS Essex who facilitated the move, including securing £1million of external funding.
It was great to visit the new Minor Injuries Unit at Thurrock Hospital today and see the difference our government’s investment is making for healthcare in Thurrock. The new facility provides more clinical space, additional treatment rooms and a larger waiting area, helping more people access care closer to home and reducing pressure on Basildon A&E.
Staff spoke positively about the move and the improvements it is already making for both patients and those delivering care. We also spoke about parking, which is an important issue for many patients and visitors, and I will continue to monitor this.
The opening of the Minor Injuries Unit is an important first step, with plans to develop the site further into an Urgent Treatment Centre, expanding the range of services available locally and ensuring more residents can receive the care they need closer to where they live.
Jen Craft MP for Thurrock
The shift of MIU from its smaller space in Orsett Hospital to a bigger home designed specifically for the service at the John Tallack Centre happened at the beginning of November.
The move has been positive for everyone. Our staff are thrilled to be working in this newly refurbished space that supports them to deliver more effective patient care that improves privacy, dignity and comfort for patients.  And we’ve had great feedback from patients about the new facilities, including the new waiting area.
Being close to the Community Diagnostic Centre is also helping us to provide a more joined-up and smoother experience for our patients and service users.
We’ve made a lot of progress in the first two weeks, and while we want to continue to improve our current minor injuries service and will be asking for patient feedback, we’re also excited by the potential to expand the service in our new space.
Brid Johnson, Chief Operating Officer for NELFT
The relocation forms part of a wider NHS Essex programme to enhance urgent and emergency care services in the area, and this is a step towards developing an Urgent Treatment Centre (UTC) at Thurrock Community Hospital.
We’ve successfully moved the Minor Injuries Unit into a new environment designed to meet current clinical standards and support future service development. Achieving this in a short time has been a great team effort by NHS Essex, NELFT and Essex Partnership University NHS Foundation Trust (EPUT) who operate the Thurrock Community Hospital site.
Samantha Goldberg, Executive Director of Commercial, Resilience & Estates at NHS Essex Integrated Care Board
As well as the clinical improvements, we’ve worked to ensure adequate parking, access and signage. It’s great to have such positive initial feedback from patients and staff.
This move is more than a change of location. It is part of our five-year plan to expand urgent care services for local people. We plan to build on this move by developing the service into an Urgent Treatment Centre that will care for minor illnesses as well as minor injuries, helping more patients and diverting people from hospital emergency departments.”

https://www.essex.icb.nhs.uk/feed/.title: Rayleigh family helping others spot the signs of type 1 diabetes sooner
https://www.essex.icb.nhs.uk/feed/.text:
Fourteen-year-old Zara Holland-Martin from Rayleigh loves singing, listening to music and dancing ballet and contemporary.
In August 2025, at 13 years old, she became critically ill and developed diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). This is a serious complication of type 1 diabetes when the body does not have enough insulin.
At one stage, her family were told to prepare for the worst. Thankfully, Zara recovered, thanks to the medical and support teams who cared for her.
Now, Zara and her mum, Mandy, raise awareness about type 1 diabetes and DKA. They bring other type 1 diabetes families together offering advice, guidance and shared experiences. This helps children and young people with type 1 diabetes meet others with the same condition.
The lead up to hospital admission
In the months before Zara became seriously ill, the signs of her undiagnosed type 1 appeared slowly. She complained about stomach pains, backaches and felt tired all the time. She was always thirsty, needed to use the toilet more frequently and suffered from dizziness. The family visited their GP practice, but the symptoms were initially thought to be related to other causes.
In early August 2025, Zara’s situation escalated during a family weekend away. Zara was visibly thinner and mentioned her clothes felt loose and big. She had to keep stopping on family outings due to exhaustion. Mandy says:
She then developed an unquenchable thirst, drinking massive amounts of fluids and using the toilet constantly. Due to the warm weather, I mistakenly thought she just needed to keep hydrated. That evening she was sick a lot.
Two days later, Zara was too exhausted to leave the car during our trip and asked to go home. When we arrived home, she was sick repeatedly and told me she couldn’t breathe. She had deep, rapid and laboured breathing. We checked her heart rate, which was 178bpm, and took her straight to Southend Hospital.
Emergency response
When they arrived at A&E, Zara was immediately triaged and diagnosed with type 1 diabetes and diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). Within 15 minutes, 17 staff members were around her bed. Hospital staff activated the Paediatric and Neonatal Decision Assessment (PANDA) protocol. A specialist team from Addenbrooke’s Hospital in Cambridge then guided her care via phone every 15 minutes.
Mandy continues:
While the medical team were asking me questions, they told me that they were wiring Zara up to a defibrillator in case her heart stopped. It was at this point that staff told me to call my family to come to the hospital, prepare for the worst, and say my goodbyes because she was not expected to live.
Zara was moved to the adult intensive care unit where she was monitored constantly. Staff told the family that cases like Zara’s are uncommon.
Making progress
She slowly began to get better. Although she was still very fragile, she continued to improve and was moved to paediatric care. Mandy says:
During her week in hospital, I remember the diabetes nurses visiting to give her a ‘Rufus Bear’ (an educational stuffed bear for type 1 diabetes children) and fitting her very first Continuous Glucose Monitor on her arm to track her glucose levels automatically.
A terrifying experience
It is hard to comprehend how quickly life changed in just a few days.
Our experience felt like a catastrophic plane crash rather than a managed emergency landing. Her siblings are still adjusting to the emotional turmoil of what they saw.
Zara doesn’t remember much of the time in intensive care but has vivid memories of certain moments and those who she formed the closest bonds with.
I live with a heavy sense of guilt that I failed her by not recognising the signs.
I had absolutely no idea what the 4Ts were, what the signs of type 1 diabetes look like or how life-threatening DKA can be.
Mandy explains
Know the 4Ts
Toilet – going to the toilet more often, bedwetting by a previously dry child or heavier nappies in babies
Thirsty – being constantly thirsty and not being able to que

https://www.england.nhs.uk/east-of-engla.title: Get your flu vaccine now to help protect yourself and your loved ones this Christmas
https://www.england.nhs.uk/east-of-engla.source: NHS England East of England news
https://www.england.nhs.uk/east-of-engla.text:
NHS organisations across the East of England are jointly urging anyone eligible for a free flu vaccination to get it now if they have not yet had it this winter. The call comes ahead of spending time with family and friends this Christmas.
The flu vaccine can take up to two weeks to build protection. NHS Essex, NHS Central East and NHS Norfolk and Suffolk are encouraging residents to get vaccinated by Friday 11 December to give the vaccine time to work before Christmas Day.
Christmas is a time when families and friends come together, and flu can spread easily through close contact. Getting vaccinated helps reduce your risk of serious illness. Vaccinating children also helps reduce the spread of flu to family members, including those at greater risk of becoming seriously unwell.
Older people, pregnant women and people with certain long-term health conditions are particularly at risk of serious illness from flu. Getting vaccinated helps reduce that risk.
Dr Matthew Sweeting, Executive Medical Director at NHS Essex, said:  “As you make your Christmas plans, please make time for your flu vaccination too. Flu can make anyone unwell, but for some people it can lead to serious complications, a hospital stay and, in some cases, death. If you’re eligible for a free vaccine and haven’t had it yet, book an appointment now rather than leaving it until the festive rush.
“If you’re a parent or carer, please also check whether your eligible child has had their flu vaccine. If they’ve missed it, make arranging their vaccination part of your Christmas preparations.
“If you can only get an appointment after 11 December, please still take it. Flu can circulate well beyond Christmas, and vaccination can help protect you through the rest of winter.”
Dr Katherine Rowe, Deputy Clinical Director at NHS Central East, said: “Christmas brings different generations together, including older people, pregnant women and those with certain long-term health conditions, for whom flu can be particularly serious.
If you’re eligible, taking up your free flu vaccine is an important step in reducing your risk of serious illness. Vaccinating children also helps reduce the spread of flu to family members. Please make vaccination part of looking after yourself and your loved ones this Christmas.”
Lisa Nobes, Executive Director of Nursing, NHS Norfolk and Suffolk ICB, said: “If you’re eligible for a free NHS flu vaccination, a participating pharmacy can help you get protected ahead of Christmas. Some pharmacies offer walk-in vaccinations, so you may not need to book an appointment.
“Please check with your local pharmacy about availability before travelling. The chances are, there’s one near you offering the vaccination.
“It’s a busy time of year for most of us, but our health and wellbeing is worth making a bit of time for, alongside all our Christmas preparations. I want people to be able to enjoy the festive season and not be in bed, or in hospital, with flu.”
Dr Eleanor Powers, Head of Public Health Commissioning (immunisation) for NHS England – East of England, said: “Last year, around 104,000 hospitalisations were avoided through people getting their jabs and protecting themselves, their loved ones, our communities and helping the NHS prepare for winter.
“So far this season, over 2 million people in the East of England have already had their flu jab, which is great news, but there are plenty more appointments available.
“The flu jab really is your best defence against winter illness. It takes just a few minutes, but it can protect you for months, helping to prevent serious illness, avoid hospital admissions and keeping the most vulnerable people safe.
“Now is also a great time to get your 2- and 3-year-olds vaccinated; little ones can get really unwell with flu. Zip off to Zurich! London Southend Airport welcomes Swiss airline Chair Airlines with new daily Zurich route
November 16, 2026
Book holiday
Book parking
Book lounge
New daily flights to Zurich launching from 27th May 2027
The new service will strengthen connections between Switzerland and the South East, supporting both outbound travel and inbound tourism
Flights go on sale from 16th November 2026
London Southend Airport is welcoming a new airline to its growing route network, with Swiss carrier Chair Airlines set to launch daily flights between London Southend and Zurich from 27th May 2027.
Chair Airlines is a Swiss airline based at Zurich Airport, operating an all-Airbus fleet. Since launching in 2019, the airline has developed a network connecting passengers with popular holiday destinations and vibrant cities.
The new service will provide passengers across Essex, London and the wider South East with a direct connection to Switzerland’s largest city, opening up opportunities for city breaks, outdoor adventures and access to the country’s spectacular mountain and ski destinations.
It will also make it easier for Swiss visitors to discover London, Essex and the wider region, supporting inbound tourism, business travel and stronger international connections.
Sharmeen Divan, Interim CEO and Chief Financial Officer at London Southend
Airport, said:
“We’re absolutely delighted to welcome Chair Airlines to London Southend Airport and to be working together on this exciting new partnership. The addition of a daily direct route to Zurich is another important step in our continued growth, strengthening our international connections and opening up new opportunities for both leisure and business travel.
The year-round route, which launches in May, will offer passengers even more choice, whether they’re looking for a European city break, a summer escape or an opportunity to explore Switzerland.
We’re excited about what this partnership brings and look forward to welcoming Chair Airlines and its passengers to London Southend.”
Shpend Ibrahimi, CEO of Chair Airlines, said:
“We see significant potential in the Swiss market for flights to London. We are confident that, with its exceptionally efficient airport operations and seamless arrival experience, London Southend will quickly become an increasingly popular choice among Swiss travellers.”
Zurich offers visitors a wonderful mix of city experiences and natural beauty. Its charming Old Town, historic landmarks, bustling shopping streets and vibrant food scene provide plenty to explore, while Lake Zurich and the Limmat River offer a picturesque backdrop to the city. Visitors can also discover the famous Lindt Home of Chocolate or soak up the festive atmosphere at Zurich’s much-loved Christmas markets during the winter months.
Beyond the city itself, Zurich provides an excellent base for exploring more of Switzerland, from boat trips and scenic day excursions to the surrounding
countryside and mountains. For winter sports enthusiasts, popular ski destinations including Flumserberg and Hoch-Ybrig are also within reach, making Zurich an attractive gateway to the Swiss Alps.
Flights will operate daily between London Southend Airport and Zurich from 27th May 2027, with tickets going on sale from 16th November 2026.
Passengers will be able to book via https://www.chair.ch/en/
For more information on the wonderful city of Zurich visit: https://londonsouthendairport.com/

I look forward to working closely with our colleagues, airline partners and stakeholders as we continue to build on the airport’s recent successes and deliver our next phase of growth.”
The airport’s shareholding, ownership structure and strategic direction remain unchanged.
The executive team, led by Divan will continue to lead the organisation on a day-to-day basis, ensuring stability and continuity for the airport’s people, partners and customers.

London Southend has taken the top spot in the UK’s airport punctuality rankings, with new UK Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) data revealing that 84% of its flights departed within 15 minutes of schedule.

The airport team were simply not prepared to settle for third place in the UK CAA rankings. They have continued to improve our performance quarter on quarter, and that hard work has now taken us to the top of the table.
What makes this achievement even more special is that we have delivered it while continuing to be the UK’s fastest-growing airport. We’re growing quickly, but we’re doing it while keeping punctuality and the passenger experience firmly at the heart of what we do.”
London Southend is now looking ahead to a strong finish to the summer season, followed by the launch of five new routes from the end of October: Belfast City, Budapest, Edinburgh, Lyon and Sharm El Sheikh.
The airport will also extend its new summer services to Jersey and Munich into the next season, taking its winter network to 26 destinations, and 30 across the whole year.

https://mediacentre.stanstedairport.com/.title: London Stansted to conduct major emergency training exercise
https://mediacentre.stanstedairport.com/.text:
An emergency training exercise designed to test London Stansted’s response to a major aircraft accident will take place next week as part of the airport's regular preparedness programme.
The exercise will be held on Tuesday 24 November and forms part of the airport's four-year regulatory testing programme. The exercise is required under Civil Aviation Authority regulations, which require UK certificated aerodromes to undertake a full-scale aircraft accident exercise at least once every four years.
Local residents and passengers are being advised in advance of the exercise, so they are not alarmed on the day by the high number of emergency service vehicles in the area.
The scenario will simulate an aircraft accident requiring a complex, prolonged, multi-agency response and is designed to test life-saving procedures, command and control arrangements, communications, and support processes for passengers, families and stakeholders.
The exercise will take place at the airport's Compass Base facility, a remote aircraft parking stand, using a decommissioned aircraft and has been carefully planned to ensure there is no impact on flight operations or passengers using the airport. A number of emergency service vehicles and personnel will be visible in the area during the exercise.
Around 400 participants will take part, including teams from across London Stansted, alongside colleagues from Essex Police, Essex County Fire & Rescue Service, East of England Ambulance Service and Essex & Herts Air Ambulance.
Also supporting the exercise will be the British Red Cross, Uttlesford District Council, Essex County Council, the Rapid Relief Team, the Air Accident Investigation Branch, the Ministry of Housing, Communities & Local Government, Ryanair, Border Force and National Express.
Nick Millar, Operations Director at London Stansted Airport, said:
"The safety and security of our passengers, colleagues and airport community is always our highest priority.
"Although an aircraft accident is an extremely unlikely event, it remains the most significant emergency scenario we could face, which is why it is vital that we regularly test our plans, procedures and response capabilities.
"The exercise will bring together airport teams, emergency services and partner organisations from across the region, giving us the opportunity to rehearse how we would work together in a highly challenging situation and identify any opportunities to strengthen our response arrangements.
"We want to reassure passengers, local residents and businesses that this is only a training exercise and there will be no impact on the airport's day-to-day operations. However, people in the area may notice increased activity from emergency service vehicles and personnel on the day."
Essex Police Chief Inspector Julia Finch, Stansted Airport Commander , said:
"We regularly test our plans and capabilities, and this is no exception.
"Taking part in these exercises are really important to ensure we are ready for any eventuality, no matter how unlikely the scenario.
"We have a really positive working relationship with Stansted Airport and we’re grateful for this opportunity."
The exercise is designed to provide assurance that emergency plans, facilities, people and partner organisations can work effectively together under realistic conditions and operational pressures, in addition to fulfilling the airport's regulatory requirements.

https://mediacentre.stanstedairport.com/.title: East of England tops regional export growth rankings
https://mediacentre.stanstedairport.com/.text:
·       Six in ten exporters increased overseas sales in Q3 — the highest proportion among the four regions covered
·       42% entered a new overseas market, joint highest alongside London
·       US leads the region’s overseas growth markets, followed by France and Australia
The East of England recorded the highest proportion of firms growing overseas sales in the last quarter, according to the latest UK Trade Barometer.
Six in 10 exporters (60%) said they increased sales to existing overseas markets in Q3, ahead of London (59%), the Midlands (55%) and the North (53%), and above the UK-wide figure of 53%.
The region also shared the top spot for breaking into new markets - 42% of East of England exporters started trading in a new overseas territory, level with London and six percentage points above the national figure of 36%.
The Barometer — from the UK’s largest airports group and London Stansted owner, MAG, and the Growing Together Alliance of business groups — surveys more than 2,000 businesses through YouGov every quarter about their export performance over the past three months and their expectations for the quarter ahead.
The US was the leading market for the East of England on both measures. Almost one in five exporters (19%) reported growing sales to America, with the same proportion entering the US market for the first time.
France was the next most frequently cited market for increased sales, at 10%, followed by Australia (7%) and Spain (6%). Belgium, Canada, Germany, Poland, South Africa and the United Arab Emirates were each identified by 4% of the region’s exporters.
For new-market entry, France again ranked second, with 9% of exporters starting to trade there, followed by Australia at 4%.
Looking ahead, one in five businesses across the East of England (20%) expect to increase sales to an existing overseas market by the end of December 2026, while 11% expect to start trading in a new market.
Those figures are below the UK-wide averages of 24% and 16% respectively, showing that the region’s strong recent export performance is not yet matched by above-average expectations for the quarter ahead.
It comes after separate data produced for London Stansted by WPI Economics, revealed the East of England continues to go from strength to strength with international services trade in the region growing by 96% between 2016 and 2023. Growth was particularly strong beyond the EU, where services trade increased by 112%.
London Stansted’s Managing Director, Gareth Powell , said:
“Businesses succeed when they can connect easily with customers, suppliers and markets around the world. The latest MAG Trade Barometer highlights the strength of the East of England's international trading community, with 60% of exporters increasing sales in existing overseas markets during Q3 and 42% successfully entering new markets, making the region one of the UK's strongest performers.
"From established markets such as the US and France to emerging opportunities around the world, businesses depend on strong international connections to grow and compete. London Stansted's extensive route network and significant cargo operation help provide those vital links, supporting trade, investment and economic growth across the East of England."
Dan Thorp, Chief Executive at Cambridge Ahead, said:
“The latest figures highlight the strength of the East of England's business base, and the leading role it plays for the UK economy on the global stage.
“With the East of England reporting the highest increase in overseas sales alongside the top spot for breaking into new markets, it is clear that our region stands out for being internationally connected and active.
“International connectivity is a vital component of the Cambridge economy, which operates at the forefront of highly international and competitive innovation sectors, and these results show why investment into the Cambridge and East of England economy are so important for the UK in a global context"

https://mediacentre.stanstedairport.com/.text:
A business networking event set up by London Stansted to help local companies win new work is celebrating its 25th anniversary.
Meet the Buyers, which takes place this week (19 Nov) at the Radisson Blu Hotel, has spent 25 years connecting small businesses with major employers, contractors and procurement teams looking for new suppliers.
Since launching in 2001, the event has helped hundreds of firms from across Essex and the East of England showcase their products and services and compete for new contracts.
Over the past 15 years alone, the event has helped businesses across London and the East of England secure more than £37 million worth of new business opportunities.
The success of the scheme has also led to it being rolled out at Manchester and East Midlands airports, with the programme generating more than £78 million in opportunities for small and medium-sized businesses nationwide.
The event works a bit like business speed dating, giving firms a chance to meet buyers from large organisations in a series of short face-to-face meetings that can lead to contracts, partnerships and long-term commercial relationships.
This year's event will bring together businesses and buyers from sectors including construction, engineering, facilities management, logistics and professional services.
Marcella M'Rabety, Head of Social Sustainability, said:
"We're incredibly proud to be celebrating 25 years of Meet the Buyers and the impact the event has had on businesses across our region. For a quarter of a century it has helped bring local companies together with major organisations, creating valuable connections and opening doors to new opportunities.
"Over the past 15 years alone, those opportunities have translated into more than £37 million of business for companies across London and the East of England. As the airport continues to grow and invest, we want local businesses to be part of that journey and benefit from the opportunities it creates."
The event forms part of London Stansted's wider efforts to support economic growth in the region by helping local businesses find new customers, expand and create jobs.

https://mediacentre.stanstedairport.com/.title: New Bond, new adventures: Step into the world of 007
https://mediacentre.stanstedairport.com/.text:
The world’s most famous secret agent has a new face, with British actor Robert Pattinson confirmed as the next James Bond, taking over the role from Daniel Craig.
And while film fans wait to see what adventures await the new 007, there are plenty of opportunities to follow in the footsteps of his predecessors, with many of the locations made famous by the franchise just a short flight from London Stansted.
From the sun-soaked streets of Italy to the spectacular mountain scenery of Switzerland, the Bond films have showcased some of Europe’s most memorable destinations over more than six decades.
Several are easily accessible from Stansted, offering inspiration for a different kind of city break or European getaway.
The airport even has its own place in Bond history.
In Tomorrow Never Dies, Stansted doubled as Hamburg Airport, where Q introduces Bond to his gadget packed BMW, famously equipped with remote-control technology.
The scenes featuring Pierce Brosnan and Desmond Llewelyn were shot inside one of Stansted's hangars in 1997.
Among the destinations where travellers can retrace 007’s footsteps are:
Italy - From Matera’s ancient streets to Venice’s canals
Italy has provided the backdrop for some of Bond’s most memorable adventures.
The ancient city of Matera featured prominently in No Time to Die, with its spectacular Sassi cave dwellings providing the setting for the film’s opening Aston Martin DB5 chase.
Venice’s romantic waterways featured in both Casino Royale and Moonraker, while Rome’s historic streets provided the setting for the spectacular car chase in Spectre. Lake Como also featured in Casino Royale, with its elegant lakeside villas.
France - Paris and beyond
Paris featured in A View to a Kill, with its famous landmarks providing the setting for one of the franchise’s most memorable action sequences.
Nearby Château de Chantilly also doubled as the estate of villain Max Zorin.
easyJet launched its direct London Stansted to Paris service in March 2026, making the French capital another option for Bond inspired travellers.
Austria - A spectacular Alpine backdrop
Vienna played host to memorable scenes in The Living Daylights, including Bond’s encounter with Kara at the city’s famous Wiener Riesenrad, the giant Ferris wheel at Prater amusement park.
Further west, the picturesque Alpine village of Obertilliach featured in Spectre, providing the dramatic setting for Bond’s plane crash landing during a high-speed mountain pursuit.
Turkey - Istanbul’s big-screen history
Istanbul has featured in several Bond adventures, most notably From Russia With Love, which showcased the city’s historic mosques, bustling markets and waterways.
Maiden’s Tower, standing on a small island in the Bosphorus, also featured in The World Is Not Enough, serving as the hideaway of Elektra King.
Turkish Airlines launched its London Stansted to Istanbul service in March 2026, offering up to 15 flights a week.
Switzerland - Where Bond takes on the mountains
Few countries have provided a more dramatic setting for 007 than Switzerland.
The spectacular Furka Pass featured in Goldfinger, providing the backdrop for the legendary Aston Martin DB5 chase, while the Swiss Alps have featured in several other films, including On Her Majesty’s Secret Service.
Switzerland also provided the setting for one of Bond’s most spectacular stunts in GoldenEye, when Pierce Brosnan’s 007 made his debut with a 220-metre bungee jump from the Verzasca Dam.
Germany - Bond’s connection to Hamburg
Hamburg featured in Tomorrow Never Dies, with the city’s streets providing the backdrop for Bond’s mission against media tycoon Elliot Carver.
The film also has a special connection to London Stansted, where one of the airport’s hangars doubled as Hamburg Airport in the scenes where Q introduces Bond to his remote controlled BMW.
Portugal - Following Bond along the coast
