https://community360.org.uk/feed/.title: Macmillan Community Voices (MCV) Workshop – Exploring the experiences of people living with cancer in Essex – LGBTQIA+ communities
https://community360.org.uk/feed/.text:
Introduction
Our workshop was the first in a series being undertaken by the Macmillan Community Voices team who are working in partnership with Macmillan Cancer Support to explore  cancer care experiences of different groups in our communities. Our programme of workshops focus on groups that data demonstrates, face significant health inequalities.
This workshop engaged with clinical and community stakeholders involved in the care and support of members of the LGBTQIA+ community who have or are, receiving cancer care.  We worked with two key partners to build our programme for the day, Transpire (based in Southend) and The Outhouse (based in Colchester) who helped to ensure that content was as useful and accessible as possible.
We wanted to take learning from our discussions and from the lived experience of community members to explore what plans and strategies could be developed to improve those experiences. We also wanted to consider what was working well and positive steps taken so far.
Our Workshop Programme
C360 presented a creative case study involving a trans woman who had previously engaged with the project, using collages to explore one positive and one negative cancer-related experience. The stark contrast between the two collages demonstrated the significant impact that being listened to, understood, and supported can have on an individual’s wellbeing. LGBTQIA+ themes and feedback gathered throughout the MCV project, alongside wider insights identified across different cohort groups were also shared, helping attendees understand common barriers and experiences within these communities.
Attendees also heard presentations from Transpire and The Outhouse, which highlighted the healthcare inequalities faced by LGBTQIA+ community. Research shared by Transpire explored concerns around access to gender-affirming care, fears of seeking healthcare due to the instability of Shared Care Agreements, and experiences of invasive questioning and perceived bias. The Outhouse outlined its Trans+ Levelling Up programme,  which aims to strengthen healthcare professionals’ understanding of Trans+ health needs, particularly  in relation to cancer screening and early diagnosis. This initiative also includes community focused campaigns to help educate and empower individuals. Following a pilot, educational gaps were identified and a new training programme developed.
The session concluded with a powerful personal testimony from a member of the LGBTQIA+ community who shared their experience of a late testicular cancer diagnosis, reflecting on both the challenges they faced and the exceptional support they received from Macmillan Cancer Support during their treatment and recovery.
Attendee Participation Session
A key focus of the event was understanding the lived experiences of LGBTQIA+ individuals affected by cancer and the importance of inclusive, person-centred support. So, we encouraged attendees to consider what they could do as a community member to improve the cancer related experiences of the community and consider what the system wide challenges are that can be worked on together.
Our Learning
Feedback from attendees confirmed that the workshop was highly informative and impactful. Participants highlighted that much of the information shared was new to them and increased their understanding of the inequalities faced by LGBTQIA+ communities when accessing healthcare and cancer services. The discussions generated a strong appetite for further learning and identified several priority areas for future development and improvement.
Key Outcomes
Increased awareness of the health inequalities and barriers to care experienced by LGBTQIA+ communities.
Recognition of the need for additional education and training for professionals and organisations supporting LGBTQIA+ individuals.
Greater understanding of the importance of engaging with LGBTQIA+ people in a confidential, respectful, and inclusive manner.

Celebrating the Heart of C360: Our Volunteers
At Colchester C360, everything we do is powered by people – people who give their time and energy to make a real difference in their community. Our volunteers are not just an extra helping hand. They are at the very core of what makes C360 such an impactful organisation. Quite simply, we couldn’t do what we do without them.
Why Volunteers Matter at C360
Volunteering is important because it brings people together, strengthens communities and helps services expand their reach. Volunteers offer time and skills that can make a real and lasting difference, whether that is through practical support, companionship or sharing specialist knowledge. At the same time, volunteering can be hugely rewarding for the individual, helping people build confidence, develop new skills, make connections and gain a strong sense of purpose through giving back.
What Volunteering Looks Like
There is no single way to volunteer at C360 – and that’s exactly what makes it so amazing. Opportunities are varied and flexible which suits different interests and skills. From being a volunteer driver to being a trustee, researcher or community group leader – there’s something to suit everyone. Every role, big or small, plays a part in shaping the experience of those who walk through our doors.
A Place to Grow
Volunteering at C360 isn’t just about giving, it’s also about growing. Many of our volunteers develop new skills, boost their confidence, and even take steps toward employment or further education. We pride ourselves on creating a supportive environment where everyone feels valued and encouraged to develop at their own pace.
It’s Volunteers’ Week!
Volunteers’ Week is a UK-wide celebration of the contribution volunteers make to charities, community groups and local causes every day. Taking place from 1st to 7th June, it is a chance to recognise the time, energy and commitment from volunteers and the impact they have on their communities. It is a moment to say thank you, celebrate volunteer stories and encourage more people to get involved in meaningful community participation.
Throughout Volunteers’ Week, we are sharing our volunteers’ stories through interviews that celebrate why people choose to volunteer, the incredible work they have done since joining us, and the personal benefits they gain from volunteering.
We are also running a workforce-wide volunteer nomination scheme ahead of a volunteer celebration and awards ceremony later this month. Alongside this, we are promoting not only our own volunteer vacancies, but volunteering opportunities more widely, to highlight their potential to strengthen communities even further.
A Big Thank You
To all our volunteers: thank you. Your dedication, kindness, generosity, and enthusiasm are what drive C360 forward. You are valued more than words can express, and this week (and every week) we celebrate you.
If you’ve ever thought about getting involved, there’s never been a better time. We also offer participation via corporate volunteer and student placements.
If you have any queries please contact us  Volunteer@community360.org.uk .
We will be at the love Colchester event at Firstsite representing the importance of volunteering in Colchester on 5th June!

Step Into Something Meaningful at VolFEST 2026
Thursday 4 June 2026 | 9.30am–4pm | Chelmsford High Street
Chelmsford, Essex – Chelmsford CVS is delighted to announce the return of  VolFEST 2026 , the city’s much-loved celebration of community, volunteering and local charities, taking place on Thursday 4 June in the heart of Chelmsford High Street.
Now firmly established as a highlight of National Volunteers’ Week, VolFEST will once again bring together around 50 local charities, community groups and support services for a day filled with conversation, connection and community spirit.
Whether you are looking for support, hoping to meet new people, or thinking about giving volunteering a try, VolFEST is the perfect opportunity to explore what is happening locally and discover how you can get involved.
Visitors will have the chance to:
Find vital help and advice from trusted local organisations
Discover flexible volunteering roles to suit different interests, ages, skills and availability
Speak directly to charities about what volunteering is really like
Meet local people already making a difference in the community
Enjoy music, activities, demonstrations, charity items for sale and a welcoming festival atmosphere
From one-off events and practical outdoor projects to charity shop roles, befriending, fundraising, youth work, administration, community gardening and skilled volunteering, VolFEST showcases the huge variety of ways people can support causes they care about.
Meet the Charities Changing Chelmsford.
Since launching in 2019, VolFEST has grown into a major annual community event, attracting thousands of visitors and helping local organisations connect with new volunteers, supporters and service users.
This year’s event will feature a wide variety of charities and community groups, including organisations supporting health and wellbeing, young people, older residents, disability support, homelessness, community safety, animals, the environment and much more.
Well-known local organisations expected to attend include Broomfield Hospital, CHESS Homeless, Farleigh Hospice, Wilderness Foundation, and City of Chelmsford Mencap, alongside many more local groups making a huge difference behind the scenes every day.
Chelmsford CVS is grateful to Chelmsford City Council for supporting this year’s event.

https://chelmsfordcvs.org.uk/feed/.text:
Wilderness Foundation UK   are seeking an exceptional Chief Executive Officer to lead the charity into its next chapter of impact, influence, and sustainability.
This is a pivotal leadership role for a values-driven, visionary CEO who can inspire people, shape strategy, and steward the charity’s mission with integrity and ambition. You will work closely with the Board of Trustees, senior leadership team, staff, volunteers, partners, and supporters to ensure the organisation thrives operationally, financially, and culturally. The CEO is both the strategic compass and the public voice of the charity, holding the big picture while remaining deeply connected to the people and places at the heart of the charity’s work.
Job Title: Chief Executive Officer (CEO)
Location: Chelmsford, Essex (with national engagement and travel as required)
Salary: £60,000 to £70,000 per annum, depending on experience
Contract: Full-time, permanent
Key Responsibilities
Strategic Leadership & Vision
Provide inspirational leadership and a clear, compelling vision aligned with the charity’s mission and values
Develop and deliver a long-term strategy that strengthens impact, reach, and sustainability
Lead organisational growth while safeguarding programme quality and ethos
Organisational Leadership
Lead, motivate, and support a skilled and passionate staff team
Foster a healthy, inclusive, and high-performing organisational culture
Ensure robust governance, risk management, and regulatory compliance
Finance & Sustainability
Oversee financial planning, budgeting, and performance to ensure long-term viability
Drive income diversification through fundraising, partnerships, grants, and trading activity
Work closely with the Board on financial strategy and accountability
External Relations & Advocacy
Act as the principal ambassador and spokesperson for Wilderness Foundation UK
Build and maintain strong relationships with funders, partners, commissioners, and stakeholders
Represent the charity within the nature, conservation, wellbeing, and youth sectors
Programme & Impact Oversight
Ensure the delivery of high-quality, evidence-based nature and wilderness programmes
Champion innovation in nature-based education and therapy
Uphold strong monitoring, evaluation, and learning to demonstrate impact
Why Join Wilderness Foundation UK?
This is a rare opportunity to lead a respected and impactful organisation where nature is not a backdrop, but the catalyst for change. As CEO, you will shape lives, protect wild places, and guide a charity that stands at the intersection of wellbeing, education, and conservation.
If you are a leader who believes that nature can heal people and people can protect nature, Wilderness Foundation UK would love to hear from you.

https://rravs.org.uk/feed/.title: Free Online Training – Preventing Radicalisation
https://rravs.org.uk/feed/.text:
Prevent is part of the UK’s counter-terrorism strategy. It focuses on offering early support to individuals who may be vulnerable to radicalisation.  For the voluntary and community sector, Prevent is about noticing when someone might need help and connecting them with the right services before issues escalate. It is purely about safeguarding, early intervention, and support—not monitoring communities.   This training is available to all staff from Voluntary and Community Sector Organisations within the County Of Essex.
What will the training cover?
Background: An overview of CONTEST, The Prevent Duty, an understanding of Terrorism legislation and the current national picture. ·

https://cvstogether.org.uk/feed/.title: Hello from Mark
https://cvstogether.org.uk/feed/.text:
Hello CVST!
from Mark Warwick (trustee)
The background…
Having spent many years visiting Clacton and the surrounding area, my wife and I decided to move from London to this lovely part of the country. We were confident that we were making the right decision and we have not been disappointed, spending lazy days on the beach, making new friends and discovering places that we never knew existed.
We felt at home straight away having found such a strong, friendly and welcoming community offering lots of different activities which has led to our foray into line dancing, bowling, yoga and singing!
Meeting CVST
One of the first places I came across when I moved to the area in April was Kennedy Way Community Gardens. I was so taken with the garden, which is a tranquil space near the Kennedy Way Surgery in Clacton with wildflowers and vegetable patches, seating and a Men’s Shed, I applied to be a volunteer. Now I spend time in the garden volunteering with some wonderful people and have helped at open day events showcasing the amazing space.
Mark in the polytunnel at Kennedy Way Community Garden
The gardens are an inclusive space for those who want to become part of the local community. It is also a safe space to help improve physical health and benefiting mental wellbeing.
I have enjoyed immensely being part of this community project, which in turn has given me the opportunity to become a Trustee for CVST.
Becoming a trustee
Having become a volunteer at the garden I began to learn more about CVST as a charitable organisation and learned about all the other wonderful projects and work it does across the district of Tendring. I couldn’t believe CVST did so much! Walks, befriending groups, craft clubs, dementia support, training, litter picking, allotments, networking, supporting other charities and community groups and more! So when the opportunity came to join the board of trustees I was excited to get involved. Communities thrive because of organisations like CVST and I’m so pleased to be able to be part of that now and help shape the future.
What I bring to the table
As well as being a Young Carer and more recently an Adult Carer, I have also worked in the health and social care sector for over twenty years in various roles, supporting vulnerable young people and adults with a wide range of disabilities and diagnosed conditions,
I have  worked on a number of projects in collaboration with organisations such as AgeUK, Mind, the NHS and various local authorities.
Although new to the post, of a Trustee I will bring my lived experience, skills and expertise to the role to complement the excellent work that the CVST volunteers, staff, senior management team and board have done over many, many years and help ensure our charity remains completely transparent and accountable, proving to our funders, volunteers, and local community exactly what a positive impact we are making.
Looking forward
I attended the 2026 CVST AGM – my first as a trustee, and loved seeing so many staff and volunteers and members of the local community. It’s a privilege to be part of such a fantastic charity.
I look forward to seeing those of you that I have yet to meet and working alongside my fellow trustees to support CVST in continuing to make a huge difference to residents in Tendring.

https://cvstogether.org.uk/feed/.title: Celebrating Volunteer Managers
https://cvstogether.org.uk/feed/.text:
At CVST, we see every day how volunteering strengthens local organisations and brings people together. Behind every successful volunteer role is usually someone quietly making sure people feel welcomed, guided and encouraged often while juggling three conversations, a printer that has given up and a meeting that started five minutes ago.
As Volunteer Managers you are not just filling gaps on a rota. You are helping people feel at home and share what they have to offer. It is quiet, steady, important work and it makes a real difference in our communities.
For those of us who support volunteers, our role is about much more than keeping things ticking over. At its heart, volunteering is about people choosing to give a little bit of themselves to something that matters. It is the responsibility of everyone within our organisations to help make people feel that they are a welcome and useful part of the team.
Warm welcomes matter
We all know the difference a friendly face can make. A welcoming hello, a proper introduction and someone taking the time to explain things can help to turn first-day nerves into confidence. A cup of tea may not solve everything, but it is often a very good place to start!
People come through your door for all sorts of reasons. They may want to learn something new, support a cause close to their heart, or simply to meet others and feel useful again. If we take time to understand what has brought them to us, we are much more likely to help them find the right place in your organisation.
Not everyone volunteers in the same way
Some people can give a regular morning every week. Others can help now and again, from home or at an event. Or maybe they can help with that one small but very important task that somehow saves the day. What’s important is that the more flexible we can be, the more people we can include.
Volunteers usually bring far more than the role they first sign up for. They also bring with them their life experience and local knowledge, their kindness, practical skills and their ideas. Sometimes our job as Volunteer Managers is simply to spot those gifts and give people the confidence to use them.
Keeping people connected
Good volunteer management is as much about listening as leading. Checking in, saying thank you and being clear about expectations and being honest when something is not working all help build trust.
Life changes too. We know that work, health, caring responsibilities and family life can all affect how much time someone has to give. If we can keep the door open even when someone needs to step back, we show that they are valued as a person and not just for the hours they can offer our organisations.
So, to every Volunteer Manager quietly keeping things moving, thank you for all you do. You help people take that first step and get involved in their communities in ways that can change people’s lives… including their own.
Join us at our next Volunteer Managers Network at Imperial House, Rosemary Road, Clacton on 2 October at 8.30am , where we’ll be discussing how AI tools can support volunteer management by saving time and enhancing volunteer recruitment, engagement and recognition.
A great opportunity to connect with peers, share experiences and learn something new over a coffee. To book, click here for the booking page or email events@cvstogether.org.uk .

https://cvstogether.org.uk/feed/.title: Spotlight on Young Minds and how CVST helped it begin
https://cvstogether.org.uk/feed/.text:
By Karen Barber
The 10-Year Fight for Answers :
After 10 years of exemplary promotions and appraisals in the civil service, I was dismissed due to poor performance caused by a disease that took a decade to diagnose. It was a relief to finally get that diagnosis. Even though medical professionals told me it was all in my mind, I knew something was wrong.
Falling Through the Gaps :
After attending a cognitive therapy course at the Kingswood Centre in Colchester Hospital, I found there was no support out there for people of my age; I simply did not fit into the more senior groups. There is such a gap for people with young onset dementia, and it is unacceptable that we are just being forgotten. I decided to help others like myself who fell through the gaps without the support we needed.
Building a Vision with Community Partners :
I am so grateful for the community partners who understood the need. The Stroke and Wellness Foundation for hiring us a hall, and Sports for Confidence who designed our logo and poster when we had no funds. To CVST who when I contacted them believed in the project, my vision, p assion, and ambition, they are a true example of how a voluntary service should work by helping with advice, policies, and providing my excellent volunteers, who have worked tirelessly and with all this support we have made it a success. Together, we opened the Young Minds Dementia Group and secured grants from Grassroots, the Tudwick Foundation, and the Essex Foundation.
Speaking Out in Parliament and the Media :
Our group is steadily growing. I am speaking out not for myself, but for everyone out there who does not have a voice. I’ve raised awareness on ITV Anglia, in Alzheimer’s Magazine, and an upcoming Daily Mail article. In May, I was invited to speak in Parliament, where I made our message clear:
Dementia needs to be a medical condition not a social care issue… We will not be silenced, we are valued members of society, yet for far too long we have been forgotten. We are the nation’s untapped capital, not a burden to be managed.”
My Vision for the Future : It shouldn’t be on people like me to establish these groups to make our own support. Unless action is taken, the vacuum of care will only deepen into a social catastrophe. My vision is to get charity status and funding to see Young Minds Dementia Groups across Essex, rectifying this inequality so that we are finally seen, supported, and valued. I couldn’t do this without the support of my excellent volunteers and community support of CVST and so many organisations in Tendring. I thank you all for believing in my vision and for not letting those with young onset dementia be forgotten

https://cvstogether.org.uk/feed/.title: Volunteering Looks Like This
https://cvstogether.org.uk/feed/.text:
Volunteers Week 2026: Volunteering Looks Like This
Volunteers Week is the time we pause, reflect and, most importantly, say a heartfelt thank you to all the people who give their time, skills and energy to support others across our community.
At CVST, we see every day the difference volunteers make – whether that is volunteering for us or for the many brilliant organisations across Tendring. From supporting weekly friendship groups, to helping teach others new skills, to bringing ideas, kindness and practical help where it’s needed most – volunteering is at the heart of a stronger, more connected Tendring.
‘Volunteering Looks Like This’
This year, our Volunteers Week campaign is called Volunteering Looks Like This , and it’s all about showing the true diversity of volunteering.
Volunteering doesn’t look just one way.
It looks like:
A volunteer trustee helping guide a local organisation
Someone giving a few hours a month to support a community group
A volunteer befriender offering time and compassion
People sharing professional skills, lived experience or simply a willingness to help
Individuals of all ages, backgrounds and abilities making a difference in their own way
Through our campaign, we’re celebrating real volunteers and real stories – highlighting that every contribution matters , whether it’s a little time or a long-term commitment.
Saying Thank You
To everyone who volunteers – whether through a charity, community group, or informally in your neighbourhood – thank you . Your generosity helps organisations survive and thrive, supports vulnerable people, and builds communities where people care for one another.
We’d also like to thank the organisations who support volunteers, create welcoming opportunities, and recognise the value of volunteering in all its forms.
Why Volunteering Matters
Volunteering matters because it changes lives.
For local charities and community groups, volunteers are often the difference between a service existing or not. They bring time, skills, passion and local knowledge that help organisations respond to real needs in their communities.
For individuals, volunteering can reduce loneliness, improve wellbeing, build confidence and open doors to new skills and opportunities. It allows people to connect and play an active role in shaping the place where they live.
And for communities, volunteering builds resilience and connection. It brings people together across generations and backgrounds, strengthens local networks, and helps ensure that support is there when it’s needed most.
That’s why at CVST, we believe volunteering isn’t just about giving time — it’s about creating stronger, kinder and more inclusive communities .
Get Involved
If you’re interested in volunteering, or if your organisation needs volunteers, CVST is here to help. We can support you to find opportunities, promote roles, and strengthen volunteering across the district.
Look at volunteering opportunities at
This Volunteers’ Week, let’s celebrate the people who make a difference — and show that volunteering really does look like this .

https://cvstogether.org.uk/feed/.title: We provide the “hidden wiring” connecting Tendring
https://cvstogether.org.uk/feed/.text:
Behind the people, the services, and the organisations in Tendring sits a layer of support that often goes unseen, the “hidden wiring” that keeps everything connected and working smoothly.
That hidden wiring is exactly the role CVST plays. Across Tendring, we work to bring people and organisations together. We help local groups navigate challenges and build their capacity to grow in ways that make them more sustainable. We advocate for the voluntary sector so that the voices of smaller and marginalised organisations are heard in the rooms where decisions are made. We help create the conditions where volunteering gives local people meaningful ways to contribute to the place they call home.
For our partners, this means having a trusted bridge into the community; an organisation that understands the local landscape and can convene the right people to help shape solutions that reflect real lived experience. For local groups, it means having someone in your corner offering the practical support that hopefully will help you to thrive rather than just survive.
.
Report highlights what makes good infrastructure
The National Association for Voluntary and Community Action’s (NAVCA) latest report on what good local infrastructure looks like really connects with CVST’s work as it talks about something that we see every day in Tendring… that when people have places to connect and services that genuinely understand their needs, the whole community becomes more healthy and confident.
https://www.navca.org.uk/news/what-does-good-local-vcse-infrastructure-look-like
What this NAVCA report highlights is that good infrastructure isn’t about a particular structure or model, it’s about relationships and collaboration. That’s why at CVST we invest so much time in listening to local groups and building strong partnerships with partners and funders. When those relationships are strong, it feels like everything else is more possible.
We run a number of different opportunities for groups and organisations to come together to share their skills, knowledge and experiences. For more information look around this website or email events@cvstogether.org.uk. If you’re a local partner, funder or voluntary sector organisations or community group who wants to work together to strengthen our area, we’re always ready for a conversation!
The NAVCA report makes a powerful point. When local infrastructure is recognised and properly resourced, the whole system benefits. Public services become more effective, voluntary and community organisations and groups become stronger, and local people feel more connected and able to take part in their communities. Who doesn’t want to be a part of that?

https://cvstogether.org.uk/feed/.title: Proud to be a Trustee
https://cvstogether.org.uk/feed/.text:
What a journey I have had over the last two years. I have always ensured I have given something back to the community I live in and have had several different volunteering roles in the past including being a chair of governors for a primary school and an Ambulance Community First Responder.
My journey into trusteeship began at the CVST AGM in September 2023. A presentation was given about trusteeship and an offer from CVST’s Yvette Wetton to provide more of an insight into what being a trustee entails and to support me in finding an organisation that my skills would align with. Following a very fruitful conversation with Yvette, I went away with a renewed passion and very soon after I applied to be a trustee at the Youth Enquiry Service. Following a successful interview and completing the mandatory Trustee training provided by the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales (ICAEW) I formally became a trustee in April 2024.
I have found my first 18 months as a trustee very rewarding, working alongside my fellow trustees undertaking a skills audit and enabling each of us to be aligned to a head of section depending on our skills and background. This has been a very supportive way to enable a collaborative approach to the challenges around funding and working differently in this uncertain time across the sector. Being there to support the CEO, offering advice and support and understanding more about the service offerings has provided me with a sense of pride in being part of an amazing organisation which supports one of our most vulnerable cohorts across North East Essex, our young people.
The time commitment as a trustee is flexible, you can give as much or as little as you are able as long as you manage your statutory duties in reviewing board meeting documents such as budget papers, heads of service reports and provide constructive feedback as part of the regular board meetings, which are held bi monthly with an option of face to face and MS teams.
If you ever want to get more involved with a ‘special community voluntary sector faith enterprise group’ in your area please do so – we all have transferable skills that could make a real difference and a greater impact than you could imagine to many people in your community.

https://cvstogether.org.uk/feed/.title: Why I became a trustee – and why you should too by Ali Blake
https://cvstogether.org.uk/feed/.text:
Why I, Alistair Blake, became a Trustee (And why you should consider it too)
Eight years ago, I became a trustee, despite concerns I wasn’t qualified enough or have enough time. Today I chair the board.
How and why, I became a Trustee
My journey with Summit Services began in 2008. Having just finished a multimedia degree and struggling to find work the media sector, I took a receptionist position at what was then called ‘The Advocacy Service’ in Clacton, where I grew up. I didn’t know what advocacy was or have any understanding of mental health services. But I quickly fell in love with the work – largely driven by amazing mentors, the passion of the staff and witnessing first-hand the impact on people’s lives.
Over the next few years, I trained as an advocate and also used my skills in unexpected ways from developing interactive and accessible materials to running music groups and sports teams.
But I still dreamed of working in media, and in late 2011, an opportunity to work for a television company came up which I couldn’t refuse. So, I moved to London and spent the next few years doing exactly what I’d always planned.
Yet something was missing. And as I became more aware of my own mental health, I reflected on how critical Summit’s work was.
That’s when I thought about trusteeship. Despite concerns about what I could offer and whether I’d have enough time, I got in contact, went through the interview process, and was appointed to the board.
What does being a Trustee actually involve?
We meet formally every 6 weeks, with occasional sub-committee work between. Some months it’s just a few hours; others require more time when we’re navigating challenges or establishing new initiatives. But it’s manageable alongside full-time work and family.
As Trustees, we provide governance and strategic direction, ensure financial sustainability, and support the CEO and staff team. It’s not about doing day-to-day work; our excellent staff do that. It’s about acting in the best interest of our beneficiaries and ensuring the organisation can continue its mission effectively.
What Have I Learned?
In eight years as a trustee, now as Chair, I’ve seen enormous change. Leadership transitions, funding and service evolution, staff and trustees moving on. What hasn’t changed is our mission: Advocating Empowerment. Supporting Independence.
Clacton has the second-highest mental health need in the country and seven areas in Tendring are among the most deprived 10% in England. While the statistics are eye-opening, behind every statistic is a person – someone struggling to access support, someone feeling isolated, or someone simply trying to live a fulfilled and independent life. Which is why this work really matters.
What surprised me most about trusteeship is how much my perspective counts. My media and business experience has practical value, but the real contribution is diverse thinking. The board needs people who aren’t necessarily mental health professionals, people who ask different questions and represent the community we serve.
I still don’t feel I give enough time. I still sometimes question what I offer. But I’ve learned that’s okay and what really matters is showing up, having a voice, and bringing genuine commitment.
What do I get out of it?
There’s the satisfaction of contributing to meaningful work, staying connected to advocacy while pursuing my corporate career. But I’ve also developed skills in governance, strategic thinking, and leadership that I would not have gained otherwise. I’ve been part of decisions that genuinely changed outcomes for people in our community.
Why you should consider it
Tendring’s voluntary organisations need trustees. Not just people with medical, legal or financial backgrounds, but people with all kinds of experiences: project management, HR, marketing, IT, lived experience, or simply a passion for the cause and willingness to learn.
If you’re thinking you aren’t qualified or don’t have time – I thought the same.

https://cvstogether.org.uk/feed/.title: Would you like a Safeguarding top-up at our next Trustee Forum?
https://cvstogether.org.uk/feed/.text:
If something went wrong in your organisation tomorrow… could you honestly say you’d done everything possible to keep people safe?
For small voluntary and community organisations, it can be easy to assume that safeguarding is “someone else’s job” or only relevant in certain settings. But as a Trustee, you hold ultimate responsibility for ensuring your organisation protects the people it serves, especially those who are vulnerable.
That means more than simply having a safeguarding policy in place. As a Trustee you need to ensure procedures are not just clear and accessible, but also actively followed, from recruitment checks to reporting concerns. It also means creating a culture where people feel safe to speak up, and where safeguarding is embedded in every activity.
Laws, best practice, and risks evolve over time and Trustees have a duty to stay informed, seek training, and regularly review your organisations safeguarding arrangements. Neglecting this could expose your organisation to serious harm both to the individuals you serve and to your reputation and sustainability.
At CVST we want to support Trustees to be able to fulfil their safeguarding obligations. At our next Trustee Forum on the 4th September at 6pm we will be welcoming Alison Clark who is the Head of Safeguarding in Adult Social Care at Essex County Council to talk about the role of  Trustees in making their organisation’s operations safer and provide information about where to go and what to do if you have concerns.
To register to attend – please contact CVST at events@cvstogether.org.uk

https://thurrockcvs.org/feed/.title: Bringing Thurrock’s Voluntary Sector Together
https://thurrockcvs.org/feed/.text:
One of the ways Thurrock CVS supports local communities is by bringing voluntary and community organisations together to share ideas, build connections and strengthen the support available to residents across the borough.
On Tuesday 30 June, we hosted our latest quarterly Sector Networking Brunch, welcoming representatives from voluntary and community organisations across Thurrock. The event provided an opportunity for local groups to discuss the projects they’ve been working on, share news about upcoming activities, and explore ways to work together to better support local people.
After an informal networking session, attendees took part in smaller group discussions, giving organisations the chance to have more meaningful conversations, exchange knowledge and identify opportunities for future collaboration. Events like these help organisations learn from one another, avoid duplication, and develop partnerships that ultimately benefit Thurrock’s communities.
It was fantastic to see so many organisations coming together with a shared commitment to making a positive difference across the borough. Thank you to everyone who attended and contributed to such a valuable morning — we’re already looking forward to our next networking event.

https://thurrockcvs.org/feed/.title: TACC Visits Inspire Future Volunteers
https://thurrockcvs.org/feed/.text:
Over the past few weeks, Thurrock Volunteer Centre has been delighted to visit Thurrock Adult Community College (TACC) at the Old Courthouse on several occasions, connecting with learners and showcasing the many opportunities volunteering can offer.
The first visit saw Thurrock Volunteer Coordinator, Eden, join a SEND learners’ class as a guest speaker. The session introduced the work of Thurrock Volunteer Centre, explained how the service supports local volunteers, and highlighted the resources available at The Beehive Centre. Learners also had the chance to ask questions about volunteering, explore the benefits it can bring, and discuss any barriers they might face.
Eden later returned to support the same group as they registered with Thurrock Volunteer Centre. The session helped learners understand the registration process, complete their applications with confidence, and learn what to expect as they begin their volunteering journey.
Reflecting on the experience, Eden said: “What a truly wonderful group of people – it was an absolute pleasure! I’m astounded by their desire to give back and their eagerness to learn. They should all be so proud of themselves!”
Most recently, Thurrock Volunteer Centre attended TACC’s Careers and Volunteering Marketplace event. Throughout the day, Eden welcomed learners from across the college to the Volunteer Centre stand, enjoyed inspiring conversations about the impact of volunteering, and met many people keen to find out how they can get involved in supporting their local community.
If you’d like to find out more about volunteering or explore opportunities that match your interests and skills, we’d love to hear from you. Contact volunteercentre@thurrockcvs.org to start your volunteering journey.

https://www.havenshospices.org.uk/latest.title: Local Swimmers Cross the English Channel and Raise Over £9,000 for Havens Hospices
https://www.havenshospices.org.uk/latest.text:
A group of five friends from Burnham-on-Crouch challenged themselves by embarking on an open water relay swim across the English Channel in aid of a local hospice charity.
James Cliff, Andrew Bell, Madeline Raymond, Clare Boston and Stuart Sargeant, also known as the Burnham Gang, finished their relay in 10 hours and 50 minutes whilst fundraising for Havens Hospices. So far, they have raised over £9,000 to support the charity in providing expert, compassionate care to local children and adults of all ages living with incurable conditions.
The route is around 21 miles long across one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes, with powerful tidal movements, strong currents and cold water at temperatures of around 18°C.
The group made the decision to take on this challenge after visiting Fair Havens and Little Havens, the charity’s hospices for adults and children, and learning about the care they provide to families within the local community.
James, who also fundraised for the charity in 2023 by swimming across the English Channel solo, said, “We are keen open water swimmers and after seeing the incredible work of hospices firsthand by visiting Havens Hospices, we decided to fundraise by setting a hard challenge that would also stay with us as an amazing group memory.
“Standout memories were certainly made. Seasickness, jellyfish stings, swimming in the dark and narrowly avoiding big tankers! We swam on the night of the Harvest Moon and as we got to Cap Gris-Nez, it shone out at us just by the famous lighthouse.
“We’re all so pleased to have completed this challenge and knowing it was making a real difference to families helped get us through the tough moments.
“To all first-time fundraisers, it’s never too early to start fundraising ahead of your challenge. Don’t be afraid to keep asking and be inventive.”
Lucy Lock, Community Engagement Manager at Havens Hospices, said, “We want to say a huge thank you to the Burnham Gang. Swimming the English Channel through the night, with jellyfish, seasickness and tankers to contend with, is an incredible achievement, and we’re so grateful they chose to do it in aid of Havens Hospices.
“All of our care and support is provided absolutely free of charge, and we rely on the generosity of our community to make that possible. The money the Burnham Gang have raised goes towards expert, compassionate care for local families, whether that’s in our hospices, in the comfort of their own homes or out in the community, making every day count for the people who need us.”
The Burnham Gang are now calling on the local community to support them in their quest to continue raising vital funds for Havens Hospices by making a donation to their JustGiving page. The charity must raise more than £225,000 a week to be there for everyone who needs them, so every donation, no matter how small, will make a difference in supporting the hospice charity.
You can support the Burnham Gang’s fundraising efforts by donating to their JustGiving page: https://www.justgiving.com/page/burnhamrelay
The post Local Swimmers Cross the English Channel and Raise Over £9,000 for Havens Hospices appeared first on Havens Hospices .

https://www.havenshospices.org.uk/latest.title: Havens Hospices launches school Santa Run campaign
https://www.havenshospices.org.uk/latest.text:
Havens Hospices is calling on local schools to organise a Santa Run, encouraging pupils to don their best festive outfits and run, walk or skip to raise funds for its expert, compassionate care.
The Essex charity has launched its Santa Run campaign, asking schools to become festive fundraisers by picking a date in December, running a route of their choice and setting up a JustGiving page to raise sponsorship.
Participation is free, and each school will receive a downloadable fundraising pack when they sign up. Resources include a poster template, an assembly video explaining Havens Hospices’ care, a certificate for those taking part, and a letter to parents and carers explaining how schools’ support makes a difference.
The charity encourages pupils and teachers to get in the Christmas spirit by wearing Santa hats, Christmas jumpers, or festive fancy dress. To make the campaign sustainable and low-cost, Havens Hospices suggests using what pupils already have at home.
By taking part, schools can help Little Havens Hospice support more children like Teddy to make every day of their lives count.
Teddy was diagnosed with Dravet syndrome at four years old, and Little Havens has supported his family ever since.
Jasmine, Teddy’s mum, says, “Little Havens provides a safe space where all of Teddy’s needs are met. If we didn’t have Little Havens, our lives would be very difficult.”
Havens Hospices must raise more than £225,000 each week to support families like Teddy’s.
£31 could pay for an hour of expert care at Little Havens, providing care during a respite break, emergency stay or support at the end of a child’s/ or young person’s life.
£50 could provide a session of complementary therapy for someone we care for, helping them to relax, ease anxiety and even reduce pain caused by their condition.
£160 could provide a pool session at Little Havens with two of our Care Team, or a family swim session. Children can feel weightless and move more freely, while lights, floats, and bubbles offer rich sensory experiences, helping reduce stress and relax tense muscles.
Schools can find out more or sign up to the Santa Run campaign here: havenshospices.org.uk/christmas/santa-run

https://www.havenshospices.org.uk/latest.title: Children’s Artwork Helps Bereaved Families Keep Connected at Little Havens
https://www.havenshospices.org.uk/latest.text:
Children supported by Havens Hospices are sharing their feelings about grief through art this Children’s Grief Awareness Week (16–22 November 2026), as the charity shines a light on how it helps bereaved children and young people stay connected to the people they love.
This year’s theme is #KeepingConnected, which focuses on helping bereaved children and young people feel connected to their friends, family, memories and grief traditions. The week is coordinated by the Childhood Bereavement Network. Continuing bonds and keeping connected recognise that grief is ongoing for adults, children, and young people.
To mark the week, Little Havens is displaying ‘My Invisible Backpack – What’s In Yours?’, a collection of artwork created by children supported by Havens Hospices’ children and young people’s wellbeing team. The pieces explore the hidden feelings children carry when someone important has died, or when they’re living with an incurable condition.
First shown at the Leigh Art Trail in July, the exhibition was on display last week in the Bistro at Fair Havens for visitors and colleagues, and is now on display at Little Havens until Friday 20 November for the children and families we care for.
When someone important dies, children can feel cut off, both from the person who died and from the people around them. Havens Hospices’ children and young people’s wellbeing team supports children and young people known to Little Havens and Fair Havens, before and after a death, including children whose loved one is being cared for at either hospice.
The team helps children stay connected to the person who died through one-to-one counselling, therapeutic play and creative work such as memory boxes, hand casts and family trees. Meeting others who understand matters too. Headspace, a group for 5 to 11-year-olds, and Griefside, workshops for young people aged 11 and over, bring bereaved children together so they feel less alone, while parents and carers get support to keep those conversations going at home. The charity also runs Horizons, a group for parents and carers whose child has died.
Jane Fieldson, Babies, Children and Young People (BCYP) Wellbeing Service Lead, said, “When someone important dies, children and young people’s lives turn upside down overnight – what they knew to be safe and secure has now gone. Children can often feel very alone, even when they’re surrounded by people who love them. A big part of what we do is helping them stay connected, both to the person who died and to other children who understand what they’re going through.”
“The artwork in ‘My Invisible Backpack’ shows just how much children carry with them, and how creativity can help them share feelings that are hard to put into words.”
Jane’s advice for parents, carers and friends supporting a grieving child is to be honest and use clear words like ‘died’ and ‘dying’, as phrases such as ‘went to sleep’ can confuse children. Keeping routines such as school, mealtimes and bedtimes the same helps them feel secure, and it’s natural for children to ask the same questions again and again as they make sense of what’s happened.
She added: “Let children know that all their feelings are okay and that what happened isn’t their fault. Play, art and talking can all help them express how they feel, and involving them in remembering the person, like making a memory box together, helps them stay connected.”
To find out more about the wellbeing support Havens Hospices offers to the children and families it cares for, visit  havenshospices.org.uk/wellbeing-care .
Published 18 November 2026.
The post Children’s Artwork Helps Bereaved Families Keep Connected at Little Havens appeared first on Havens Hospices .

https://www.havenshospices.org.uk/latest.title: Local business partners raise over £150,000 for children’s hospice care
https://www.havenshospices.org.uk/latest.text:
Neil Cohen, Stephen Lewis and Michael Lewis first began supporting Little Havens in 2008, both personally and through their original business, The Underfloor Heating Store. They then continued their commitment to the charity through their next venture, Fastwarm, the UK’s number one supplier of underfloor heating products.
Since being established six years ago in 2020, Fastwarm and its team have continued this longstanding support of Little Havens through a variety of fundraising activities and initiatives. These have included sponsoring the charity’s much-loved Race4Business event in Chelmsford, organising seasonal fundraising initiatives such as Christmas jumper days, and donating 10p from every online order, a scheme that has raised more than £3,000 in just over a year. Neil Cohen has also personally supported the charity by running the London Marathon.
Most recently, Neil, Stephen and Michael have further strengthened their commitment by joining the Havens Hospices Corporate Membership programme. The programme brings together a network of local businesses working collaboratively to make a lasting difference to hospice care in the community.
Joining at Platinum level, each has pledged £300 per month, together totalling an incredible £10,800 annually. This generous commitment will provide vital, sustainable support, helping Little Havens continue delivering its much-needed expert care to local children and their families.
Neil Cohen, Chief Executive Officer at Fastwarm, said: “We’ve collectively supported Little Havens for 18 years, both personally and through our businesses, and we’re proud to continue that support today through Fastwarm. As a local business, we feel it’s important to give back to our community. Supporting Little Havens means helping local children and their families receive expert care and we’re proud to play a small part in the wonderful work they do.”
Little Havens, based in Thundersley, provides free, expert care to babies, children and young people living with incurable conditions across Essex. As a charity, it relies on the generosity of its local community and supporters like Neil, Michael and Steve to continue delivering its vital services to children and their families.
Steve Yeung, Fundraising Officer at Havens Hospices, said: “We can’t thank Neil, Steve and Michael enough for all their support over the past 18 years. Their continued generosity and commitment to Little Havens has made a real difference, helping us provide vital care and support to children with complex and incurable conditions, and their families.
“It’s fantastic to see their support continue to grow, and their decision to join our Corporate Membership programme is another wonderful example of their commitment to making a difference locally. We’re incredibly grateful to have them alongside us.”
To find out more about Havens Hospices and how more companies can support the charity, visit www.havenshospices.org.uk/corporate

https://www.havenshospices.org.uk/latest.title: Hospice calls on community to help them say “Yes!” this Christmas
https://www.havenshospices.org.uk/latest.text:
Havens Hospices is calling on people, schools and businesses across Essex to help its nurses make Christmas wishes come true for people living with incurable conditions.
This Christmas, hundreds of people with incurable conditions, and their families, will turn to Fair Havens or Little Havens Children’s Hospice, part of Havens Hospices, for care and support. For many, it will be their last Christmas – and that’s why the Essex charity is asking the community to help it say “Yes!” to every one of them.
The idea behind its Big Yes! appeal is simple: the hospice’s nurses can only say “Yes!” to the people they care for if the community says “Yes!” to Havens Hospices.
For Fair Havens nurse Ali, her reason for working at the charity is personal. “Before I joined Fair Havens, I had always been inspired by palliative care,” she said. “But it was when my mum was supported by her local hospice that I truly understood the difference hospice care can make. Seeing how well she was cared for, how comfortable she was, and how much support was given to our family inspired me to work in hospice care myself.”
Ali says Christmas holds a special place at the hospice. She said “Christmas can be a particularly special time at Fair Havens. As well as sad times, there are lots of happy times – like the time we had reindeer visit us at the hospice. Seeing the happiness on someone’s face; it reminds me why I started working at Fair Havens.”
These moments show what hospice care is really about. It isn’t only care at the end of life; it’s about quality of life, with comfort, choice and dignity, and making every day count for people and the families around them. This Christmas, Havens Hospices wants to say “Yes!” every time someone has a special request, and that depends on the generosity of local people.
Just £31 could pay for one hour of specialist nursing care for someone over Christmas, where the Care Team can say “Yes!” to moments that really matter. Every donation helps support children and adults living with complex or incurable conditions, at Christmas and all year round.
You can give a Christmas gift to the appeal at www.havenshospices.org.uk/christmas . This year, Havens Hospices is also asking schools, companies and groups across Essex to get behind it.
Businesses and companies: From festive jumper days and office bake-offs to donation matching or rounding up sales for charity, there are lots of ways your team and customers can make a real difference this Christmas.
Schools, groups and clubs: Dress-up days, bake sales, sponsored singalongs and craft fairs are all fun, festive ways to get involved.
To find out more or to give a gift, visit www.havenshospices.org.uk/christmas or call 01702 220 305. Your support this Christmas will help Havens Hospices say “Yes!” to someone who needs them over the holidays.
Published 16th November 2026

https://www.havenshospices.org.uk/latest.title: Tee-rrific Fundraising as Sandon Golf Society raises £20,000 for Little Havens at its 20th Golf Day
https://www.havenshospices.org.uk/latest.text:
Sandon Golf Society has marked its 20th Golf Day in aid of Little Havens by raising £20,000 for the second year in a row, matching last year’s record-breaking total.
The event took place on 7 August at Braintree Golf Club, where golfers came together for a day of friendly competition. Their generosity means the society has now raised more than £212,000 for Essex’s only children’s hospice over the past two decades.
The funds were raised at the sell-out event through entry fees, a lively auction, a raffle and on-the-spot ‘Fun Fines’.
Members of the Sandon Golf Society recently visited Little Havens, the children’s hospice based in Benfleet, to see firsthand the difference their incredible fundraising has made over the years. They met the team and saw for themselves the care their fundraising supports, from the hospice’s welcoming rooms to its gardens.
The £20,000 raised by the society is enough to fund nearly 650 hours of expert, compassionate care at Little Havens -providing care during a respite break, emergency stay or support at the end of a child’s life
Last year’s Golf Day was held in memory of founding member Gary Carlile, who died in November 2023, and this year the Society were proud to carry his commitment forward again.
Ella Huber-Brown, Head of Fundraising & Marketing at Havens Hospices, the charity which Little Havens is part of, said: “It was wonderful to welcome members of Sandon Golf Society to Little Havens and show them the difference their support makes. Reaching 20 Golf Days is an amazing milestone, and to raise £20,000 for the second-year running is a real testament to everyone who plays, organises and gives so generously.
“Over two decades, the society has raised more than £212,000 for Little Havens. Their support goes towards the care we give babies, children and young people with incurable conditions and their families, helping them to make every day count. We’re so grateful to every golfer for standing by us for so long, and we can’t wait to see what the next 20 years bring.”
Little Havens cares for babies, children and young people with incurable conditions across Essex, and supports their families too. The team helps every family make every day count, with comfort, choice and dignity throughout life’s journey.
Little Havens needs to raise £83,000 every week to care for every family who needs it. If your club, school or community group would like to fundraise for Little Havens, the team would love to hear from you. Visit www.havenshospices.org.uk/fundraising to find out more.

https://www.havenshospices.org.uk/latest.title: Havens Hospices invites community to remember loved ones with special robin decorations
https://www.havenshospices.org.uk/latest.text:
Havens Hospices is inviting the local community to remember loved ones this winter by dedicating a robin decoration in their memory.
The charity has launched its Robins of Remembrance appeal for the third year, following the success of last year when 1,000 beautiful robin decorations adorned Christmas trees outside the hospices throughout December.
For £18, supporters will receive a limited-edition robin decoration to hang on their tree at home, while a matching robin will be displayed on Christmas trees at either Fair Havens in Prittlewell or Little Havens in Thundersley throughout December and into early January.
Each robin hung on the hospice trees will be dedicated to a loved one, creating a beautiful display celebrating the lives of those who are missed. The trees will be on display outside Little Havens and Fair Havens from 1 st December to 3 rd   January for everyone to see.
All proceeds from the appeal will help fund expert, compassionate care and support for people of all ages living with incurable conditions across Essex. Robins are often seen as a sign that loved ones are near, making them the perfect symbol for this time of year. These robins are more than just a decoration – they are a small act with a huge impact.
Karen Summers, Individual Giving Fundraising Manager at Havens Hospices, said: “We were overwhelmed by the community’s response to Robins of Remembrance last year, with over 1,000 dedications adorning our trees. This appeal offers families a meaningful way to honour their loved ones while supporting the specialist care we provide.
“As they fly into their third year, our beautiful traditional robin decorations are collectively displayed on our hospice Christmas trees, each one representing a life remembered and a love never forgotten. Your matching robin decoration to be placed on your tree at home, or anywhere else that brings a sense of comfort and peace, is a unique way to honour the memory of someone special to you.

Havens Hospices invites the community to ‘Light up a Life’ this Christmas in memory of their loved ones.
‘Light up a Life’, kindly supported this year by S. Stibbards & Sons, gives supporters the opportunity to honour those special to them by dedicating a light on the hospices’ Christmas trees in their memory. Those taking part will also receive a special keepsake card remembering those no longer with us, and a tag for supporters to hang on their own tree at home.

One of those dedicating a light to celebrate the lives of loved ones is Vicki George. Having previously lived in Southend-on-Sea with her husband Tony, Vicki dedicates a light in his memory every year. This annual Christmas tradition began around thirty years ago when Tony and Vicki became supporters of Havens Hospices by dedicating a light in memory of their parents, Nelly and Albert George, and Connie and Sydney Deane. Vicki visits Southend Crematorium every year before Christmas and loves to see their names in the Books of Remembrance.
Vicki has continued their tradition since and says, “Although my family never used Havens Hospices’ services, Tony and I always felt it was a worthwhile cause. I have a strong connection with Southend after visiting my grandparents in Westcliff during the summer holidays at school. My father grew up here, and Tony and I lived here together before retirement, so I continue to support Havens Hospices even after moving away.”
When speaking about ‘Light up a Life’, Vicki added, “I take part because it makes me feel like my loved ones are being remembered. ‘Light up a Life’ is a reminder that they are not forgotten, and when taking part, it feels as though you and those special to you are helping another family receive the care they need.”
Every dedication will help raise vital funds so Havens Hospices can support every child, young person, and adult needing their expert, compassionate care.

https://www.businesswire-essex.co.uk/fee.title: Retail sales rise, but uneven recovery continues to challenge high street businesses
https://www.businesswire-essex.co.uk/fee.text:
“One strong month isn’t a recovery”: the leading accountancy firm Price Bailey urges retailers to look beyond turnover ahead of the crucial Christmas trading period.
The latest retail sales figures, released by the Office for National Statistics (ONS) today, offer some encouragement for the retail sector, with total sales volumes increasing by 0.7% in October, outperforming economists’ expectations. Sales volumes also rose by 2.3% compared with October of last year.
However, accountancy firm Price Bailey says the headline figures mask a more uneven picture across the sector, with some retailers continuing to face challenging trading conditions despite the overall improvement.
Some of October’s growth appears to have been driven by increased supermarket purchases of long-life goods, including tinned food and UHT milk, following the Government’s Be Ready campaign. Food store sales volumes increased by 0.8% over the month.
Meanwhile, performance across non-food retail remains mixed. Although other non-food retailers recorded a 3.1% increase in sales volumes, department stores saw a 1.2% decline and household goods retailers experienced a 1% fall.
The figures also highlight the continued importance of online retail, with online sales values increasing by 9.7% year-on-year in October. Online spending now accounts for 29.2% of total retail sales, reinforcing the importance of digital channels as consumer shopping habits continue to evolve.
Stella Athanasiadou , Audit Partner and Retail sector specialist at Price Bailey, comments: “While the increase in retail sales is encouraging, it’s important not to mistake one month’s growth for a sustained recovery. The figures demonstrate just how varied trading conditions remain across the sector, with some retailers performing well while others continue to face considerable pressure.
“Online retail continues to grow, presenting both opportunities and challenges for traditional high street businesses. Retailers are having to think carefully about how they balance the costs of physical premises with the investment required to compete online, while ensuring that growth across different channels is translating into sustainable profits.
“As we approach the Christmas trading period, retailers should be looking beyond turnover and paying close attention to their cash flow, stock levels and profit margins. Understanding which products and sales channels are delivering the strongest returns, managing overheads and planning for different trading scenarios can all help businesses navigate uncertainty.
“Ultimately, those retailers that maintain strong financial discipline and understand their numbers will be better placed to withstand challenging conditions and take advantage of opportunities as they arise.”

https://www.businesswire-essex.co.uk/fee.title: NEETS review ‘a missed opportunity’
https://www.businesswire-essex.co.uk/fee.text:
“A missed opportunity. Milburn’s review shows a fundamental lack of understanding of how jobs are created and how emplo yers decide to invest in talent.  Minimum wage rates, employment taxes, workers’ rights and welfare handouts are the root cause of youth unemployment.  Tinkering with employment programmes and promising subsidy-driven non-jobs won’t change this.”
This is the somewhat damming verdict offered by Chris Hodson, Programme Director at Pitman Training in Essex on a major review by former minister Alan Milburn which has proposed widespread changes to help get young people who are not in education, employment or training (Neet) into work across the UK.
Alan Milburn’s review calls for a fundamental overhaul of how Britain supports young people who are not in education, employment or training (NEET). Nearly one million young people aged 16–24 are currently in this position, around one in eight, and the report warns that the figure could rise significantly if no action is taken. Its ambition is to reduce the NEET rate to around 5% over the next decade.
Milburn argues that the problem is not simply a lack of motivation among young people, but a failure of the systems designed to support them. He proposes a new network of local Youth Opportunity Services, bringing together employment advisers, education providers, health services and other support under one roof. Every young person would receive individual guidance and a personalised plan aimed at getting them into work, education or training.
The review proposes two key guarantees: an Opportunity Guarantee , providing a route into employment, training or education, and a Support Guarantee, ensuring young people receive the practical, financial and health support needed to take advantage of those opportunities. This could include apprenticeships, college places, subsidised employment, work placements or, as a last resort, a government-funded job.
Employers would be encouraged to recruit young people through financial incentives, including grants of up to £3,000, reduced employment costs and simpler access to government support. Apprenticeships would be expanded, with a target to double participation, while schools would place greater emphasis on work readiness, practical skills and identifying pupils at risk of disengagement.
Health is another central theme. The report recommends quicker access to mental health services and support without young people having to wait for a formal diagnosis before receiving help.
However, the proposals also involve tougher expectations. A new under-25 benefits system would link financial support more closely to participation in employment, education or training. Young people who repeatedly refuse opportunities or support could face benefit reductions, although the report stresses that assistance must be available before sanctions are imposed.
Milburn estimates the reforms could help around 440,000 additional young people into work by 2036. His message is that tackling youth disengagement requires long-term investment, coordinated government action and a stronger partnership between employers, education and young people.
The central argument is that Britain must move away from a system that manages youth unemployment towards one that actively creates pathways into work, skills and independence.
The review has received a mixed reaction. Peter Richardson, Publishing Editor at BusinessTime in Essex magazine, said: “It’s an incredibly complex and difficult issue to resolve, but I’m with Chris Hoidson here What is being proposed is a bit like rearranging the deckchairs on the Titanic as the vessel sinks below the surface of the water. Governments and all the reviews they’d care to commission don’t and won’t create jobs. Jobs are created by businesses who feel confident enough in the economic climate to expand and take on more staff. Governments are responsible for creating that economic climate.

https://www.businesswire-essex.co.uk/fee.title: A message from Essex Wildlife Trust
https://www.businesswire-essex.co.uk/fee.text:
A message from Justine Addison, Corporate Partnerships Manager at Essex Wildlife Trust.
This year we have again felt humbled by the support of businesses like you.
One of the greatest privileges of our work is getting to know our supporters and understanding why nature matters to them personally. Through conversations, visits and events, we hear stories about favourite places, treasured memories, family connections and the comfort and inspiration that nature provides. Those conversations continually shape our thinking and remind us why our work matters and why nature is great.
We know these are unsettled times. Many of us are feeling the pressures of change in our daily lives, whether at work, at home, or in our communities. This summer’s extreme weather brought home the reality of climate change. Here in Essex, with our long, wiggly coastline and dry weather, we are witnessing those impacts first hand. At times, the scale of the challenge can feel overwhelming.
And then there is nature.
And the outdoors.
And taking a breath.
In a rapidly changing world, nature helps us reconnect with what is important. It grounds us, restores us, and reminds us that positive change is possible.
As Essex Wildlife Trust nears to its 70 th birthday, we are reflecting not only on what has been achieved, but on what comes next. Over the decades, we have helped bring species back from decline, protected precious landscapes, restored habitats, and provided opportunities for countless people to experience and benefit from nature. For many, our reserves and green spaces have become a Natural Health Service: places where wellbeing, learning and connection grow.
This Christmas, our appeal will celebrate what makes nature great and what makes Essex special. It will tell the story of how nature enriches our lives, how our supporters have helped us make a difference over the past decades, and how together we can build on that legacy for the next 70.
Importantly, it will also launch an ambitious goal. Over the next three years, we aim to raise £1million to support the long-term protection and restoration of nature across Essex. This investment will help us care for and enhance the landscapes in our stewardship, protect vulnerable species, improve the health of our waterways, provide opportunities for people to connect with nature, and ensure that robust scientific evidence continues to guide our work. It will strengthen our ability to take practical local action, creating lasting benefits for both wildlife and people.
We believe that now is not the time to feel disheartened; it is the time to act . The appeal will last for three years as the next three years are critical – we are working towards a global goal to restore 30% of land and sea by 2030. The challenges facing nature are significant, but so too is our collective ability to make a difference. Every restored habitat, every protected species, every child inspired by the natural world begins with people who choose to invest in a better future because they understand what makes nature great.
As our Essex business community, we hope you will help us tell that story through The Great Nature Appeal and will help us write the next chapter.
Any donations made to The Great Nature Appeal between 1 st and 8 th December 2026 will be doubled by The Big Give.  Double Your donation. Double your Impact.
Thank you for your continued trust in the Essex Wildlife Trust , your generosity, and your belief in what we can achieve together.
For more information on Essex Wildlife Trust, visit www.essexwt.org.uk

https://www.businesswire-essex.co.uk/fee.title: Nina steps up to support bowel cancer research
https://www.businesswire-essex.co.uk/fee.text:
An Essex mum who overcame bowel cancer has raised vital funds towards research into the disease.
Nina Murton, who lives in Alresford, successfully completed the Walk 45 Miles Challenge in aid of the Bowelbabe Fund for Cancer Research UK.
The annual challenge is in memory of Dame Deborah James, the prominent cancer campaigner who died from bowel cancer in 2022 after a six-year battle.
Mother-of-one Nina was also diagnosed with the condition in 2016, but was fortunate the cancer was caught early, and, after surgery, she has made a full recovery.
Nina took on the challenge during October, supported by her dog Rosie and, on one of the days, her husband Terry and 16-month-old granddaughter Ada Rose. So far, Nina has raised almost £600.
Nina, who works as a Senior Tenancy Manager for estate and lettings agency Boydens in Colchester, said: “It is thanks to advances in research that my cancer was caught early. I had surgery to remove a section of my bowel but didn’t have to have chemotherapy. My cousin was less fortunate as her condition was diagnosed later, but she has also now recovered.
“I was 42 when I was diagnosed, which is quite young for the condition, and I am so grateful to the doctors and nurses who treated me and to the researchers who are doing such an amazing job undertaking cutting edge research into bowel cancer.
“It felt right to take on the challenge this year as I was diagnosed in the October 10 years ago.
“Most of my walking was done from my home in Alresford, along the creek to Wivenhoe. It’s a lovely scenic walk, particularly at this time of year when we are going from autumn into winter. It’s peaceful and great for your wellbeing.
“I’m delighted to have completed the challenge and for all the donations I’ve had from friends, family and colleagues at Boydens.”
To donate go to https://fundraise.cancerresearchuk.org/page/ninas-giving-page-41730

BASICS Essex is proud to announce that it has been awarded the King’s Award for Voluntary Service , the highest award given to local voluntary organisations across the United Kingdom. Often described as the equivalent of an MBE for voluntary groups, the award recognises the outstanding contribution made by volunteer organisations and the people behind them.
BASICS Essex provides specialist pre-hospital emergency medical care across Essex through a team of highly trained volunteer clinicians who respond to patients suffering serious illness and injury. Working alongside the ambulance service and other emergency services, BASICS Essex delivers advanced medical interventions at the scene when they are needed most.
The award recognises not only the dedication of BASICS Essex’s volunteer doctors and paramedics, but also the trustees, fundraisers, supporters and operational volunteers who help ensure the charity can continue delivering its lifesaving service.
BASICS Essex is one of 250 charities, social enterprises and voluntary groups to receive the prestigious award this year. Their work, alongside other recipients from across the UK, highlights the vital role volunteers play in strengthening communities and improving lives.
The King’s Award for Voluntary Service recognises outstanding work by local volunteer groups supporting their communities. It was created in 2002 to celebrate Her Late Majesty Queen Elizabeth II’s Golden Jubilee and continues under His Majesty The King.
Paul Gates, Chairman of BASICS Essex, said:
“We are incredibly proud to receive the King’s Award for Voluntary Service.
This recognition belongs to every volunteer who has given their time, skills and commitment to BASICS Essex over the years.
Our volunteer clinicians respond day and night to support critically ill and injured patients across Essex, backed by an incredible team of supporters, fundraisers, trustees and volunteers. This award reflects the passion, professionalism and dedication of everyone involved with BASICS Essex, and we are honoured to receive it.”
Representatives of BASICS Essex will receive the award crystal and certificate from the Lord-Lieutenant of Essex in the coming months.
In addition, two volunteers from BASICS Essex will attend a Royal Garden Party at Buckingham Palace in 2027, alongside other recipients of this year’s award.
