https://www.businesswire-essex.co.uk/fee.title: 44% of CEOs consider cyber security when deciding who to do business with, new research shows
https://www.businesswire-essex.co.uk/fee.text:
Microsoft’s global outage puts business resilience in the spotlight as new Price Bailey research reveals cyber security is increasingly influencing commercial relationships.
According to experts at leading accountancy and business advisory firm, Price Bailey, Microsoft’s global outage serves as another reminder that IT and technical continuity is now a financial and operational risk that belongs on the board agenda.
This comes as a recent survey conducted by Price Bailey, which assessed 500 senior financial decision makers, found that cyber security ranked among the top four factors when assessing whether to trade with another business. The weighting was higher still for CEOs, with 44 percent counting a business’s cyber security as one of the most important factors to consider before trading with another company.
While Microsoft has ruled out a cyberattack and attributed the incident to elevated load on its systems, the consequences for businesses are the same, and sensible planning starts from the assumption that an outage will happen again, not if, says Price Bailey.
Chand Chudasama , Chairman at Price Bailey and an expert in strategic corporate finance, comments: “The harder issue is the concentration of risk with a major outage like this. Resilience planning often assumes failures are isolated, but a cloud outage is the opposite. One supplier fails and thousands of businesses lose the same capability at the same moment, with no easy workaround because everyone is affected together.
“While you cannot prevent a supplier outage, you can prepare in advance and consider how much it might cost you. The businesses that have coped best with recent outages did the thinking before the systems went dark.”
Price Bailey highlights that major outages are becoming a more regular feature of business life. In July 2024, a faulty software update from CrowdStrike took an estimated 8.5 million Windows devices offline, grounding flights, freezing payment systems and affecting businesses around the world. The insurer Parametrix put the cost to US Fortune 500 companies at roughly $5.4bn.
Just over a year later, in October 2025, an accidental configuration change in Microsoft’s Azure Front Door, took down Microsoft 365, Xbox and a long list of third-party services that rely on Azure, from airlines to banks.
James Hart , Senior Manager and cyber security sector expert at Price Bailey, comments: “Events such as the Microsoft outage will ultimately highlight where critical dependencies sit within many businesses and I would encourage senior decision makers to use this as an opportunity to review their systems and map out a continuity plan. Resilience is a business decision before it is a technical one, and the question to ask is simple: if our core systems were unavailable for a working day, what would we lose, and what is our plan?”
To discuss business resilience and continuity planning, contact Price Bailey.

https://www.businesswire-essex.co.uk/fee.title: Basildon Cybersecurity Event Brings Local Businesses and Industry Experts Together
https://www.businesswire-essex.co.uk/fee.text:
Businesses from across Essex gathered in Basildon for a morning of live cybersecurity demonstrations, practical advice and expert insights, as local IT provider Sunrise Technologies hosted Cyber Security Live 2026.
Held at the Holiday Inn Basildon on Thursday 29 October, the event brought together representatives from Essex Police, the Cyber Resilience Centre for the East and global IT solutions provider Kaseya to explore the growing importance of cybersecurity for local businesses.
Organised by Basildon-based Sunrise Technologies, the event aimed to move beyond traditional cybersecurity presentations by demonstrating how cybercriminals operate, the risks businesses face and what effective recovery from an attack can look like.
The morning began with a presentation from the Cyber Resilience Centre for the East, which provided attendees with practical advice and resources to help businesses understand and reduce their exposure to cyber threats.
Essex Police followed with an interactive, escape-room-style challenge, demonstrating how criminals can use publicly available information to build convincing false identities and manipulate individuals. The activity highlighted the risks associated with social engineering and how seemingly insignificant pieces of information can be combined to facilitate cybercrime.
Attendees were then given a live demonstration by Kaseya, showing how businesses can recover following a cyber incident when effective backup and recovery systems are in place. The demonstration showed a recovery process taking approximately five minutes, illustrating the potential benefits of well-managed recovery technology.
The event concluded with a presentation from Sunrise Technologies examining the hidden vulnerabilities that can exist within business IT systems.
Using the analogy of open doors, the team encouraged attendees to consider whether they fully understand the potential weaknesses within their organisations, from outdated software and access controls to business continuity arrangements and cybersecurity policies.
Sunrise also introduced its Business IT Risk Assessment, designed to help organisations review five areas of their operations: compliance, technology, risk management, operational resilience and foundational security.
The assessment aims to give businesses a clearer understanding of their existing IT arrangements and identify areas where improvements may be required.
Cybersecurity remains an important consideration for businesses of every size, particularly as organisations become increasingly dependent on digital systems, cloud services and interconnected technologies.
Events such as Cyber Security Live provide opportunities for local businesses to engage directly with cybersecurity specialists, understand emerging risks and gain practical knowledge that can be applied within their own organisations.

https://www.businesswire-essex.co.uk/fee.title: Brits lose £619 million to expired gift cards, and last Christmas’s could be next
https://www.businesswire-essex.co.uk/fee.text:
Be Clever With Your Cash – is it time for a legal minimum expiry period as millions risk losing money they’ve already been given?
UK shoppers have lost around £619 million to gift cards that expired before they were spent, according to new research from consumer finance website Be Clever With Your Cash (BCWYC). With many cards running out 12 months after purchase, anyone who received one last Christmas could see it expire within weeks.
The survey of 2,000 UK adults found that three in ten (31%) have had a gift card or voucher expire before using the full value in the last five years. Those affected lost an average of £36.20 each, and nearly one in five (18%) lost £50 or more. Two respondents even revealed that they’d missed out on expired gift cards valued at £500 or more, and dozens have lost between £100-£149.99.
And it can happen to anyone. Millennials aged 30 to 45 are hit hardest, losing an average of £51.50, well above Gen Z (£29.30), Gen X (£30.40) and Boomers (£28.40). Londoners lost an average of £44.60, the highest of any region.
Gift cards remain a brilliant present for the person who’s impossible to buy for, or for friends and family clubbing together for something bigger. The problem is the small print. The UK has no legal minimum expiry period for gift cards, so retailers can set their own deadlines, and when a card runs out, the money stays with them.
Other countries have already acted. Ireland introduced a five-year minimum expiry period in 2019, and the US has had one since 2009. Is it time for the UK government to follow suit and introduce a minimum expiry period, so consumers don’t lose money that has already been spent on them?
Amelia Murray, Money Expert at Be Clever With Your Cash, said:
“Someone paid good money for that gift card, and it’s simply not right that it can quietly vanish back into a retailer’s pocket because of a date hidden in the small print. Before you buy a single present this Christmas, dig out any gift cards in your drawers and wallets and check those expiry dates.”
BCWYC’s top tips for gift cards
Check your drawers now. Gather up any gift cards and vouchers, check the expiry dates and balances, and spend the ones closest to running out first.
Spend before you shop. Use existing cards for Christmas shopping before reaching for your own money.
Read the terms before you buy. Check how long a card lasts and whether there are any fees or restrictions before giving one as a gift.
Register your card. Where retailers allow it, registering a card can help if it’s lost or stolen.
Don’t sit on them. Gift cards may not be honoured if a retailer goes into administration, so it pays to spend them promptly.
Consider cash for group gifts. If several people are clubbing together for a larger amount, a bank transfer or cash may be a safer option than a single high-value card.

https://essexjewishnews.co.uk/feed/.title: Southend Reform celebrates 80 years with special service
https://essexjewishnews.co.uk/feed/.text:
Words by Simon Rothstein
Pictures by Ashley Jay Brent Photography ( ajbrent.com / visualsbyash.com )
Southend and District Reform Synagogue (SDRS) marked its 80th anniversary with a Shabbat service on Saturday 24 October, exactly 80 years after the community was founded. The occasion brought together synagogue members, civic leaders and guests from across the Jewish community to celebrate eight decades of Jewish life in Southend.
Among those attending were Southend East MP Bayo Alaba, Southend West MP David Burton-Sampson, Southend Council Leader Daniel Cowan, Councillor Donna Richardson, and representatives from the police, Jewish Joint Burial Society, Jewish Care and other local synagogues.
Chair Lewis Miller and the current SDRS Council were joined by past Chairs Sue Levitas and Fern Potter. Ninety-nine-year-old Synagogue President Irene Klyman, whose parents were among the founding members, took part via Zoom.
The service was led by Rabbi Warren Elf MBE, who has worked with the community since 2001, with the sermon delivered by Rabbi Josh Levy, Co-Lead of The Movement for Progressive Judaism.
Rabbi Warren said: “It was a pleasure to lead our 80th anniversary Shabbat morning service, which was a true celebration. It was wonderful to host both of Southend’s MPs, the leader of the city council and our other guests from religious and civic life.
“I have enjoyed working with this special community for 25 years and hope to continue for a few more!”
Rabbi Josh’s sermon, which can be read here , centred on a teaching traditionally attributed to the sage Yehudah ben Tema: “ Ben shmonim ligvurah ”, meaning “The age of 80 for strength”.
He explored what strength means for a community, and how it lies not only in resilience and an ability to overcome challenges, but in the pursuit of justice, peace, equality and making the world a better place.
Rabbi Josh Levy presents Southend and District Reform Synagogue’s Chair Lewis Miller and Rabbi Warren Elf with a certificate of recognition for its contribution to Progressive Jewish life in Essex
Rabbi Josh presented the community with a certificate of recognition and concluded: “May 80 be a year of special strength for you – may this community always have the strength to keep safe, the strength to persevere, and most of all the strength to be a beacon of Progressive Jewish values in Southend and beyond.”
Southend Council Leader Daniel Cowan praised the synagogue’s contribution to the city over eight decades.
Reflecting on Rabbi Josh’s “thoughtful and moving sermon”, he said: “The strength of a community is found in its people. In the friendships built across generations, the traditions passed from parents to children, and the determination to preserve identity, faith and belonging through changing times.
“Eighty years is more than a milestone. It is a testament to the resilience of a community that has continued to grow, support one another and enrich our city.”
The community began as Southend Liberal Synagogue in Leigh-on-Sea in October 1946, when a group of local Jews came together to establish a Jewish community to meet their religious needs. Initially meeting and praying in one another’s homes, the group began holding weekly Shabbat services in a hall above shops in Leigh Road in 1947.
The synagogue moved to its present building in Westcliff-on-Sea in 1961 and became known as Southend Progressive Synagogue. In 1972, following a decision to move from Liberal to Reform Judaism, it adopted its current name, Southend and District Reform Synagogue. Today, it is a member of the newly united Movement for Progressive Judaism.
The anniversary service was part of a series of events taking place throughout the year, culminating in a musical gala evening in November.

https://essexjewishnews.co.uk/feed/.title: Theatre review: By Royal Appointment
https://essexjewishnews.co.uk/feed/.text:
★★★★½
Review by Simon Rothstein
Pictures by Robert Day
“My clothes say what I can’t…”
So says Queen Elizabeth II in Chelmsford Theatre’s By Royal Appointment, and this fascinating play about the late monarch’s wardrobe reveals just how much she could communicate without saying a word.
The first thing to say is that the costume design is fantastic, recreating some of the Queen’s most memorable looks and bringing key moments in recent history to life through her eyes.
There is the blue-and-yellow hat worn for the State Opening of Parliament after the Brexit referendum, and the striking green outfit she wore on her historic visit to Ireland in 2011, when the colour itself carried a message of welcome and goodwill.
Other costumes have more personal associations, including those chosen for family weddings and funerals, or the brooch worn when meeting the infamous Mrs Simpson.
The attention to detail is wonderful, and the first thing you will do after leaving the theatre is look up photographs of the original events to see just how closely they match.
But what sets this play apart is that it is about so much more than what the Queen wore.
Daisy Goodwin’s writing takes us into the lives of the four very different central characters: Queen Elizabeth II (Jane Asher), her dresser (Laura Main), her designer (David Robb) and her milliner (Matthew Cottle).
As we follow their lives over several decades, we see them deal with love, infidelity, coming out, divorce, death, disability and the ageing process that finally catches up with us all.
Some of the story is based on real people and events, while other elements have been introduced for dramatic effect, but you become genuinely invested in all four lives.
The chemistry between the actors is excellent. Stage legend Jane Asher brings real presence to the Queen, capturing the person behind the familiar public image, while Call the Midwife’s Laura Main is superb as the dresser from Wigan who strikes up an extraordinarily close relationship with a woman from a background that couldn’t be more different.
David Robb and Matthew Cottle are equally impressive, bringing their own personalities and vulnerabilities to the designer and milliner. Together, the four create a convincing picture of people who work closely together, sometimes liking each other and sometimes not, but ultimately learning to respect and look out for one another.
Laura Matthews also does a great job as the fifth character in the show, the curator, introducing the exhibition that frames the story and helping to place the Queen’s outfits in their historical context before each is revealed.
The play has plenty of laughs, but is ultimately about something much more poignant.
Without wishing to spoil the narrative, there is a powerful sadness in the play’s exploration of what happens when someone who has devoted their life to a particular role is no longer needed. It is a message that goes well beyond the Royal household, and one that stays with you long after the final curtain.
Best of all, we get to enjoy all of this in the intimate surroundings of the gorgeous Chelmsford Theatre, where the story feels all the more personal.
As Daisy Goodwin puts it: “It is the greatest feeling in the world to come to a theatre like Chelmsford and see people really enjoying themselves. In London, audiences are spoiled, but in Chelmsford the audiences are so appreciative and it is a privilege to serve them.”
By Royal Appointment is funny, moving, beautifully costumed and full of fascinating historical detail.
Some of the descriptions of dresses and hats go on a little too long, although, as a middle-aged man, I may not be the target audience for that part of the show!
Ultimately, this is a play that offers a fresh perspective on a Monarch we have all seen depicted many times, while reminding us that behind the carefully constructed outfits and public image were real people with complicated lives, relationships and emotions.

Pat Lidiker reports on her memorable visit to Jewish Care’s Sugar & Ronson Campus
Resident Naomi with her husband Norman and daughter Nicole as she moves into to The Sugar Family Care Home
When the Essex Jewish News was invited by Jewish Care for an incredibly tasty salt beef lunch and personal tour of the charity’s new Sugar & Ronson Campus in Redbridge, both this paper’s editor Simon Rothstein and I thought we’d wandered into a five-star hotel by mistake.
I’m seldom at a loss for words, but trying to describe this incredible building leaves me in danger of running out of superlatives!
New Prime Minister Andy Burnham has described Jewish Care as the “gold standard” for the adult social care sector, and it’s easy to see why.
First impressions are of spacious, welcoming, stylishly designed and decorated eating and meeting areas, café’s, lounges, wide corridors and sheer comfort for all who make this their home, or their home from home.
The Sugar & Ronson Campus brings together care, community and support services for the local Jewish community under one roof, continuing the legacy of more than 50 years of Jewish Care services on the site.
The 66-bed Sugar Family Care Home provides residential, nursing, dementia and end-of-life care, as well as respite stays.
Alongside it is The Ronson Community Centre, a vibrant hub offering a programme of activities including live entertainment, dancing, card games, exercise classes, bridge, yoga, table tennis and Jewish festivals and community events.
One resident, Corinne, had just had her hair and nails done in the ground-floor salon available to care home and community centre members.
“It looks like a hotel, never in a million years did I think I’d be in a place like this!” she beamed happily.
Michael, a resident at The Sugar Family Care Home, added: “The whole building is fabulous. There’s everything here, they’ve done a wonderful job and the garden’s gorgeous too.”
Social care coordinator Jacklin Stephenson with Michael who is a resident at The Sugar Family Care Home
Jewish Care continues to make the most of a unique opportunity to create a new hub for the whole new community in the heart of Essex.
At The Ronson Family Community Centre on-site café, members of the community can meet friends for breakfast, lunch or tea and join in a variety of different events.
People of all ages can come in simply for a coffee, or a meal with their relatives. And the Campus is designed as a gentle pathway to attend an activity, while also having access to services such as social work, Meals on Wheels, specialist dementia support and mental health services from Jami if and when they need them.
The Dennis Centre, specifically designed for people living with dementia, is also part of the campus. Dementia-informed design runs throughout this part of building – that has its own secure entry and exit – with furniture, flooring, lighting and colour choices helping to support orientation, safety and independence.
One regular member there, Rita, was blown away when she first arrived, saying, “It’s really wonderful and the staff can’t do enough for us.”
Our lunch was hosted in the excellent café, open to the wider community, and serving kosher meat meals, somewhere that it’s easy to meet, eat and socialise. This includes an incredibly tasty salt beef lunch which will be on the varied menu once a month and will also features at the legendary Salt Beef Suppers.

https://essexjewishnews.co.uk/feed/.title: Building Jewish connections across Essex
https://essexjewishnews.co.uk/feed/.text:
By Peter Wynch
When I moved back to Woodford in 2021, after almost a decade in North West London, I saw there was a particular gap for Jewish people in their 30s, 40s and 50s to meet each other socially – especially singles.
After talking this through with Rabbi Odom Brandman at Chabad Buckhurst Hill, I decided to do something about it.
With his initial support, I organised a walk through High Beach in September 2024. Six of us turned up on a warm late-summer day. That was the start of Essex Jewish Socials.
Since then, the group has gradually evolved. We have visited cultural landmarks in London, walked around Fairlop Waters, taken part in quizzes, gone bowling and enjoyed L’chaims in and around north-east London and Essex.
The ethos is simple: openness, inclusivity and keeping things local. Most events cost very little and people can come and go as they please.
Although singles are an important part of the group, I was determined from the outset that it would not become a dating forum. Couples, including those with non-Jewish partners, have also joined us. Genuine friendships have emerged.
The King William IV in Chigwell has proved our most popular venue so far. As we move forward, I would like to organise more walks, as well as potentially introducing Friday night dinners, discussion events and film screenings.
There is certainly scope for the group to grow, but that depends on people getting involved. My advice to anyone considering coming along is simple: have no expectations and enjoy the event for what it is. Everything else can develop from there.

https://essexjewishnews.co.uk/feed/.title: A life well lived: A tribute to Manny Robinson
https://essexjewishnews.co.uk/feed/.text:
Manny Robinson – the wonderful Editor of this newspaper for more than 40 years – had a saying when somebody died in old age.
He’d tell his sons: “When it’s a life well lived, of course, you are going to be sad, but these things should also be more about celebrating a life than mourning someone lost.”
When we remember Manny – who died in May aged 93 – we remember his wonderful career in the media, his love for our Essex Jewish community and his amazing EJN columns that continued right up until his final days. It truly was a life well lived.
Emanuel Rabinovitch was born on April 11, 1933, the first child of Ray and Sidney. He was close throughout his life with his brother Jeffrey and sister Gilda, whose passing in January of this year, which left him ‘last man standing’, affected him profoundly.
They grew up in Whitechapel in a block of flats called Chelsea Buildings in Princelet Street. His father was a Hoffman presser, his mother a seamstress.
On the night of 19 April 1941, the Luftwaffe launched one of its heaviest attacks on London, dropping a bomb on St Peter’s Hospital in Stepney, where Manny was being treated for dysentery.
His mother wouldn’t know for four days whether he had survived the bombing or not, only then finding out that he, together with the other survivors, had been evacuated to the village of South Mimms. He retained a vivid memory of tulips in the fields outside where he was staying. He was evacuated to Tylorstown in the Welsh valleys for the rest of the war, even attending chapel every Sunday.
Back in the East End, as youngsters, they had nowhere really to go, other than to the local dance hall, the Lyceum or the Royal, or to the local cinema, though sometimes a lack of money meant he often couldn’t afford to go to either.
And so, he joined a new club for Jewish boys, Brady. The purpose of the club, he once said, was to instil some sort of character. To him, Brady was his university. It was a place where they learned how to speak, how to respect their elders, and how to develop loyalties. It was also where he learned to dance – a skill to be shown off at simchas for years to come.
He became the first boy to edit the club’s magazine, once writing about the visit of Princess Margaret to the Brady Girls’ Club. He also used to go to watch Brady teams at football matches and started to write reports about their games.
And then on a Sunday afternoon after the match, he would write a report and take it down to the local newspaper, the East London Advertiser, and was chuffed when they used his report in the paper without changing a word.
Manny during his time at the Evening Standard
That planted the seed in his mind that maybe he could become a journalist. Committing to this, he would spend his weekends in Fleet Street delivering photographs from picture agencies to national newspapers. It was his way of finding his way round, and from five o’clock in the afternoon until nine o’clock at night, he would be paid 10 shillings, but it gave him an ‘in’.
After National Service, he applied for work on the Stratford Express. The paper served the supporters of two professional football teams, West Ham United and Leyton Orient, and so he was given a job, on the heady salary of £4 a week.
Having told the Editor he liked football, he subsequently found out that none of the other journalists wanted to cover football because it meant working weekends. So he was appointed Sports Editor at the age of 21 and started sending snippets of news from the two clubs to the Evening Standard.
Journalism, at that time, wasn’t really a go-to career for a young Jewish guy from the East End of London. In fact, he became Manny Robinson when it was explained to him that his name needed to change if he wanted a by-line as Emanuel Rabinovitch was just too long to fit across a single column of type.
Eventually he was approached by the Evening Standard and offered a job there. And at 23, he became the youngest journalist at that point ever to get in

https://essexjewishnews.co.uk/feed/.title: Cable Street 90 festival to celebrate stories of courage and sacrifice
https://essexjewishnews.co.uk/feed/.text:
By Linda Newman
To mark the 90th anniversary of the historic clash at The Battle of Cable Street, the Board of Deputies of British Jews presents Cable Street 90 , a festival of Jewish culture, history, and solidarity in which a whole kaleidoscope of fascinating events will be taking place
As part of the festival, historian and AJEX archivist Martin Sugarman whose work we featured in our current issue (p 10 ) will be giving a talk on October 8 th titled  Jews Against Franco: The Jewish Contribution to the Spanish Civil War. Martin’s talk will explore the Spanish Civil War as one of the defining struggles against fascism of the 20th century – in which Jews played a remarkable part.
The Battle of Cable Street took place on October 4, 1936. Just months earlier, in July 1936, the Spanish Civil War erupted. For the Jewish youth of East London, Oswald Mosley’s Blackshirts at home and General Franco’s fascists in Spain were the same enemy. Many of the very same young Jewish men and women who stood at the barricades shouting “No Pasarán” (They Shall Not Pass) at Cable Street went on to volunteer for the International Brigades in Spain to continue the fight.
Thousands of Jews from around 53 countries became involved in the Republican cause. Many joined the International Brigades and travelled to Spain to fight Franco; others supported the struggle through fundraising, political activism, refugee aid and humanitarian work. Some went openly as Jews, while others adopted aliases. Some fought alongside fellow nationals, while others joined different national units. Some were refugees from antisemitism and political persecution; others left relatively secure lives in democratic countries to fight fascism.
Martin’s talk uncovers these often-overlooked stories of courage, idealism, international solidarity and sacrifice – and asks why the Jewish contribution to the fight against Franco remains so little known.
CABLE STREET 90
Running from 1–11 October 2026, Events will be taking place across iconic East London and central venues (locations revealed upon booking); the varied programme includes discussions, artistic performances, films, live performances and tailored black cab history tours of Whitechapel, Spitalfields, and Brick Lane.
For further info and to book, please go to: https://bod.org.uk/cable-street-90/

https://essexjewishnews.co.uk/feed/.title: Theatre review – Operation Mincemeat
https://essexjewishnews.co.uk/feed/.text:
****
Review by Simon Rothstein
Photos by Matt Crockett
The wonderful Operation Mincemeat, now playing at the Cliffs Pavilion in Southend, probably never should have made the big stage at all.
A historical musical spy comedy set during World War II, with an ensemble cast who frequently swap roles and genders, it started life in an 80-seater studio not long before the pandemic hit and its plans were interrupted.
However, post-lockdowns and carried by word of mouth, momentum soon built, with awards and glowing reviews following not far behind – leading to it becoming a huge West End and Broadway hit.
Now touring theatres around the UK, and indeed the world, it opened right here in Southend-on-Sea, Essex. Future stops will include Chicago, Los Angeles, Boston and cities in China and Australia, as well as Norwich and Crawley a little closer to home.
While not the original cast, four of the five principal performers – Christian Andrews, Seán Carey, Charlotte Hanna-Williams and Holly Sumpton – reprise roles from the West End production, joined by new recruit Jamie-Rose Monk.
All are superb, mixing high comedy with thrilling spy escapes – while bringing a sweetness that makes you really care about their characters and the mission’s success.
That mission was the extraordinary true story of a 1943 British deception operation, in which a dead man was given a false identity and planted off the coast of Spain carrying fake military documents. The elaborate ruse helped convince Hitler that the Allies intended to invade Greece rather than Sicily, drawing German forces away from the real target.
The show is also a tribute to the hugely important role of our intelligence services, who often operate with no public thanks or glory until decades later.
One key reason to see the production, other than its great entertainment value, is therefore keeping this history alive for future generations!
Back to the stage and two things that stand out are the clever choreography, with genuine ‘how did they do that’ moments, and a set design that does a wonderful job of transporting you back to the era.
The five performers, swapping between multiple parts, mix song, farce and intrigue, with the tunes moving the story along and the fast pace rarely letting up.
Some of the songs went on a little too long and they aren’t the type you’re still singing the next day, while a few of the gags missed the mark.
But overall this is a show that is funny, thrilling and full of things to learn, culminating in a happy ending and a lovely tribute (I won’t say any more so as not to spoil).
Judging by the standing ovation in Southend, it is clear that Operation Mincemeat has lost none of its ability to win over an audience as it heads on tour.

https://essexjewishnews.co.uk/feed/.title: Theatre review – Dial M for Murder
https://essexjewishnews.co.uk/feed/.text:
*****
Review by Simon Rothstein
Photos courtesy of Phil&Ben Productions
A true joy of being the Editor of the Essex Jewish News is travelling around our glorious county discovering its hidden gems.
One of those is undoubtedly the Palace Theatre in Southend where stepping through the doors is like stepping back in time.
A Grade II listed Edwardian building, first opened in 1912, it’s a truly beautiful venue with original features preserved – giving you the same layout, atmosphere and experience those watching plays there 100 years ago would have enjoyed.
Of course, any theatre is only as good as the shows it puts on – which is why I’m pleased to report that Dial M for Murder, which is playing all this week, truly is a classic thriller fit for a Palace.
Brought back to the stage for 2026 by Phil&Ben Productions, in association with PW Productions, it is showing in Southend until Sunday (16 August) before heading off to Harrogate, Blackpool, Coventry and Peterborough. It previously toured Eastbourne, Crewe, Fareham and Swindon.
For a Frederick Knott play that first premiered in 1952 – made famous by Alfred Hitchcock’s 1954 film version – it may seem strange of me not to want to give any spoilers, but with every twist and turn being so impactful, I’m keen not to ruin any of them.
The story, as fans of the film will remember, begins with English former tennis professional Tony Wendice plotting to kill his wealthy wife Margot after finding out she’d been cheating on him with Mark Halliday, an American crime-fiction writer.
Blackmailing an old classmate turned con man, Charles Swann, into doing the deed for him – Tony feels he has the perfect murder planned as he explains to Charles, and therefore us, in great detail.
Things, as you can imagine, don’t go as expected, leaving Charles to come up with a second dastardly plan. But is his web of lies and latch keys enough to fool Inspector Hubbard and get him the inheritance he wants?
The direction from Josh Mathieson is one of the best I’ve seen in a small theatre, adding moments of dramatic pause to the gripping script to really allow you to take everything in and wonder what happens next.
You, of course, hate the dastardly Tony (played masterfully by Pete Ashmore), but there’s a moment where Margot (Tanya-Loretta Dee) chooses to walk with Max (Simon Pothecary) instead of Tony that really makes you wonder where your sympathies lie – a credit to the acting and directing.
Phil Stewart may be having the most fun as the slightly hapless Charles Swann, while you never know how much Katy Dean’s Inspector Hubbard really knows – keeping you guessing until the end.
Dial M for Murder is a whodunnit where you know who did it, how they did it and why they did it… yet it remains gripping throughout.
There were a mix of ages in the theatre, including my own teenage children, and all were hanging on every word.
Listening to conversations afterwards, the audience was a combination of those who know and love the film – like us – those who have seen it but forgotten the twists and turns, and those coming to the material for the first time. All enjoyed it equally.
Not only was this a five-star show, right here on our doorsteps, but it is also part of an important effort to strengthen the future of touring drama in towns and smaller cities across the UK.
As Phil and Ben said: “We believe audiences in towns and smaller cities like Southend deserve regular access to outstanding live drama, and that the appetite for it remains strong.
“This is an exciting production in its own right, but it also stands for something larger: a commitment to restoring confidence in mid-scale touring theatre and building lasting partnerships with venues and audiences.”
So if you’re looking for a great night out at a very reasonable price, just Dial M and get to the Palace.

https://essexjewishnews.co.uk/feed/.title: Local MP Wes Streeting takes on top Government job
https://essexjewishnews.co.uk/feed/.text:
By Pat Lidiker
Since joining the Essex Jewish News 10 years ago, I have become increasingly aware of the growing reputation of our local MP, Wes Streeting. I have met and interviewed him on many occasions, so I was delighted to offer him mazel tov on behalf of the paper on his recent appointment as Secretary of State for Defence.
A Christian, Wes has forged close relationships with members of the Redbridge Jewish community and is a familiar and welcome face at local shuls, schools and organisations. He has also been a vocal campaigner against the growing threat of antisemitism.
At 43, Wes has already held one of the most demanding jobs in government, serving as Secretary of State for Health and Social Care from 2024 until May this year, before returning to government as Defence Secretary in July.
He also laid bare much of his personal history in his autobiography, One Boy, Two Bills and a Fry Up, published last year. I found it impossible to put down and admired his willingness to confront his past so openly.
Wes continues to live in his Redbridge constituency with his partner Joe Dancey, a communications and public affairs consultant. How much time they will now have for weekends away in the area remains to be seen.
His new role comes at a challenging time, with responsibility for Britain’s defence, security and armed forces.
On receiving our congratulations, the new Defence Secretary replied: “It is a huge honour to be taking on this role. Keeping our country safe is the first duty of government and since my appointment, we’ve been straight to work speaking to allies, including Ukraine, to make clear that we will continue to stand steadfast alongside them. I am also absolutely committed to ensuring our armed forces have the resources they need.
“I would like to wish your readers a Shanah Tovah this Rosh Hashanah. Chag Sameach!”
Wes Streeting with the EJN’s very own Pat Lidiker and Phillip Leigh in 2023

Sir John Whittingdale MP has written to the Home Secretary calling for plans to accommodate up to six asylum seekers in Tillingham to be reconsidered.
He has raised concerns about the village’s isolated location and limited public transport, as well as access to essential services. He has also highlighted the potential for community tensions arising from the proposed accommodation.
The Maldon MP believes that Tillingham is an unsuitable location both for local residents and for the individuals who would be accommodated there.
Sir John has requested urgent discussions with the Government to raise these concerns and seek a reconsideration of the proposals.
The letter forms part of his efforts to represent the concerns surrounding the proposed asylum accommodation in Tillingham and its potential impact on the village.

https://www.johnwhittingdale.org.uk/?fee.text:
Sir John Whittingdale had the privilege of chairing the Foreign Affairs Committee when it received evidence from Vladimir Kara-Murza, a leading Russian opposition political activist, author and former political prisoner, as part of its ongoing inquiry into Russia and the UK’s strategy towards the country.

https://www.johnwhittingdale.org.uk/?fee.title: Local Government Organisation
https://www.johnwhittingdale.org.uk/?fee.text:
Sir John Whittingdale MP challenges the Government over delays and uncertainty surrounding local government reorganisation in Essex, following the decision to scrap the previous reform proposals and reconsider the plans. He warns that the lack of clarity is disrupting local decision-making and questions how elections can proceed in 2028 when voters and candidates may not know which authorities will be in place. The exchange highlights concerns about the timetable for Essex local government reform, democratic representation and the need for clear decisions from the Government.
Debate Highlights
John Whittingdale Conservative, Maldon
Six weeks ago, the Government announced that they were scrapping the local government reform proposals for Essex and going back to the drawing board. That announcement created yet more uncertainty and further paralysed decision making, yet the Minister has not even mentioned Essex, and he has provided no additional clarity whatsoever. How can he expect elections to go ahead in 2028, when we will not even know what authorities the candidates will be elected to until next year?
Jim McMahon Parliamentary Under-Secretary (Housing, Communities and Local Government)
I definitely accept the right hon. Member’s point that having an itinerary of areas, with a clear date alongside them, would do what he has asked, but that is not where we are. We have decided that we ought to confirm the decision for an area as soon as possible, rather than waiting for this to be patched up, in the way that may have happened previously. On whether elections should go ahead, I have made the point that these district councils will be in place until the vesting days of the new local authorities. We cannot have elections being cancelled, creating a democratic deficit. Councils must have representatives around the table, with a mandate given to them by the public.

https://www.johnwhittingdale.org.uk/?fee.title: Falkland Islands Oil Reserves
https://www.johnwhittingdale.org.uk/?fee.text:
Sir John challenged the Prime Minister to confirm the Government will oppose Argentina’s efforts to prevent oil exploration authorised by the United Kingdom around the Falkland Islands. Sir John pressed for a firm commitment to defend the UK’s position, drawing attention to concerns over sovereignty and the Government’s approach to the strategically important Chagos Islands. The Prime Minister did reaffirm the Government’s support for the Falkland Islanders’ right to self-determination and for keeping the islands British and Sir John will continue to hold the government to account on this matter.
Debate Highlights
John Whittingdale Conservative, Maldon:
Unlike the Government’s shameful attempts to hand over the sovereignty of the strategically important Chagos islands, will the Prime Minister confirm that this time the Government will strongly oppose the case being made by the Government of Argentina to the international tribunal to try to stop the exploitation of oil reserves around the Falkland Islands, which is authorised by the United Kingdom?
Andy Burnham Leader of the Labour Party, The Prime Minister:
Indeed we will, and I am happy to make that clear again today. We will take the firmest of action to support the Falkland Islands—the right to self-determination of the islanders, who chose to remain British not so long ago. The Defence Secretary has met his counterparts to reiterate that position, and the Foreign Secretary too. I raised the matter with President Trump. There is no diminution in our strong support to keep the Falkland Islands British.

https://essexpolfed.org.uk/feed/.title: Call For Breast Cancer Screening Funding
https://essexpolfed.org.uk/feed/.text:
Essex Police Federation is calling for partners to help fund breast cancer screening for the force’s female officers and police staff.
Last year, Essex Police’s Women’s Forum ran a pilot scheme and was able to secure 37 breast cancer ultrasound screenings for officers and staff; this year the Federation is helping raise funds to do the same again. The scheme is aimed at women aged under 50, who may not be eligible for routine NHS screening.
One woman who was screened last year as part of the initiative was told that a breast implant had ruptured.
She had no symptoms that indicated this and she would not have known if she hadn’t taken part in the screenings. She has since been able to avoid referral waiting times because she was able to send the scans that the screening consultant provided straight to her doctor, and already has an operation booked in to remove the damaged implants.
Alfie McPhilimey, Federation Vice-Chair and Lead for Equality and Wellbeing, said: “It’s really important that the Federation supports this initiative, because otherwise it might not happen. We are here to support our members and our women in policing, so I think it’s vital that we get behind this. We have seen positive results from last year’s screening, and we want to see that rolled out further to more officers.”
Alfie said he was speaking to member services who he hoped would come on board as sponsors. Any organisations that are interested in getting involved can email Alfie.McPhilimey@polfed.org .

https://essexpolfed.org.uk/feed/.title: Essex Police Federation Pay & Morale Survey 2026
https://essexpolfed.org.uk/feed/.text:
93% of Essex Police officers do not feel fairly paid for the stresses and strains of the job, and 75% are dissatisfied or very dissatisfied with their overall pay and allowances, new figures show.
According to the 2026 Police Federation of England and Wales Pay and Morale Report, 26% of officers frequently cannot meet their household’s financial needs.
54% say their workload is too high or much too high, and 44% have had at least one rest day cancelled in the past 12 months.
22% say they are satisfied with their job, and 16% intend to resign from the service either within the next two years or as soon as they can.
The survey also showed that 75% do not feel valued in the police and 73% would not recommend joining the service.
70% of respondents are not confident in their force’s ability to resource appropriately for day-to-day operational demands, and 49% say their team has been fully staffed on very few or no shifts in the past three months.
73% say their force relies heavily on officer goodwill to meet routine operational demands, and 64% have felt unsafe on duty because of staffing levels in the past three months.
And 66% of officers who responded to the survey are too fatigued to carry out their duties. In Essex Police, 49% of officers have been physically attacked by a member of the public in the past 12 months, and 71% do not have access to double crewing at all times while on duty.
Essex Police Federation Chair Steve Martin said: “All ranks should be getting a fair pay for the work they do. We know how difficult it is as a police officer in this day and age, and we need the Government to stand up and actually start rewarding us properly.
“They need to listen to what we say in the pay surveys, they need to listen to what we say from a morale point of view in those surveys, and realise that we’re not just… the comment a number of years ago from Theresa May, we’re not crying wolf.
“This is a genuine crisis in policing. We’re struggling with retention in force, we’re losing lots of good people and actually there’s probably some easy things that we could do about it, some really easy wins and one of those is probably starting to look at pay properly.”
The survey also showed that 83% of respondents had experienced stress, low mood or anxiety in the past 12 months, and 40% find their job very or extremely stressful.
54% have sought help for stress, low mood, anxiety or other mental health difficulties, and 60% rate their force’s support for officers and their wellbeing as inadequate or requiring improvement.
The survey also showed the effect that policing has on officers’ personal lives. In Essex Police, 28% of officers often or always pressured to work long hours and 51% had annual leave requests refused.
73% of respondents say they have been so fatigued that it has interfered with their family or social life in the past month, and 62% have had to cancel personal plans due to last-minute work requirements in the past 12 months.
30% have worked during annual leave to catch up, 16% have had at least one free day cancelled in the past 12 months and 9% have had their roster changed more than 10 times in the past 12 months.
For the first time, the survey asked about how policing affects parents and carers, with 69% of mothers and 39% of fathers in Essex Police saying they have had to change job roles or teams to meet their obligations as a parent.
The survey is based on 419 responses received from Essex Police officers.

https://essexpolfed.org.uk/feed/.title: Policing A Low Government Priority
https://essexpolfed.org.uk/feed/.text:
Policing is clearly low down the Government’s list of priorities, Essex Police Federation has said.
Chair Steve Martin was speaking at the Police Federation of England and Wales conference, which neither the Policing Minister nor the Home Secretary attended.
He said: “It is really disappointing that our current Government is not here to listen to the issues facing police. The current Prime Minister doesn’t appear to mention policing ever, which for me demonstrates where we sit on his order of priorities.
“It is really positive that we’ve had the Shadow Home Secretary and the Leader of the Opposition, but I think the lack of Government presence speaks volumes as to where policing is currently seen under the current government agenda.”
Steve was joined by Rep Amy Sage, who spoke about a powerful presentation by a former officer from West Midlands who spoke about her experience of sexual assault and misogyny in the workplace.
Amy said: “Actually seeing the impact of it and how it’s affected her, I think it’s very powerful and that’s something I’ll probably take with me for the rest of my career.
“It’s small stories like that that let you kind of sit down for a minute, pause and think you actually are changing lives, and how you are as a Federation Rep matters and impacts people.”
As a new rep, Amy added that it was a useful learning experience for her to come to conference: “I think in terms of learning about the pay, how the PIP procedure is changing, how Regs procedure is changing, I just find it really impactful because obviously this is my first couple of months being a rep.
“I’ve always heard the other side but actually being in the room I think it’s just really powerful how such a big group comes together, and obviously we’re all here because we care and actually seeing that the change is being made.”
Steve added: “Amy has not been a rep for long but she’s clearly demonstrating what, as Branch Chair, I expect to see from our reps. Someone that wants to come in, make a difference, help people where they can.
“I think it’s really important to come to conferences so that they can actually see different viewpoints. You can see that some of the problems that we talk about in our Branch are replicated across the country.
“We’re all fighting the same challenges, we’re all trying to be that one Federation and now we’re transforming and we’re doing some meaningful transformation, hopefully we’re going to be changing the Federation for the better.”

https://essexpolfed.org.uk/feed/.title: Federation sets out six-point plan to combat the suicide crisis affecting policing
https://essexpolfed.org.uk/feed/.text:
More than 100 police officers and staff died by suicide between 2022 and 2025. At least 70 police officers have died during that time and there have been more than 200 attempted suicides.
The Police Federation of England and Wales (PFEW) is today calling for the silent crisis of police suicide to end – as this new data reveals the devastating scale of this crisis killing officers.
47 of the 70 suicides and 173 of 236 attempted suicides are attributable to officers involved in misconduct or criminal investigations against them.
In 2025 the link was even stronger, with 12 of 13 police officer suicides that the Federation is aware of involving officers under investigation.
Police forces are not required to record suicide or attempted suicide, meaning the Federation’s data is likely to significantly undercount the real figures.
The lack of recording means that policing is not currently regarded by the Office for National Statistics as an “occupation at risk”.
The Federation has set out a six-point plan to combat the crisis:
• Chief Constables need to agree today to begin recording and reporting on suicide and attempted suicide in the workforce.
• Police conduct regulations need to mandate a 12-month limit for disciplinary investigations into police officers, whether that is by the IOPC or police forces.
• Health and Safety legislation needs to treat police suicide as an incident at work and therefore reportable and investigated under ‘RIDDOR’ rules.
• All forces should implement the STEP (Suicide Trauma Education Prevention) campaign, launched by Hampshire Police Federation. The campaign calls for the downloading by forces of the Stay Alive app and mandatory TRiM (Trauma Risk Management) interventions for any officer attending a suicide.
• The coronial system needs to reflect the unique aggravating or contributory factors of the role of police officers in suicide and ensure that the crisis is dealt with nationally rather than through a patchwork of “prevention of future deaths” reports after individual inquests.
• The Police Covenant needs to be funded to better support the welfare and wellbeing of police officers in the same way that the Armed Forces Covenant and Covenant Trust does.
For more information about the Stay Alive app, visit stayalive.prevent-suicide.org.uk. Officers and police staff members who are struggling should know that they are not alone, and that there are people there to help.
This includes, for immediacy: Samaritans: call 116 123 and Oscar Kilo’s Mental Health Crisis Line: call 0300 131 2789.

https://essexpolfed.org.uk/feed/.title: More Police Officers Awarded Elizabeth Emblem
https://essexpolfed.org.uk/feed/.text:
The families of 30 UK police officers who have died on duty have seen their loved one’s sacrifice be recognised by the King with the Elizabeth Emblem.
This includes the families of DC Mick Swindells, of West Midlands Police; PC Alan McMurray, of Lothian and Borders Police; and PC Sandra Edwards, of South Yorkshire Police.
Also receiving the award will be the families of fallen officers PC Laurence Brown, of the Metropolitan Police; PC Andrew Winterburn, of West Yorkshire Police; PC John Alcock, of Grampian Police; PC Kenneth Adams, of Hampshire Constabulary; and from Norfolk Constabulary PC Bernard Brown, PC David Protheroe Davies and DC Terence Glister.
The Elizabeth Emblem recognises the sacrifices made by public servants who have lost their lives as a result of their duty. It is the civilian equivalent of the Elizabeth Cross, which recognises members of the UK Armed Forces who died in action or as a result of a terrorist attack.
This is the third list of Elizabeth Emblem recipients to be published. The next of kin are awarded the national form of recognition.
The design of the Emblem incorporates a rosemary wreath, a traditional symbol of remembrance, which surrounds the Tudor Crown.
It is inscribed with ‘For A Life Given In Service’, and will have the name of the person for whom it is in memoriam inscribed on the reverse of the Emblem.
It includes a pin to allow the award to be worn on clothing by the next of kin of the deceased.
The full list of those to be awarded the Elizabeth Emblem is here:  https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-elizabeth-emblem-application-guidance-and-eligibility/list-of-recipients-of-the-elizabeth-emblem-15th-january-2026

https://essexpolfed.org.uk/feed/.title: Christmas and New Year Message from Essex Police Federation Chair Steve Martin
https://essexpolfed.org.uk/feed/.text:
As Christmas fast approaches, I just wanted to take a moment to look back on what’s been a year of progress and teamwork for the Essex Police Federation team.
2025 has brought plenty of change and growth.
We welcomed lots of new faces to the Branch Council – all with fresh ideas and energy that will help shape the future and continue the support and representation of you, the members. At the same time, we said goodbye to our previous Chair and Secretary, Laura and Dean, who retired after years of dedicated service.
A huge thank you to them for everything they’ve done (and continue to do in their new roles).
Nationally, the Federation has continued to transform into a more professional organisation, and locally we’ve worked hard to make sure we’re more visible and accessible than ever.
Whether it’s advice, support, or representation, we’re here when you need us.
We’ve invested in training and development for our new reps and strengthened our relationships with other branches, staff associations, support networks and our external service providers – because working together makes us stronger.
Most importantly, we’ve kept doing what matters most: supporting colleagues, whether that’s helping with compensation for injuries, providing access to medical assistance, assisting with representation during misconduct or criminal matters, or just day-to-day advice.
This is the heart of what we do, and I am proud of the difference we make.
Sadly, this year hasn’t been without loss. We have said goodbye to friends and colleagues, and their absence is deeply felt. Over Christmas, please take a moment to remember them and their loved ones. And for those working over the festive period – please stay safe.
Looking ahead to 2026, I’m optimistic. We’ll keep building on what we’ve achieved this year, making sure every member gets the support they deserve.
From all of us at the Essex Police Federation, have a great Christmas and a peaceful New Year. Thank you for everything you do for Essex and for each other.

https://essexpolfed.org.uk/feed/.title: 2026 subscription changes confirmed following conference vote
https://essexpolfed.org.uk/feed/.text:
Delegates at the Police Federation’s Annual Conference have voted to introduce a £2 per month increase in member subscriptions from 1 January 2026. This will take the gross monthly rate from £24.31 to £26.31.
In addition, the current student officer 50% discount will end, meaning that from 1 January 2026 all new members joining the Federation will contribute at a single standard rate from their first day of membership. There will be no change to the rate for current student officers.
Motions proposing the subscription fee increase and ending the student officer discount passed with heavy majorities after voting at the Federation’s AGM on 18 November.
We know cost of living pressures continue to bite, and no one welcomes paying more. But maintaining the current rate is no longer sustainable if we are to protect, represent and support members in the way they expect and deserve.
Subscriptions have only risen twice in the past decade. In that time, we’ve absorbed rising costs, delivered more than £1 million in annual savings through restructuring, and continued to secure significant outcomes for members.
Demand for our legal and welfare support continues to grow rapidly. Case volumes have risen by almost a third in three years, and this year alone we’ve secured more than £41 million in compensation for members. The cost of expert legal representation and specialist welfare services continues to increase at pace.
What the £2 increase will deliver
The increase is expected to generate around £3.36 million a year. This funding will help us to:
Ending the student officer discount
The discounted rate for student officers, while well-intentioned, generates less than 0.3% of our total income. Our data also shows that newer officers often rely most heavily on Federation support.
Moving to one fair rate for all ensures consistency, sustainability and equal access to the same level of protection and support from day one.
Our role is to stand beside you on your toughest days, in the moments that matter most, and in the national debates shaping the future of policing. These changes are about securing the Federation’s ability to do that, not just now but for the long term.

https://essexpolfed.org.uk/feed/.title: Better Support Needed On Suicide Prevention in Forces
https://essexpolfed.org.uk/feed/.text:
Forces need to step up to record the numbers of police suicides and provide welfare support to officers, particularly those who are under investigation, the Police Federation of England and Wales Annual Conference heard.
In the session, ‘Code Zero: Policing’s Suicide Crisis’, delegates heard from PFEW national Health & Wellbeing Leads Richie Murray and Paul Williams, and Hampshire Police Federation Chair Spencer Wragg, who spearheads the STEP (Suicide Trauma Education Prevention) campaign.
Tragically the conference was told there have been at least 10 suicides of police officers and staff around the country this year.
Richie said he wrote to all Federation branches asking how many of their officers had died by suicide between 2022 and 2024. Two large forces are yet to respond, but so far PFEW has been told about 55 officers who took their own lives in this period, of whom 34 were under investigation. In addition, 120 had reported attempting to take their own lives, 71 of whom were under investigation.
Richie said: “There is a huge causal link between officer suicides and investigations. And I think everybody in this room will say investigations are taking too long, and that it has to have an effect.”
Paul agreed, saying: “We arrest criminals, we send them through the Criminal Justice System. We prosecute, they go to court, they serve a sentence, potentially a prison sentence. Now that criminal could be released back on the street a lot quicker than a police officer who’s been served a basic misconduct form and put under investigation by their own force.”
In addition, forces should carry out a documented basic risk assessment on misconduct investigations and provide the officer with wraparound care, Paul said: “Allocating a welfare officer is sometimes just not good enough.”
Paul said that there needed to be “common minimum standards across the country”. He continued: “We heard yesterday that there’s a postcode lottery of wellbeing in forces: 43 different Chiefs, 43 different personalities.”
PFEW has been successful is getting a motion tabled with the House of Lords to amend the Police and Crime Act to mandate the recording of suicide and attempted suicide in forces.
Another proactive step is for forces to put the free Stay Alive app from Grassroots Suicide Prevention on all officers’ work phones, said Spencer. Spencer spoke about how he and the Martis Media team have promoted the STEP campaign around the country and succeeded in getting the Stay Alive app put on 8,000 officers’ phones in Hampshire and Thames Valley Police. He said: “We’re asking and pushing for Chiefs to put that on job mobile phones, which will cost them absolutely nothing.”
It is important for officers who are struggling to know they are not alone, and that there are people there to help.
This includes, for immediacy, the Mental Health Support line from Oscar Kilo 0300 131 2789.

https://essexpolfed.org.uk/feed/.title: ‘Policing Becoming Unaffordable Profession’
https://essexpolfed.org.uk/feed/.text:
Policing risks becoming an unaffordable profession for officers as the cost of living goes up and officer pay and conditions continue to stagnate.
National Secretary John Partington told the 2025 PFEW conference that potential recruits risk being priced out of the job because pay and conditions are so inadequate for the role that officers carry out.
He also said that equal percentage pay rises are unfair as higher ranks end up taking home more than those on the front line because of their higher baseline salary. He said lower earners – who spend almost their entire income on essential costs – need higher awards to maintain real terms pay.
He said: “A superintendent and a constable face the same inflation, but not the same pressure. Identical percentages create inequality.”
He suggested that lower earners should get higher percentage pay rises to redress this balance.
John said: “Equal percentage pay awards might look fair on paper, but they’re not fair in practice. When everyone gets the same percentage rise, those on higher salaries keep far more of their income after the bills are paid, while those on the frontline see their disposable income vanish.
“Federated rank members today spend almost everything they earn just on living. Housing, energy, and fuel have risen far faster than pay, and what used to be a modest but secure income has become a financial struggle. Simple research for credible sources will show how rent has risen more than police pay.
“This isn’t about generosity – it’s about fairness. A superintendent and a constable face the same inflation, but not the same pressure. Identical percentages create real-terms inequality, not parity. Without correction policing risks becoming unaffordable to those who deliver it.
“That’s why the next pay settlement must recognise this truth: lower earners deserve a higher pay award. Because pay that protects buying power is what keeps people in the job, keeps policing professional, and keeps faith with those who hold the line every day.”
John explained that police conditions should also be improved – to mandate sufficient rest, recovery and resilience because of the unique demands of the job.
He told delegates: “This job affects your mental health, your family life, and your personal wellbeing like few others.
“The risk of assault, the threat of injury, the emotional toll, all of these are part of policing today. And they must be met not just with decent wages, but with conditions that support rest, recovery, and resilience.”
He also highlighted the urgent need to reform police recruitment, calling for mandatory psychological and psychometric testing for every applicant and throughout initial training.
He said: “This is about safeguarding the integrity of policing. Resilience, empathy and moral strength cannot be assumed – they must be tested and proven.”

https://www.transporteast.gov.uk/feed/.title: Takeaways from the European Transport Conference: ABMs, Crisis Resilience, Futures
https://www.transporteast.gov.uk/feed/.text:
This year’s European Transport Conference (ETC) provided a valuable showcase of where transport analytics, data science, and modelling are heading. From agent-based simulations to knowledge graphs and futures frameworks, here are the core technical insights from the sessions.
Agent-Based Models (ABMs) take centre stage
ABMs had a major presence at this year’s conference with BERTIE – Transport East’s Activity and Agent-Based Model – having contributed to or been the subject of five separate talks, four of which reflected innovation enabled by BERTIE and delivered with Arup for the Department for Transport, National Highways, as well as by researchers at University College, London.
Key analytical applications covered in these sessions included the challenges and opportunities for A2BMs in economic appraisal, and actionable insights for modal shift using BERTIE’s ‘VAMoS’ (Viable Alternative Mode Selector) tool. VAMoS leverages a granular understanding of the options and choices of agents, across different segments of the population, to help identify realistic opportunities for mode shift.
Practical application of this work was undertaken for Basildon Borough Council, where Arup applied BERTIE and VAMoS as part of a data-led and people-focussed approach to testing the Local Plan and potential interventions to support the plan’s equitable and sustainable credentials.
The increasing importance of crisis resilience
Resilience was another important theme across the conference. DfT and Arup presented on the Crisis Resilience Digital Twin, which is bringing together Agent-Based Models to test crisis scenarios with Knowledge Graphs to embed that knowledge and support crisis response capability.
Complementing this, TIS presented the RURAL framework – a recovery framework designed for post-disaster scenarios. Developed in response to increasingly frequent severe climate hazards in Portugal, RURAL addresses a common gap: isolated and rural communities are frequently the last to see critical transport infrastructure restored.
Transport futures in decision-making
It was encouraging to see a dedicated session on transport futures, featuring a joint presentation by DfT and Mott MacDonald on how DfT is embedding futures thinking directly into strategic planning and transport decision-making.
Targeted EV Investment and inclusion from Suffolk
Suffolk County Council’s Amy Rushton delivered an excellent session to close Day 2, focusing on targeted use of government funding allocations for EV charging.
The talk demonstrated how to make optimal use of funding, in a large and sparsely populated county like Suffolk, to improve mobility and the conditions for social inclusion in largely rural geographies.

https://www.transporteast.gov.uk/feed/.title: National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) published: what this means for vision-led planning in the East
https://www.transporteast.gov.uk/feed/.text:
The Government’s publication of the NPPF marks a major shift in planning. The new framework uses vision-led planning at the core of its decision making. This means transport and land-use planning should be integrated even further, so new homes and employment space are well-connected to existing communities, essential services and jobs. By linking transport to wider economic growth and prioritising good design, the NPPF supports the East to plan sustainable communities.
A key part within the new framework is the introduction of Spatial Development Strategies (SDSs). In our area, two SDSs are set to be established – one for Greater Essex and a combined SDS for Norfolk and Suffolk. As long-term strategic plans, SDSs will coordinate housing, transport, infrastructure, and economic growth across local authority boundaries.
Transport East is fully committed to collaborating with local authorities as they develop their SDSs and implement the NPPF. Our evidence can help our partners plan for the future of the East with a clear understanding of how our growing communities connect to each other, to our neighbours and the rest of the UK.

https://www.transporteast.gov.uk/feed/.title: Transport for healthier communities – Esme Yuill
https://www.transporteast.gov.uk/feed/.text:
It might be because my social feed is full of videos of 80 year olds lifting heavy and ads for collagen – but staying healthy for as long as possible is starting to become a more of a motivator for me.
Keeping people healthier for longer is also becoming a bigger policy focus for government. Healthier people can stay in work longer, can volunteer for longer, can stay involved with their communities and generally just be happier. People staying healthier for longer will also reduce costs and demands on the NHS, the benefit system and social care.
This challenge cannot be solved by health professionals alone. It is a cross-government issue that needs attention at all levels – including those of us working in transport.
How to create places that support people to live healthier lives for longer was the topic of the Coastal Navigators Network Healthy Aging Summit, held in Southend last month. The contents were a real eye-opener for anyone involved in planning for the future – and transport came up as a regular issue in the workshop discussions.
The challenge of ageing healthily in the East
The East has an older and ageing population. According to the ONS, by 2040 the number of over 65s in the East of England will increase by over 145,000 to 770,000 and the number of people living to over 90 will almost double to over 47,000.
Our coastal areas are older still – for example 25% of Canvey Island residents are over 65 and over half of all adults on the island have multiple health conditions. Our coastal towns are also, literally, at the end of the line – for road and rail connections, making it harder to access services and opportunities.
Fig 1 – National ageing trends for coastal towns. Source: Coastal Navigators Network
There is also a significant link between deprivation, age, health and coastal communities. People in our coastal towns are more likely to be poorer and less healthy than those in inland places.
Fig 2: Map showing health & disability deprivation for the East. Source: Health & Disability | Local Deprivation Explorer
Our work on Transport Related Social Exclusion explores the connections between transport and deprivation, which is a strong factor in healthy living. Of the top ten districts with the worst levels of transport related social exclusion – 6 of them are largely coastal districts.
The transport/ health connection
So how can the decisions we take on transport help people living in the East stay healthier as they age?
Transport and health interact in a myriad of ways.
Safer pedestrian and cycle routes encourage people to get and stay active through day-to-day journeys – helping meet the Chief Medical Officers physical activity guidelines
Transport to work, training and volunteering keeps people earning, learning and engaged with their communities
Regular bus services with more space for wheelchairs and mobility aids, visual displays and audio announcements help people access the services they need and reduce isolation
Health and social care workers need to be able to access work locations -complicated by shift patterns and multiple sites.
Well maintained pavements with dropped kerbs at junctions and without parked vehicles make it easier for people to get around their neighbourhoods – without trips and falls
Lower levels of air pollutants like CO 2 and particulate matter reduces lung diseases, heart diseases and strokes
Community transport provides an essential link for those with disabilities and age-related health conditions to get to treatment and social activities
Regularly accessing green and blue spaces, like parks, rivers and the sea front can improve mental health
Healthy Streets with benches to stop, safe crossings and shade from trees make it easier to walk further
Fig 3: Data on the health benefits of physical activity. Source: DfT Gear Change 2020
This work needs to be preventative too. We can’t just be making it easier for older people to stay more active – we need to be making it easier for everyon

The pod locations have also been selected to align with local hotels and the Shotley Marina, giving visitors to the area ready access to the facilities and encouraging them to stay longer.

“The e-bike network has the potential to encourage more sustainable travel, support local tourism and improve connectivity for residents and visitors across the area.”

https://freeporteast.com/feed/.title: Build on £6.4 billion investment: new report urges government to unlock Freeport growth and jobs
https://freeporteast.com/feed/.text:
£6.4 billion invested, 6,000 jobs supported: UK Freeports have already attracted substantial private investment, according to the report.
Thousands more jobs forecast: Thames Freeport aims to create 21,000 jobs by 2045; Freeport East forecasts 11,350 new jobs.
Key lever to deliver Reindustrialisation: Freeports link Government ambition on industry and jobs with delivering growth in every postcode, especially coastal communities
15 recommendations for government action: strengthen investment incentives, align infrastructure funding and tackle grid and transport barriers to turn investor interest into projects.
Thames Freeport and Freeport East today publish Free to Grow: Unlocking the potential of England’s Freeports , calling on the UK Government to work with Freeports to deliver even greater impact through strengthening tax certainty, delivery powers and infrastructure funding.
Written by Jack Shaw of Groundwork Research, the report sets out 15 recommendations to turn investor interest into projects, jobs and lasting benefits for communities across England. Alongside Government, Freeports can deliver stronger multi-region investment propositions to international investors, go further on tackling skills deficits and use their unique public-private investment role to support Mayors and other local authorities deliver stronger regional growth.
UK Freeports are working.  They have attracted £6.4 billion in private investment and supported 6,000 jobs, according to the report, as well as delivering a range of wider benefits on new skills and innovation infrastructure, strengthening trade links and investing in local SMEs.
The opportunity is substantial: Thames Freeport aims to attract more than £4.5 billion and create 21,000 jobs by 2045; Freeport East forecasts 11,350 new jobs and a £5.5 billion contribution to its local economy. By primarily using investment incentives to encourage investment, Freeports are low cost – no investment means no cost to Government, while success delivers economic growth and new opportunities for local communities.  But factors outside the control of Freeport bodies, such as planning delays, limited electricity grid capacity, transport constraints and skills gaps risk holding back investment.
The report encourages ministers to solidify tax incentives and give Freeports greater flexibility to finance infrastructure and develop sites. Government, regulators and network operators must work together to tackle electricity and transport bottlenecks. Four priorities are:
Give investors certainty: extend existing tax incentives to 2040 to avoid cliff-edges and give investors the long-term certainty they need when commencing complex projects.
Allow flexibility on designating freeport sites together with funding for infrastructure: create mechanisms to support borrowing against future business-rate income retained locally, with safeguards, and agree changes to tax-incentive sites.
Use Freeports as a platform for wider Government action on productivity: align investment in grid connections, transport and access to innovation funding and allow Freeports to drive regulatory trials.
Deliver local benefits and attract investment: improve reporting on local jobs and job quality and promote joint investment opportunities through the UK’s overseas trade network.
In their joint foreword, Rt Hon Ruth Kelly, Chair of Thames Freeport, and Mark Lemmon, Chair of Freeport East, write:
“Freeports have an important role to play and the case for Freeports has become more compelling as the UK confronts a changing economic landscape.
Freeports should be given greater certainty over their future, greater autonomy to overcome barriers to investment and a more clearly defined role in the Government’s plans to ‘rewire the state’. With these changes, Freeports can build on what has already been achieved and realise their full potential. ”
