I associate myself with your remarks, Mr Speaker, regarding the outgoing Clerk of the House, Tom Goldsmith. We have spent many an hour sitting in various meetings together, and I very much appreciate his wise words.
E-bikes and e-scooters are an incredibly important part of active travel. My constituency has a trial of e-scooters that has been going on for several years. That is fabulous, but unfortunately it has led to a rise in illegal e-scooters. When I met Essex police recently, it told me that illegal e-scooters are difficult to intercept, but when it does confiscate them, they are difficult to store because of concerns about battery fires. The problem is that so many people, when they buy e-bikes or e-scooters, do not realise that it is illegal to ride them, and we really need to do something about that. It is the people who buy them who end up paying the price if they do not understand that they cannot use them, and Essex police has to pick up the pieces.

https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.title: Major Trauma Centres: Helipads - [Sir Alec Shelbrooke in the Chair] | Backbench Business | Westminster Hall debates
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.text:
My hon. Friend makes an important point. Air ambulances have specialist expertise on board, so they do not just provide transportation; they provide lifesaving interventions along the way.
The advantage of the speed of an air ambulance can be completely lost if it cannot land on top of a hospital. Broomfield hospital, run by the Mid and South Essex foundation trust, is the main hospital that serves my Chelmsford constituency—it is not in my constituency, but it is just outside it—and it has a helipad. I pay huge tribute to Essex and Herts Air Ambulance; the crews and the communities that fund it are doing absolutely phenomenal work. However, when I met representatives from the air ambulance, they told me that every day when they do their briefing to the crews, they hold their breath a little bit and roll their eyes, because they know the answer to the question, “Will Broomfield’s helipad be open for long today?” is usually no.
Frustratingly, I have tried to persuade Mid and South Essex foundation trust to work with Essex and Herts Air Ambulance, Air Ambulances UK and the HELP Appeal to implement a solution—which does exist; it is just about getting the will for it—but I have met with so much reluctance from the hospital trust to do that or even to have meetings and listen to the problem. I get pushback and pushback, and it is incredibly frustrating. That is one of the reasons why we need to have national leadership on this issue. Although we can individually try to influence it, sometimes we just get pushback.
I know that hospitals and hospital leaders are under lots of constraints, but the solution seems so obvious when we already have a helipad at Broomfield hospital. Yes, it needs upgrading, but there is a solution for that, and yes, it needs to be staffed, but there is a solution for that. Getting pushback from the hospital itself is incredibly frustrating. I should say that Broomfield hospital is a major trauma centre, and its helipad is listed in the APPG report as one that needs to be open 24/7—but it is not. The hospital also has a specialist burns unit, so it is part of the national asset list. Of course, with burns, like so many other things, the speed of treatment is incredibly important.
When Essex and Herts Air Ambulance helicopters cannot land on top of the hospital, they have to go elsewhere. Their alternative landing site is Chelmer Valley high school, which is a few minutes down the road. There is a lot of traffic around the hospital a lot of the time, which adds to journey times, but landing there also means that an ordinary ambulance has to come to meet the helicopter. That takes up the time not just of an air ambulance, but of an ordinary road-based ambulance.
There were 12 or maybe even 14 road-based ambulances queuing up at the A&E department at Broomfield hospital just a few days ago. Members will know that we are not awash with loads of ambulances. If an ambulance’s time is being taken up unnecessarily—or necessarily, as it turns out, but it should not be the case—by having to meet an air ambulance, then it is not available to do other work. That ambulance transfer is also estimated to cost anywhere between £200 and £600 per journey. That is crazy. We are throwing away money when, if we just got the helipad at Broomfield open 24/7, it would be so much better.
Burns patients sometimes do not even end up coming to Chelmsford; they end up going to Thames Valley instead, which I find ridiculous. We also need to think about national security and the assets that are around London. Broomfield is not very far from our capital city. If there were a major incident in London, Broomfield hospital, just outside Chelmsford, would surely be one of the centres asked to respond, so having its helipad open would make so much sense.
Other hospitals in the east of England—I am an east of England MP—are also in the report, such as Addenbrooke’s, which has a red rating because it has serious problems with 24/7 access. It is

https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.title: Underperforming NHS Trusts: Government Oversight - [Graham Stuart in the Chair] | Chetwynd Bridge | Westminster Hall debates
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.text:
I thank all Members who have taken part in this important debate and the Minister for her response. Hon. Members from across the House have pointed out that rural constituencies are not the same as urban constituencies, and that they have very different needs. They have pointed out that we need investment in the infrastructure at our hospitals. Some hospitals are failing because their buildings have been neglected for decades. That needs to be fixed. None of us is here just to criticise. We are all listening to our constituents, to patients and to staff. It is our duty to call problems out and demand better, and that is what we have done today.
I do not like hyperbole, and often when people talk about life and death, it is hyperbole. That is not the case here. It is literally life and death for people on waiting lists. People have tragically died because they have been on a waiting list too long or because they have been mistreated or misdiagnosed, as we have heard from Members.
I make a final plea not to concentrate only on the finances. Finances will help with rural issues and infrastructure issues, but they will not help with cultural issues. The CQC did a well-led inspection of the Mid and South Essex trust recently. The stark line coming out of it was that staff are afraid to speak up for fear of reprisal. Money is not the problem with that system; it is a cultural problem, and we need to do something about it.
The Minister said that we could meet again. I gently say that we have not actually met yet, so I would love to take her up on the opportunity to meet for the very first time. I thank her for her response, and everybody who took part in the debate.
Question put and agreed to.
Resolved,
That this House has considered Government oversight of underperforming NHS trusts.

https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.title: Child Sexual Offender Data - [Dame Siobhain McDonagh in the Chair] | Westminster Hall debates
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.text:
While this debate is very welcome, it is on the broad range of sexual offences against children and the gathering of data about the perpetrators. I suggest, and certainly my constituents in Clacton suggest, that there is something uniquely evil and awful about mass-rape gangs. That is not in any way to diminish sexual abuse committed in the home or elsewhere by trusted people, but there is something uniquely evil about what is going on.
I certainly speak for many of my constituents in saying that there is a feeling that for a couple of decades the authorities at all levels have not done the job of genuinely pursuing justice because of racial sensitivities. I was unaware of the problem, its scale and the cover-up until the Rotherham by-election in 2012, when the current hon. Member for Rotherham (Sarah Champion) was elected. In the intervening years she has spoken out more bravely on the issue than most Members of this House. I was genuinely shocked by the stories I was told by families who came forward, and stunned that the police, social workers and local councillors had received multiple reports of what had happened. When I say mass rape, in some cases we are talking about individual girls being raped by hundreds of men over a period of time. Something genuinely shocking had happened.
In the intervening years, we have had the Jay report, the Casey report, attempts by Home Secretaries and current attempts to find out the truth about what has gone on. While a handful of people have been held to account, the truth is that the vast majority have not. I was surprised that during 14 years of Conservative Government, we did not have a proper judicial inquiry with the necessary powers. I have done my best to encourage the current Prime Minister to do the same, but sadly to no avail.
There are two things that it strikes me would be helpful. First, we ought to get published, with redacted names, all the reports of police and social services over the past 40 years, across the whole country, as a public record that everybody can read. But the thing that really surprises me is the reluctance of Members of Parliament to realise their own powers. We are in the Palace of Westminster, in this remarkable historic building, and we are all privileged to be here. We have enormous powers. They were last effectively used back in 2011 by the Public Accounts Committee, which in the wake of the global financial collapse of 2008 used the powers of this Palace to turn Committees into courts. That means that they have powers of subpoena; it means that people can be brought into Committee Rooms like this, under oath, and could face charges of perjury if they do not tell the truth.
My suggestion is this: rather than waiting for this Home Secretary or the next one, who may come soon—who knows?—to act with full judicial power and the ability to subpoena, why don’t we, as Members of Parliament, forget party affiliation, recognise the upset, concern and fear of our constituents that we are increasingly living in a two-tier justice system in this country, come together and force the Government to have a powerful Committee in this place? Let us call the heads of social services, let us call senior police officers and let us call former or serving councillors, or even former or serving MPs, and get to the truth.

https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.title: Power to Cancel Local Elections - [David Mundell in the Chair] | Westminster Hall debates
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.text:
No taxation without representation is quite a powerful political adage, and it has worked well over the years. What people were facing in many parts of the country was paying their council tax, but not being able to have a say and, in certain cases, elected county councillors staying in position for a full seven years.
However, it was not just the Minister that did this. It was done with the connivance of the Conservative party, which did everything it could to deny the vote in Norfolk, Suffolk, East and West Sussex, and initially in Surrey—doing its best to stop people voting for two consecutive years. And the Lib Dems got in on the act in Cheltenham, although, granted, in slightly different circumstances.
Talking of the Lib Dems, I have been having a very good chat with a prominent Liberal Democrat who I get on rather well with, Sir Bob Russell, who represented Colchester for many years. He made the point that there was last fundamental local government reorganisation in England 50 years ago, but no one suggested that elections should be cancelled, delayed or postponed. In fact, the debate about the shape of local government reorganisation became part of the campaigns and an issue upon which people voted.
I am proud of the fact that 153,000 people signed the petition, but I am even prouder that 4.6 million people will get the vote on 7 May because of the judicial review that I took against the Government. I am proud of that, and Reform will go on fighting for proper, open democracy.
It is clear that section 87 of the Local Government Act 2000 delegates way too much power to a Minister of any Government, and that elections are completely fundamental to liberty and freedom in our country. We need to change section 87—I ask the Government to support this—to make sure that, in the future, any delays to elections, for whatever reason, must be the subject of primary legislation, open debate and a vote by all Members of Parliament. If we do that, we will never finish up in this awful mess and with this lack of trust in politics again.

https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.title: Higher Education Funding - [Valerie Vaz in the Chair] | Westminster Hall debates
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.text:
I thank my hon. Friend the Member for Sheffield Central (Abtisam Mohamed) for securing this debate. I declare an interest as a member of the University and College Union and the all-party parliamentary university group.
Everybody in this debate wants to see young people and lifelong learners succeed in their chosen path in life. Most would agree that the Government have done a great deal to invest in education and skills since 2024, and I want to pay tribute to that. We have seen that uplift in schools, special educational needs and disabilities provision, youth hubs, colleges and apprenticeships.
This debate, however, is focused on the situation in higher education. My discussions with those who work in and represent that sector give me cause for concern, as I know is the case for other hon. Members present. Other south Essex MPs and I have spoken in this Chamber and elsewhere about the very significant challenges that my former colleagues at the University of Essex have faced over the past year. The university closed its Southend campus and made large numbers of staff redundant there and at its main Colchester campus.
The University of Essex is not alone, as we have heard, in facing these painful challenges: many universities are closing departments and issuing redundancies. At least two other universities are considering campus withdrawals or closures. The University of Buckingham has withdrawn from its Crewe campus, to be replaced as the main operator by Apollo Education. The University of Brighton is closing its Eastbourne campus and is considering closing its Falmer campus.
Other institutions are merging: the University of Kent with the University of Greenwich; City, University of London with St George’s; and King’s College London with Cranfield University. These new arrangements are the start of a new era in higher education. They raise the very thorny issue of how universities that were brought into being by the Privy Council via royal charters merge with those that were brought into being as companies limited by a guarantee. I suspect that this is a policy rug nobody really wants to lift. Other universities are being bought out or privatised. Lincoln Bishop University, for example, is now operated by Global University Systems, a global body with millions of students around the world.
This new era of campus closures, redundancies, mergers and buy-outs comes at a time when many in the sector face huge financial challenges. The Education Committee has already been referenced. It recently reported:
“The higher education sector in England is facing a financial crisis that now poses a real risk of institutional insolvency.”
This situation requires our close attention. We need our universities to thrive in our rich research and teaching ecosystem—they are part of an ecosystem. Our industrial strategy depends on that, as does our ability to create sovereign innovations in every sector.
Universities are very ready to adapt, and have adapted over the years, but they need us in this place to have more open conversations about how they can best do that. I ask the Minister to continue to champion our universities, but to support them by enabling more open conversations like this one about the scale of the challenges that they face.

https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.text:
It is a pleasure to contribute to this debate in memory of Sir David Amess. Sir David, as we have heard, was a tireless advocate for his Southend constituency, so I felt it was fitting to focus on an issue —the role of the University of Essex—that connects Southend with my own constituency of Colchester.
Like fellow Essex MPs, I have been very concerned about the impact of the decision to close the university’s Southend campus. Southend city centre has benefited enormously from having a university presence. I remember growing up there, so I understand the difference that presence would have made at that time. The loss of that presence is already being felt keenly by residents, staff and students. The university has said that it has taken the decision with great reluctance in response to the significant financial pressures facing the wider higher education sector. It has confirmed that its teaching will be consolidated in Colchester, although it also confirmed job losses at that campus.
As a former colleague to many staff there, my thoughts, and I am sure those across the House, are with those suffering right now as they face a very uncertain summer. They have been robustly supported by their trade unions, the University and College Union and Unison, over the past year. They are right to continue to raise concerns about jobs, workloads and the long-term sustainability of our universities. They have my support and that of the MPs who represent Southend—I am nodding to my hon. Friends in the Chamber behind me.
At a time when higher education across the country faces major challenges, I am very pleased to see that Universities UK is continuing its “Future Universities” initiative, urgently exploring how the sector can better support jobs, innovation, communities and students. The message is clear: our universities are central to the economic and social prosperity of our country. I hope that they are very high on the priority list of our new Prime Minister. In Colchester, we see that value every day.
The University of Essex supports thousands of jobs, encourages investment and enriches our cultural life. It is a source of enormous local pride. We can see that very clearly right now through the many joyous graduation ceremonies that will be happening over the next fortnight. I wish all our new graduates well, and I wish everybody in the House—colleagues, staff, friends and my own team —all the best for a very restful summer.

https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/25.source: Neil Hudson MP (Epping Forest) in Parliament
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/25.text:
The theme of this year’s autumn Budget was said to be one of hope. It raised our hopes akin to the title of a “Star Wars” film, yet for many of my constituents in Epping Forest, and indeed for families and businesses across the country, that hope has been sorely dashed. I have huge respect for the Chancellor, who is a deeply honourable man. He resigned as Defence Secretary, calling for 3% of GDP on defence spending by 2030, but sadly, even his hopes for this clear commitment and plan have been dashed by this Government.
In Epping Forest we are fortunate to have fantastic local businesses, restaurants, cafés and pubs, yet many are struggling to stay afloat under this Labour Government. It is deeply regrettable that this Budget did not take up the sensible proposals from the Conservatives on scrapping the family farm tax and family business tax in full, abolishing inheritance tax on family homes and scrapping business rates for 250,000 businesses nationwide.
One thing my constituents in Epping Forest will have noted was the Chancellor’s talk of a British data centre covenant. Many of my constituents are rightly concerned about the implications and environmental impacts of AI data centres, including the proposal in Loughton, with major concerns about their huge water and energy usage. Also, a speculative and completely inappropriate proposal is being worked up for a data centre near Chigwell that will threaten our precious green belt. Many of my constituents have reached out to me, alarmed by the Chigwell proposal and by the fact that it comes in the context of a Labour Government who have outrageously taken away large planning decisions from Epping Forest district council and who are arbitrarily and spuriously moving to reclassify green belt as grey belt in order to achieve their development targets.
We have seen this, too, with inappropriate large-scale housing developments being proposed on green belt in Theydon Bois and around Epping, and with solar developments on farmland between Thornwood and Epping Upland. I urge the Labour Government to do the right thing, listen to my Epping Forest constituents, leave our green belt alone and pull the plug on these damaging top-down policies and inappropriate developments.

I thank my hon. Friend for that powerful intervention. I was not going to talk about my own experiences growing up, because they are quite difficult for me to talk about, but I grew up in a military family, and crying was seen very much as something that men did not do—“Men don’t cry.” My hon. Friend is right; if men do not feel comfortable opening up about their mental health and sometimes having a good cry, that can have a long-term negative effect on their mental health. Whenever I have suffered a personal tragedy such as the loss of a family member—when both my grandads died—I went into a corner and had a good cry for 15 minutes. It did me a hell of a lot of good, so my hon. Friend is right to say that.
I pay tribute to some of the safe spaces in Harlow, and I thank Rory at Harlow Playhouse. When I worked for a homeless charity in Harlow, Streets2Homes, Rory was very helpful in providing safe spaces for some of my clients who suffered from mental health issues in the way that my hon. Friend the Member for Hyndburn (Sarah Smith) has talked about, and sometimes even more severely. I also pay tribute to Harlow men’s shed, which provides a safe space for men to talk and have a cup of tea. It is currently making me something out of wood—it does that sort of thing. It is really important to have those safe spaces.
I do not know any dad jokes to finish on, I am afraid. [Hon. Members: “Oh!”] Well, maybe later. My son is very little, and although I am confident that I will get at least two terms as the MP for Harlow—obviously—it is not very likely that I will still be an MP when he is an adult. I am taking this opportunity—although he will look back on his dad in Hansard in 20 or 30 years’ time and go, “Oh my God, he is so embarrassing!”, because that is what kids do—to send him a message. I want him to be happy, I want him to be healthy, but above all, I want him to be kind. That is really important.
You have tempted me into this, Madam Deputy Speaker. What is the favourite wine of the Whips Office and the shadow Whips Office?

https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.text:
It was perfect timing for my hon. Friend’s phone to go off—not a problem on the Opposition Benches—as I was about to say that if any Members lose their mobile phone, my son will find it for them, which is terrifying. It is really important to me that he also sees the value of reading.
On International Men’s Day, I also reflect on my experience of being a teacher. Earlier, I briefly mentioned in my usual haphazard way my experience of being a young teacher, and finding myself very early on in my career having to be a male role model for young men in my class. I reflect on what happens to young men whose father figures are absent from their lives, and what impact that has on them. There can be some really positive substitutes for that father figure—I have spoken about the wonderful volunteers at Harlow Sea Cadets, Harlow Air Cadets and Harlow Scouts, and I pay tribute to Matt Brace, who is the district leader of Harlow Scouts. I always forget to shake his left hand whenever I see him, so I apologise to him now. However, there are also some really bad substitutes. My hon. Friend the Member for Lowestoft (Jess Asato) , who I can see hiding in the wings, is very aware of the huge danger that the internet—especially social media—will provide negative substitutes for that missing father figure. This debate is, therefore, as timely as it has ever been.
I will take the opportunity to mention Harlow a few more times. I pay tribute again to Leo Shephed, who I mentioned in a previous intervention; he is a young man who has been a victim of domestic violence and does a one-man show on that topic. I always say to Leo that the reason his one-man show is so powerful is that, unlike me, he is really cool. I know that that sounds like a silly thing to say, but it is important that someone like Leo, who is cool—he is into his music and his drama—can tell that story, so that young men who may have been victims of domestic violence do not think there is something wrong with them because of it. It is important to make it clear that if you are a victim of any crime, you are not the problem.
I also pay tribute to some other men in Harlow. I cannot fail to mention Vic Goddard—anyone who remembers “Educating Essex” will know that he was, and still is, the headteacher of Passmores school. I did not watch it myself, because I was a teacher at the time, and the idea of watching a programme about teaching horrified me. Vic is someone who cares passionately about every young person in his school. There is a brilliant story I tell about him. One boy who was not normally the best behaved student, had done something really well in class, and Vic was so excited to hear that this boy had written a fantastic essay in whatever subject it was, that he ran out of his office down to the classroom to congratulate that young boy in person, and then realised he had not put his shoes on. That gives Members some idea of the commitment and passion that Vic Goddard has for supporting his students in his school, whoever they are.
I pay tribute, too, to Rod Wainwright, who I mention regularly. My hon. Friend the Member for Kensington and Bayswater (Joe Powell) will know who I am taking about, as Rod was one of the first responders at the terrible Grenfell Tower disaster. Subsequently, he has had some huge issues with his mental health and has been medically retired. I will not go into the details—I have shared them in this place before—but Rod has really been on a journey. He has been forced to confront his own mental health challenges, and I think he has found that really hard. He has been very open with me about how he does not want his children to see that side of him, but as one of my hon. Friends said earlier, it is okay to cry. It is okay to show your children that you can be upset and you can cry as well; it is not a weakness. Thank you, Madam Deputy Speaker. I particularly thank you for encouraging me to participate in this debate—you have done your bit to support men today. I thank my hon. Friend the Member for Bracknell (Peter Swallow) for bringing this debate forward and for his powerful opening speech. A huge number of powerful speeches have been made by hon. Friends throughout this debate, so it is a real pleasure to go last, because I get the opportunity to talk about some of them.
My hon. Friend the Member for Sittingbourne and Sheppey (Kevin McKenna) challenged us as men to think about what being a man means to us. The way he described it was really personal—it is a personal question that we have to ask ourselves. I probably did not know that until a few years ago. When young men are asked to consider what it means to be a man—effectively, what it means to be them, whether that is questioning their sexuality or trying to deal with the fact that their sexuality might not be what they thought it was—it is okay to have questions. We do not need to have all the answers at a young age. I certainly did not; until I had a row at the age of 27 with my friend who was a Tory, I did not know that I had any particular ambition to become a Member of Parliament, let alone a Member of Parliament who mentions Harlow on a regular basis. It is okay for young men to not know where they are and to discover that, and it is important that they should not be scared of that.
My hon. Friend the Member for High Peak (Jon Pearce) spoke about the challenges of being a father. I found his words particularly relevant; as you will be aware, Madam Deputy Speaker, I am a fairly new father, and always feel guilty about being an absent one. Representing the constituency of Harlow is the third greatest honour of my life—as I am talking about being a father, I should be careful how I word this—after marrying my wife and having my son. Being in this place and representing the town and the community that I love so much—and mention quite regularly—is a huge honour, but I am aware that it comes with some sacrifices. It was interesting to hear from the Chair of the Education Select Committee, my hon. Friend the Member for Dulwich and West Norwood (Helen Hayes) , about the importance of reading for pleasure, because since my son was born, I have read more books than ever before, because I am determined that he should see the value of books and not of my mobile phone. I have to say to hon. Members—[Interruption.]

https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.text:
It is a pleasure to serve under your chairship, Ms Lewell. I start by thanking my hon. Friend the Member for Bexleyheath and Crayford (Daniel Francis) for securing this incredibly passionate and well-informed debate. I know this issue is personal for him, and he talks about it with such passion both in Westminster Hall and in the main Chamber. I thank him for that, and for mentioning Harlow so many times in his speech. I also thank my two work experience students, Gaby and Tamsin, who are in the Public Gallery, for providing me with a very useful briefing. Members from across the House will agree that I am better briefed than I normally am—no comments.
I thank David from NAPA, who is also in the Gallery. I first came across NAPA when David kindly invited me to visit his clinic in Harlow. I was blown away and very emotional about the work done there, and I was incredibly keen to invite some of my parliamentary colleagues to visit NAPA. I am pleased that the Minister for Equalities and my hon. Friend the Member for South Derbyshire (Samantha Niblett) , who has a constituent who attends NAPA, had the opportunity to visit and see at first hand the work that David and his staff do.
What struck me more than the work I saw with the young people at the clinic was a graph—a very simple graph showing a bump and then a larger bump—of quality-adjusted life years for young people with cerebral palsy, and David explained how it was improving. We recognise that people with cerebral palsy and other disabilities will always have challenges in their lives, but NAPA is working to increase that quality of life. Ultimately, is that not what we want for everyone—to have the best possible quality of life?
I believe that the way we improve quality of life for young disabled people is through work on early intervention and specialist support. David’s colleagues use really innovative techniques to improve young people’s balance. Although I recognise the fantastic work that the Government have done to bring down waiting lists, as of September this year there are still 18,000 young people waiting for occupational therapy, 20,000 waiting for physiotherapy and 50,000 waiting for speech and language therapy. I welcome the work the Government have done so far, but there is clearly more to be done.
I want to talk briefly about some of the challenges and barriers. I again pay tribute to NAPA, which has worked with 344 children across the UK. I had the opportunity to speak to one family who came from Harrogate, and they talked about the significant logistical challenges. The parents have another son, so they had to take it in turns to travel from Harrogate to Harlow to visit NAPA. Obviously, during that time, they had to spend money to stay in a hotel, which is obviously an additional cost. My hon. Friend the Member for Bexleyheath and Crayford mentioned his 110-mile round trip, and that is the reality in terms of affordability, the postcode lottery and the geographical challenges. The barriers are clearly great.
David spoke to me about his son Angus, who was born in 2017. David saw at first hand how hard it was to get physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech and language therapy for a disabled child, as we have mentioned. David was taught how to use a feeding tube, so that Angus could be fed at home through his nose. Between 2018 and 2023, he and his family had to travel to NAPA in Boston 15 times for therapy. Obviously, that comes at a huge cost. We thank David for bringing NAPA to the UK, and particularly for bringing it to Harlow.
There are challenges, but there is still plenty to be positive about in the Government’s approach. We know they have a 10-year health policy to shift care from hospitals into the community. We also know the work this Government are doing to reform SEND by investing over £40 million over three years to develop educational psychology and speech and language therapy, which is another development that we should welcome.

https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/10.title: Submarine Service 125th Anniversary | Westminster Hall debates
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/10.source: Mark Francois MP (Rayleigh and Wickford) in Parliament
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/10.text:
It is a pleasure to serve under your chairmanship, Sir Roger. I congratulate my hon. Friend the Member for Dumfries and Galloway (John Cooper) on securing this important debate on the 125th anniversary of the Royal Navy’s submarine service, and for introducing it so ably.
I declare two interests: first, my late father, Stoker First Class Reginald Francois, served in the Royal Navy during the second world war, although he was a minesweeper man, not a submariner; and secondly, I am, by virtue of my father’s service, a long-standing honorary member of the Rayleigh branch of the Royal Naval Association. Members of the Rayleigh RNA were out in force on Remembrance Sunday, led by their chairman Mike Sandbrook, who is a former submariner. I am wearing my RNA tie this evening.
Despite Admiral Wilson’s strictures, which we heard about from the hon. Member for North Devon (Ian Roome) , the Royal Navy’s first operational submarine, the Holland 1, entered service in 1901. It was built in Barrow-in Furness, which is where BAE Systems builds our nuclear submarines today. The submarine service began the first world war with some 60 submarines. Those gave good service to the King, as evidenced by the fact that five of the 14 Victoria Crosses awarded to the Royal Navy during the great war went to submariners. The Royal Navy began world war two with a similar number of submarines, although by 1945, that number had more than trebled. RN submarines operated in the Atlantic and Pacific, but perhaps most famously in the Mediterranean—my hon. Friend the Member for Dumfries and Galloway has already mentioned the exploits of HMS Upholder.
During the cold war, the Royal Navy transitioned to primarily nuclear propulsion, and our first nuclear attack submarine, HMS Dreadnought, was commissioned in 1960. RN submarines played an important role in the Falklands war of 1982. That includes the HMS Conqueror famously torpedoing the Argentinian cruiser, the General Belgrano, and returning to port flying a Jolly Roger. Later classes of attack submarine—the Swiftsures and Trafalgars—continued the noble tradition of protecting the seas, as is now performed by the latest Astute class.
In 1968, the Royal Navy assumed the role of providing our nuclear deterrent from the Royal Air Force, and the Resolution class of ballistic missile submarines entered service. From then onwards, at least one Royal Navy nuclear deterrent submarine has always remained at sea, in the ocean depths, providing the ultimate guarantee of our national security. That mission, known as the continuous at-sea deterrent, or Op Relentless, has been successfully performed for more than 57 years. That is an amazing tribute to the professionalism and endurance of Royal Navy submariners.
The Royal Navy also has an extremely proud tradition of utilising its nuclear attack submarines to monitor potential adversaries, particularly the Russian navy as it seeks to operate in the High North and the north Atlantic. Nevertheless, as we have already heard, there are also concerns about the availability of our attack submarine fleet.
It is an oft-forgotten fact that Vladimir Putin’s father was a submariner and Putin has continued to invest heavily in his submarine fleet and increase the monitoring by Russian submarines of undersea cables around the British Isles that are absolutely fundamental to our commercial life.
In the light of that, it is deeply worrying that, for a period of several months earlier this year, not a single one of our attack submarines was at sea, as is well known to the Chinese and the Russians. Perhaps when the Minister responds to this debate, he can explain why that was the case and, even more importantly, what is being done to fix that situation. It is simply unacceptable that the Astutes, which cost £1.5 billion each, are tied up alongside for long periods when the Russians are roving at will in the north Atlantic. The wall of silence about the chronic unavailability of the Astute class

https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.text:
I welcome this Bill, because I know from experience how important it is. Before becoming the Member of Parliament for Southend East and Rochford, I was fortunate enough to be involved in the London 2012 Olympic games, the Euro 2020 football championships and the 2022 FIFA world cup. I have seen at first hand what it takes to make a major sporting event a success and the benefits it can have for the wider community. These events have taught me that while venues, organisation and promotion are all important, the most crucial factor is support from Government and local authorities. Unfortunately, that support is not consistent across the country. While some areas have the relationships, expertise and capacity to help sporting events thrive, others start from scratch each and every time. That is why the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Committee has called for a national strategy for major events, and I welcome the Government’s commitment to publish one.
The Committee has also called for responsibility for major events to be moved from the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport to the Department for Business and Trade. That move would highlight the role of events in driving investment, tourism and growth. The importance of major sporting events is not just their financial contribution, but their ability to create and celebrate community. We also see that in grassroots events, such as Rochford Hundred’s Remembrance Day fixture, which recently brought the community together in an extraordinary way. That event was not a global spectacle, but it showed the true power of sport in building community. I commend the club’s president, Ray Stephenson, and its chairman, Steve Maguire, who made that match happen.
I finish by encouraging colleagues to think back to the successful sporting events of the past few decades, and specifically their ability to make the whole country feel united. In these times, we all know how important it is to stay united. This Bill strengthens our ability to deliver those moments and ensures that the benefits reach every community in the country.

https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.title: Clause 1 - Introduction | Northern Ireland Troubles Bill | Commons debates
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.source: Bayo Alaba MP (Southend East and Rochford) in Parliament
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.text:
I am pleased to be able to participate in today’s debate. I did not serve in Northern Ireland, but I did spend time as a Parachute Regiment reservist—an experience that laid the foundations of my path to becoming the Member of Parliament for Southend East and Rochford. It afforded me opportunities I would never have otherwise experienced, and I know the same is true for countless others.
Paratroopers served alongside members of our armed forces and the Northern Irish security forces throughout Operation Banner, often in the most dangerous situations. They were asked to do an immensely difficult job in the hope of delivering lasting peace. Many of those soldiers, now in their 70s and 80s, have spent decades fearing a knock at their door. The unjust reality is that most who are fearful of historical prosecutions are largely working-class men who served in their late teens or 20s.
I want to speak to the point made by the hon. Member for Foyle (Colum Eastwood) about justice for victims and civilians, which I fully understand. What I would say is those young service personnel are victims, too. They saw and experienced things that they cannot unsee. They were deployed to Northern Ireland on the instructions of the British Government and fulfilled their duties as commanded by their chain of command. That is why I feel so passionately about the Bill and the protections it must offer.
For more than a quarter of a century, the job of properly addressing the legacy of the troubles has been kicked down the road by successive Governments. This legislation is an attempt to end that unwillingness and to deliver justice to all those affected. What it is not is an attempt to unfairly target British soldiers with legal proceedings or to reopen wounds that are barely healed. The truth is that if this legislation is not passed, those who served in Operation Banner would be completely exposed to spurious prosecution and would lack the immunity that they were falsely promised.
This legislation will offer veterans new protections, including strict guidelines on what can be considered new and compelling evidence, measures to adequately recognise the context in which soldiers were operating, and the explicit rejection of equivalence between service personnel and insurgents. That is why, despite my concerns about certain details of the Bill, I have worked extensively with the veteran community, most notably the Parachute Regimental Association, throughout this process. I commend it for the good-faith nature in which it has engaged.
This Bill is not perfect, but it is a marked improvement on the flawed legislation passed in 2023. The consequences of not getting this Bill right are very real, and while the failure of the process would belong to us all, its impact will be felt hardest by those we claim to support. If we are unable to talk, listen and make good-faith compromises, we risk repeating the mistakes that this legislation seeks to correct. No one here wants to see our children and our grandchildren patrolling the streets of Belfast again. We have a duty to prevent that cycle of violence from reigniting. I want this Bill to go even further in protecting our veterans, and I will keep working with the veteran community and the Government to make that happen. We do need justice, we need closure, and families need answers, but, most of all, we need long-lasting peace.

https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.text:
I am deeply honoured to have the opportunity to speak in the Sir David Amess debate. Sir David’s life was defined by public service, including the 24 years he spent representing the constituency of Southend West. Indeed, it was in Sir David’s memory that Southend was granted city status in 2022.
That passion for our stretch of south-east Essex coastline is something I share, and something that makes sense when we consider what it has to offer. From Wallasea Island and Shoebury east beach to Southend pier and the Kursaal, there is plenty to shout about along our shores. Yet although the coast is crucial to Southend East and Rochford’s character, it also poses its own unique set of challenges. Bordered by water on three sides, we are physically isolated, an obstacle compounded by a single century-old link road and our location at the end of the railway line. I regularly hear from local residents, business owners and farmers about the impact that regular cases of standstill traffic has on their daily life and work. The cost of that, however, is felt most acutely by our young people. Teenagers in coastal areas like ours suffer worse adult health than their inland counterparts, achieve below-average GCSE results in maths and English, and go on to earn lower wages.
There is, however, good reason to be hopeful. Southend is one of the country’s fastest-growing seaside resorts, with more than 7 million visitors choosing the city for their seaside day trips each year. That is unsurprising when you consider the regeneration efforts of recent years, which I have been proud to play a part in. It is a particular pleasure to see the steps being taken to return our iconic Kursaal to public use.
Coastal communities are also beginning to feel the benefit of the turning economic tides generated by this Labour Government. The promise of local government reorganisation and devolution is also set to pave the way for greater community control of spending. In Southend and Rochford district, we know what the solutions to our problems are. We know how to unlock the huge potential for growth that exists along our coast, and in our towns and in our rural areas.We recognise the impact that a new link road would offer, and the opportunities that would be created by improved access to high-tech skills training. That is why I am proud to be reigniting the mission to secure a new link road into south-east Essex, and why I am working to attract new industries and investment into our area.
As I believe Sir David Amess understood, the success of south-east Essex is defined by our spirit of hard work and self-improvement. If our communities are given the tools to succeed, I have no doubt that we can achieve incredible things.

https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.title: Northern Ireland Troubles Bill (Carry-over) | Commons debates
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.source: Bayo Alaba MP (Southend East and Rochford) in Parliament
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.text:
This debate is deeply personal for me, because, in addition to being the Member for Southend East and Rochford, I am a proud former paratrooper.
For me and countless others with military backgrounds like my own, the legacy of the troubles is not a distant memory but something that our community continues to carry the weight of. Back in November, I brought members of the Parachute Regimental Association, together with officials from the Northern Ireland Office and the Ministry of Defence. I had one simple aim: to ensure that veterans had a voice and their concerns about the Bill were heard clearly and directly. I thank those officials for their attendance and engagement.
Let me be clear: the legislation passed by the Conservative Government must be updated. This is not myth or fallacy; indeed, even some Conservative Members have acknowledged that the current legislation is inadequate. It troubles me when colleagues from this House head over to Parliament Square, as they did this afternoon, not to engage with former colleagues or members of their local military associations, but to “virtue signal”, as my teenage daughter would put it. Our duty as parliamentarians is to lead, make difficult decisions and speak with honesty and sincerity. It is not to spew negative and dangerous rhetoric, as some across this Chamber seem intent on doing. They parade around with lapel badges larger than some solar panels and bearing the slogan, “Proud of my country, ashamed of this government.” That does not help or resolve this issue, and it is certainly not why the public voted us into this special place. It is dangerous and unproductive noise.
However, I must be equally clear that, as it stands, the Bill leaves many questions unanswered and needs additional work. We cannot afford to rush it. Although justice must be delivered, we must also take the time to ensure that the legislation delivers the protections that our veterans need and deserve. Those who served in Northern Ireland followed orders and put their lives on the line to defend our country, and they cannot be an afterthought in this process. So I say to the Government that we should take the time to get this right, to continue our engagement, to listen to those who serve and the families who lost loved ones, and to ensure that before the Bill moves to its next stage veterans can have full confidence that it will deliver what is intended without creating serious unintended consequences that cannot be later undone.
In conclusion, I say that, to every member of our armed forces community who has served and those who continue to serve, we owe a debt that cannot be repaid. And to those watching from the Gallery today, I say thank you: thank you for standing up for the memory of those we have lost and for standing together to protect those who are yet to serve.

https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.text:
I start by thanking my right hon. Friend the Chancellor for the measures that he laid out in his Budget last week, and for his focus on giving my constituents breathing space as we navigate through tough global headwinds. Like him, I pay tribute and offer my thanks to the former Chancellor, my right hon. Friend the Member for Leeds West and Pudsey (Rachel Reeves) . It is clear that through her work and clear focus on fiscal discipline, she helped to stabilise the economy, despite the significant headwinds, and to create the headroom that has enabled us to take the positive actions set out in this Budget.
I am lucky to have my office on Leigh Road in Leigh-on-Sea. Along with Leigh Broadway, it is a thriving high street, full of small independent shops and hospitality businesses, including Tiny, a sandwich shop, Juice Bay, which does fantastic smoothies and juices, and Float On Records. They are all new businesses and it is great to see so many new businesses opening despite the challenges we have faced of late. That shows me that there is confidence in our economy and belief in our country. And it is not just in Leigh: Mez, a delicious Turkish restaurant, recently opened in Westcliff—I can vouch for that as I had my dinner there on Saturday.
However, I have listened to businesses in my constituency that tell me that sometimes things can be challenging. That is why I am delighted by the Government’s announcement that more retail, hospitality and leisure businesses will be completely exempt from business rates, meaning that around 52% of those types of business in the east of England will pay absolutely no business rates whatsoever. That is help for businesses. An additional 484 businesses in my constituency will have their business rates frozen in real terms until 2029, giving business owners time to plan ahead, while many others will see their business rates reduced.
When my constituents get home from their days out shopping, they will know that they have support with paying their bills. In addition to extending the 0% rate of VAT on electricity, an enormous 39,520 households in my constituency will benefit from the £100 payment to combat rising energy costs. I know that will help many people, from young families through to pensioners.
Speaking of pensioners, I welcome the excellent news that pensioners on low incomes will not have to pay income tax on their state pension. I am glad to hear the announcement that pensioners who rely solely on their state pension income will get to keep all of it. The Budget also provides the security that comes with knowing that pensions will continue to rise in line with earnings, while the adjusted triple lock will mean we can focus on providing a high-quality national care service.
Finally, I was really glad to hear that self-employed fathers and partners will now get statutory paternity pay. I have personally championed that, alongside many colleagues, and I pay particular tribute to my hon. Friend the Member for Portsmouth North (Amanda Martin) for her work in this area and in championing this cause.
This Budget shows that the Government are listening to people in my constituency and taking action to fix the issues they have raised. The constituents I spoke to at the weekend know that the times that we are in and that we face are difficult, and they are grateful for everything this Government are doing to support them.

https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.source: David Burton-Sampson MP (Southend West and Leigh) in Parliament
https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.text:
I thank my hon. Friend the Member for Redditch (Chris Bloore) for securing the debate and my hon. Friends the Members for Lichfield (Dave Robertson) and for Corby and East Northamptonshire (Lee Barron), and many other hon. Members across the House, for their work on this matter. My constituents in Southend West and Leigh, like those of so many other hon. Members, have been rightfully disappointed in the service provided by Royal Mail. I concur with much of what I have heard.
Southend was the original pilot area for the optimised delivery model, so we have been experiencing these issues locally for well over a year. It was deeply concerning that the clear indications that the ODM was not working in Southend did not prevent it from being rolled out nationwide. It is increasingly frustrating for my constituents, who feel that they are not getting the service they are paying for. For many people, the poor service has been not just inconvenient but disastrous, and we have heard many stories tonight about how it has been replicated across the country.
NHS letters are not the only urgent post not being delivered. One constituent lost a job opportunity when a Disclosure and Barring Service certificate failed to arrive in time and another man, who was terminally ill, experienced unacceptable delays in receiving the paperwork he had requested to arrange his own funeral. I heard many such stories at a public meeting I held back in April, which gave residents the chance to put their concerns directly to Royal Mail’s regional management. Improvement was promised at the meeting, but guess what? It never came.
In July, I held a consultation, which received 122 responses in just a couple of days. I am sorry to say that the feedback was overwhelmingly negative. Of those 122, 102 said that they were “dissatisfied” or “very dissatisfied” with the postal service. Only one person considered the current standard of service acceptable.
Throughout this time, I have regularly met the CWU—the union that represents postal workers—and heard from it that postal workers in my constituency have been overworked, under immense pressure and unhappy with the standard of service they have been able to provide. They are equally unhappy at the massive variations between the old and new contracts, but I do not have time to talk about that.
I was heartened to hear—a bit of positivity—that after a visit in August, having requested my fourth visit to the depot, Southend sorting office, in partnership with CWU reps, was ready to trial a new system that would rebalance the round loads and help reinforce the local link between the postie and their area in an amendment to DM26 that is about to be rolled out. Posties are much more efficient when they know the layout of their rounds, so it is clearly not rocket science to have them on a dedicated round.
The trial took place in Leigh-on-Sea in my constituency. A month later, I was glad to visit the sorting office again and see the racks empty—but this time the CWU assured me that things had worked well and that, in that particular round, they were back in control. As of 19 October , the new system has been rolled out across our whole sorting office area. I will be keeping a watching brief, but it is showing real positive signs. I hope that those at Royal Mail will look at the success of the local pilot and roll it out across the rest of the country. If it is working, why would they not?

I beg to move,
That leave be given to bring in a Bill to make provision about the marketing, advertising and offering for sale of wet wipes; to make provision about the labelling of wet wipes; and for connected purposes.
The city of Southend has 7 miles of beautiful beaches, and Leigh-on-Sea is well known as a picturesque fishing village that still has a vibrant cockling industry. My constituency is also home to many wild swimming groups such as the Bluetits, who find that the refreshing waters of the Thames estuary provide great exercise as well as benefits to their mental and physical wellbeing—although I have to say that when I took a dip in December for charity, I did not find it too relaxing.
All of this might help the House to understand why water quality is so important to my constituents and to me. Like so many, my constituents were rightfully outraged at the sewage dumps that sadly had become routine during the years of the former Conservative Government, so the people of Southend West and Leigh did what they so often do: they came together to make a difference on something they care about. They worked together to form quarterly water summits in 2024, giving residents the opportunity to hold water companies directly to account and to collaborate with the council, Ofwat, the Environment Agency and many more to find solutions to our water problems in Southend. It was the first summit of its kind in the country, and those summits continue to this day. I thank my constituent Daniella Boon, who is in the Gallery today, for her leadership on those summits and in this area.
It was through chairing those water summits as a newly elected MP that I came to learn just how complex the issues affecting water quality and sewage discharges are. Certainly, water companies play the most important role, and I welcome the work being done by this Government to hold them to account. However, sewage discharges happen when the water system fails on so many different levels. Councils, the community, planning decisions, green spaces, and even whether or not a person chooses to pave their driveway all come together to influence outcomes.
Last year, when spending time at our local sewage treatment plant, I learned that blockages are a leading cause of sewage discharges. When the sewers block, there are only two places for sewage to go—in Southend, it will be out into the estuary, or back up into people’s homes and toilets. We will all have seen in the media that those blockages are often caused by fatbergs. The pictures can be very shocking. The Guinness world record belongs to the fatberg found in Whitechapel in London in 2017, which was 250 metres long—longer than Tower bridge.
With blockages of that size, it is no wonder that our sewerage system sometimes struggles to cope, and alongside grease and fat, those bergs are mostly made up of wet wipes. In Anglian Water’s network alone, around 500,000 wet wipes are flushed every single day. Instead of breaking down, many wet wipes remain largely intact. They snag on roots, pumps and rough surfaces within sewers, and they combine with fats, oils and grease to create these large blockages. In my constituency alone, Anglian Water dealt with 610 blockages last year, all caused by unflushable items.
This Government have brought in legislation to ban plastic in wet wipes, a measure that my constituents and I welcome. At our water summits, Anglian Water will often remind us that there is no such thing as a flushable wipe. When I visited Anglian Water’s water treatment plant on Stock Road I got to see a whole skip—yes, an entire skip—filled with long stringy fibres from wet wipes that have been fished o

https://www.theyworkforyou.com/rss/mp/26.text:
I am grateful to my hon. Friend for his intervention. It is a bit like “Beetlejuice”—you mention ferries and he appears; it summons him. He is absolutely correct that ferries should prove a vital part of public transport infrastructure.
Let me turn to the huge and important role that the Tilbury ferry played in our public transport infrastructure locally. It ran continually until 2022 when, unfortunately, due to historic bankruptcy by the then Conservative council, it was unable to pay the subsidy needed to keep the ferry running, and it came to a close. That was an absolute tragedy for my area. Not only did the ferry provide a vital commuter route for a number of people, but a number of my constituents used it to attend schools in Kent, for example—they are now having to make a journey that is about an hour and a half each way, and they are encountering problems at the Dartford crossing that could have been avoided by a quick 10-minute hop across the water.
Gravesend High Street in Gravesham used to lead directly on to the ferry terminal, and those businesses have been hit so hard by the loss of this vital transport link. In my patch, there are fond memories of the ferry, not just for myself and my family but for so many of my constituents. I put a call out for people to share their memories of the Tilbury ferry and to sign my petition, and the numbers hit the thousands within a couple of days. People are desperate to see it return.
The main issue with the return of the ferry is the cost of the subsidy for running it. There is public will to get it back, and there is will from businesses in the area—the Port of Tilbury, Forth Ports, DP World and a whole host of others really want to see it, because they know it provides that link and enables them to encourage people to come and work for them from both sides of the river. Furthermore, if we are trying to get people off our road networks, a large number of people who use the Dartford crossing are projected to use the lower Thames crossing for short hops either side of the river, and the ferry would allow them an alternative, so that they could make that journey in a much more sustainable way, which is much better than adding to the congestion that already exists. It is a much greener way of travelling.
I ask the Minister to seriously consider putting aside a very small proportion of the tolls to be paid on the lower Thames crossing—I am talking about 0.01%, which is less than a penny—to enable the Tilbury ferry to be funded in perpetuity. There is precedent: the Dartford crossing used to fund the subsidy for the Tilbury ferry, until that was given over to the two local authorities at the time, Kent county council and Thurrock council. A levy on the lower Thames crossing would allow the Tilbury ferry to be insulated from potential shocks, such as we saw with the bankruptcy of Thurrock council. It would allow the ferry to keep running well into the future, so that it can serve my children and my grandchildren. It would take people off the already overloaded road network. It would bring life back to Gravesend High Street. It would make sure that people on my side of the river can visit their relatives, go to their hospital appointments, go to work, go to school and just enjoy a really nice day out, and it would prove to people in my patch that we can have nice things and we do deserve them.
This ferry is a crucial part of our infrastructure, and given that people in my patch will be bearing the brunt of the construction and operation of the lower Thames crossing, I believe that they deserve this. I ask the Minister to seriously consider allowing this piece of infrastructure to fund a critical part of the local transport infrastructure and to help me bring back the Tilbury ferry for good.

This has been an interesting debate. I genuinely believe that the House should view with caution any provision that grants tax-raising powers that, to be blunt, will harm businesses in all our constituencies across the United Kingdom. In my constituency and throughout Essex, we are alarmed by these plans.
The tourism, leisure and hospitality sector is worth an estimated £3.75 billion to the Essex economy. It supports approximately 77,000 jobs; about 57,000 are directly in leisure, hospitality and tourism, and a further 20,000 are throughout other industries. We are worried about what this levy will mean for those jobs, and this sector is already under pressure. It is estimated that more than 52 million visits are made to Essex’s attractions every single year, around 2.4 million of which are overnight stays. Those will clearly be impacted and affected by this tax.
We have heard Government Members almost trivialise the impact of this tax on households and families. They have said that it will cost just a couple more quid for working families, but every additional tax and burden that Labour imposes puts jobs and investment at risk and puts pressure on household budgets. These are families who love travelling around the country, and we should back them and support their taking staycations. We have had many representations already from Government Members talking about their constituencies —beautiful parts of the country where we want to encourage tourism and hospitality, as we do in Essex—but families and jobs in this important sector will be under strain from this Bill.
As you will know, Madam Deputy Speaker, Essex has many incredible attractions, and I never tire of speaking of Essex in this House. We have Colchester zoo, which is in my constituency, Langford Museum of Power, Layer Marney Tower, Cressing Temple Barns, Markshall Estate and Abberton reservoir, just to name a few. We are the home of Rossi’s ice cream, which is a great landmark in Essex. In the Maldon district, we have the promenade and the Combined Military Services Museum. We are on the Blackwater estuary, and of course we have a very famous county cricket club, Essex, which is based in Chelmsford. We host wedding venues, hotels and resorts such as Five Lakes, Prested Hall and Braxted Park. We are strategically placed for inward tourism, because we have Stansted airport and Southend airport.
Essex is competing, if I can politely say it, not just with the rest of the United Kingdom, but globally and internationally. We attract tourists who have the option of travelling across the world, but they choose to come to Essex. We want more people to come and enjoy our fabulous county, and to stay overnight in our wonderful hotels. While those businesses face significant pressures and challenges—we have heard about many of those challenges already—they are still fighting to invest. They want to invest; they want to create more jobs; and they want to promote Essex. They want to promote their sector and give young people the opportunity of a job, which we should all back and support in this House.
Given rising prices and uncertainty, the wider economic climate is tough enough, but we have a Labour Government who are anti-business and obsessed with treating business—and this particular sector—like a piggy-bank to be robbed. We have experienced the burdens of the Employment Rights Act 2025 and the changes in business rates, which, even with new multipliers and reliefs, have caused venues to face higher costs. The cleansing power of fungus is being trialled in a pioneering project which could help tackle Britain’s river water quality crisis.
Researchers from the School of Life Sciences are testing whether mycelium, the root-like network of Fungi can support wetlands in filtering polluted water before it flows into rivers and other systems.
The study could offer an environmentally friendly way to tackle water pollution, helping protect aquatic wildlife and people enjoying Britain's waterways.
PhD researcher Lucinda Robinson , has helped create a 'living lab' at the University's Colchester Campus to put the natural filtration system to the test.
The sacks packed with mycelium used in the experiment
Lucinda Robinson testing water quality in the 'living lab'
Six experimental wetlands, known as mesocosms, were constructed to investigate whether adding mycelium to constructed wetlands can remove harmful bacteria, including E. coli, and excess nutrients that contribute to damaging algal blooms.
Over 12 weeks, the wetlands were subjected to controlled contamination, with researchers regularly monitoring water quality across a series of experiments.
Lucinda said: "Everyone deserves to be able to swim in natural water ways and enjoy nature without the risk of getting ill.
"This natural filtration method could help to improve water quality in our waterways.
"This is an exciting project that could have real benefits on the environment and really highlights how versatile and useful mycelium could be.
"Wetlands can help with this, and we want to know whether by adding mycelium we can support them to further enhance safety for recreational users, restore currently damaged aquatic habitats, all while creating new wetland habitats where wildlife can thrive."
Looking to the future - Lucinda hopes her work will have real impact
As part of her research Lucinda has also tested river water quality
Previous laboratory studies suggest mycelium can remove pollutants and neutralise bacteria without the need for synthetic treatments.
The Essex project aims to establish whether these promising findings can be replicated in real-world conditions, potentially paving the way for wider use of the natural treatment.
Lucinda is now analysing the results to assess how effectively the mycelium-treated wetlands remove pollutants compared with conventional constructed wetlands.
If successful, the approach could eventually be scaled up to help tackle water pollution across the country.
Professor Tom Cameron , who is supervising the project, said: “It’s a very exciting area of research, where increasingly we find that the natural world already has the capacity to provide functions and services that let us live healthier lives, if only we give it room to do so.
“It may mean living differently and accepting more of nature on our doorstep so that it can provide for us.”

A computer scientist who is using AI to detect skin cancer has been named in a top 50 power list of innovative researchers in the UK.
Universities UK (UUK) has highlighted Dr Haider Raza’s work in its 50 Future Innovators list, which celebrates the groundbreaking innovations and scientific breakthroughs that are reshaping industries such as healthcare and engineering.
UUK, which represents more than 140 universities, has launched the list as part of a campaign to push for further investment into higher education research.
Dr Raza, a Senior Lecturer in the University of Essex’s School of Computer Science and Electronic Engineering, has worked with Check 4 Cancer through a Knowledge Transfer Partnership (KTP) to create SKINTEL, a diagnostic tool that determines if suspicious lesions are malignant.
The tool, which is 99 per cent accurate, uses 22 patient characteristics and image analysis to deliver a diagnosis.
SKINTEL, designed to support clinicians and doctors rather than replace them, will speed up skin cancer diagnoses, reduce waiting times, and save lives by detecting the most dangerous skin lesions at the earliest opportunity.
Dr Raza said: “I'm honoured to be recognised as one of Universities UK's Future 50 Innovators.
“This recognition reflects the collaborative work undertaken with colleagues at the University of Essex, Check4Cancer and other partners to develop SKINTEL.
“What excites me most is the opportunity to demonstrate how trustworthy and explainable AI can deliver real-world impact in healthcare, helping clinicians and patients alike.”
UUK hopes its power list will inspire the next generation of innovators and secure more funding. It wants to see external investment in university innovation double to £100bn by 2035.
Professor Noam Lubell, Essex’s Pro-Vice-Chancellor for Research, said: “Dr Raza has deservedly been recognised for his dedication to using AI in healthcare and is a wonderful example of the power of research at Essex.
“His work with Check 4 Cancer has the potential to transform skin cancer diagnostics around the world and ensure interventions are made at the earliest opportunity.
“Investment in Essex’s research has allowed our academics to work with businesses and organisations to come up with innovative ideas like Dr Raza’s. It is this kind of investment that is driving change in industries and allowing universities to make a real impact in people’s everyday lives.”
Alongside his work on SKINTEL, Dr Raza is the co-founder of Seniswise AI, which helps organisations assess their AI readiness and build custom, ethical AI and agentic systems for measurable business impact.
He has also advised UK policymakers on the use of AI in healthcare, as well as trained National Emergency Department professionals in emerging technologies.
Dr Raza is able to share his expertise and knowledge with students at Essex, where he teaches Data Science and decision-making. He also mentors postgraduate researchers.
Dr Raza added: “Beyond healthcare, this recognition also highlights my broader mission through Sensiwise AI to support organisations in adopting AI responsibly and effectively. Whether working with clinicians, businesses or policymakers, my goal is to ensure that AI remains transparent, accessible and focused on delivering meaningful societal benefit.”
Malcolm Press, President of Universities UK, said “UK universities sit at the cutting edge of the breakthroughs that define our age, from life-saving treatments and clean energy to artificial intelligence. The innovations coming out of our world-leading universities anchor Britain’s leadership in the industries that will power the global economy.
“These 50 future innovators, supported by universities the length and breadth of the UK, are just the tip of the iceberg. By celebrating these individuals and their innovations we hope to inspire the next generation of founders right across the country.”

A unique project exploring the life and legacy of one of Britain's most influential twentieth-century designers is being launched thanks to a partnership between the University of Essex and the Warner Textile Archive in Braintree.
The University’s School of Philosophical, Historical and Interdisciplinary Studies is seeking applicants for a fully funded doctoral studentship which will support a researcher to uncover the remarkable life and work of pioneering textile designer Marianne Straub, who worked for Warner & Sons in Essex for two decades from 1950 onwards.
Straub’s innovative designs helped shape everyday life in post-war Britain, appearing in London Underground trains, buses, airports, public buildings and homes nationwide, reflecting her belief that high-quality design should be accessible to everyone.
The successful applicant will become the first to study the Archive’s collection of design records, textile samples and business archives alongside her personal diaries and correspondence, helping to shed new light on the role of women, migration, industry and innovation in post-war Britain.
Dr Alix Green, who is lead supervisor alongside Dr Matthew Grant, said: “We’re delighted to be able to offer a studentship focused on a designer whose iconic fabrics furnished post-war Britain but whose life and work have been largely lost from view. It’s a project built on years of collaboration between historians at the University of Essex and the Warner Textile Archive – and one that will set Straub’s legacy within the county’s long weaving and design heritage.”
The new project, titled Fabric of Everyday Life: Marianne Straub, Textile Innovation and Design, 1950-1970, is supported by a prestigious Collaborative Doctoral Award and will give a doctoral researcher unprecedented access to a nationally significant collection of materials held by the Warner Textile Archive, alongside newly acquired personal papers that are yet to be fully catalogued.
As part of the project, the doctoral researcher will work closely with the Warner Textile Archive , the UK's largest publicly accessible archive of a single textile manufacturer. Located in Braintree, the archive preserves more than 150 years of textile manufacturing history and holds over 100,000 records, designs and artefacts linked to Warner & Sons and the wider British textile industry.
Straub's impact as a designer, innovator and educator will be explored through the project which will also examine wider themes of industrial decline and renewal, sustainability, globalisation, women's work, mass consumption and the changing nature of British identity after the Second World War.
Dr Sam Woodward, Digital Threads Project Manager at the Warner Textile Archive, said: “We are delighted to be working with the University of Essex to offer this postgraduate Collaborative Doctoral Award. As the first doctoral research project to explore the Marianne Straub Collection in such depth, it presents an exciting opportunity to generate new insights into the life and work of one of the twentieth century’s most significant, yet often overlooked, industrial designers.”
The research project forms part of Digital Threads, an ambitious programme at the Warner Textile Archive that is creating a comprehensive digital archive collection. The programme aims to transform access to the Archive’s collections, establish a nationally significant resource for design, education and research, and widen participation to help ensure their long-term sustainability.
Alongside their research, the doctoral candidate will gain hands-on professional experience in archival cataloguing, digitisation, conservation, public engagement and exhibition development. They will also contribute to educational and outreach activities designed to bring Straub's story to new audiences.
The deadline for applications is 10 February 2027.
